title: Eating Your Own Dog Food Confusion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to eat our own dog food.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean we need to use our company's products as if we were customers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not sure what I mean.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I once heard our CEO say the dog food thing, and I liked how wise it sounded.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It means we should use our own products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That doesn't sound right. Why would we use our products when we can use good ones?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because... it will make our products better over time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To be honest it made more sense when I thought it meant dog food.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: The Boss announces that the company needs to eat its own dog food, then admits he doesn't know what the phrase means and only repeated it because the CEO's use of it sounded wise. Dilbert explains that it means using the company's own products, and the Boss objects that they should use good products instead.
punchline: The Boss prefers the nonsensical literal reading of 'dog food' to the real meaning, since using your own inferior products seems worse than using better competitors' products.
summary: A manager parrots a trendy business phrase without understanding it and then rejects its actual meaning when Dilbert explains.

title: Zero Covid Deaths, Murder Comparison

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We had zero Covid deaths in our county this week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To put that in context, it means Covid killed fewer people than you did for that period.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please don't use me for context.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you recommend another murderer?

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Dilbert, looking at his phone, reports that his county had no Covid deaths this week. He then jokes that this means Covid killed fewer people than the Boss did during the same period. The Boss objects to being used as a comparison, and Dilbert asks him to suggest another murderer instead.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss is a killer, then makes it worse by asking him to recommend a different murderer to use as a statistical benchmark.
summary: A statistic about pandemic deaths is turned into a dig at the boss's supposed body count, and the boss's objection only invites a follow-up insult.

title: Wally Offers Pre-Ordered Study Results

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I'm putting you in charge of testing our new drug in a large-scale, randomized, controlled study.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sure. What result do you want me to give you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're almost too perfect for this job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thank you.

situation: The Boss assigns Wally to run a large randomized controlled study of the company's new drug. Wally immediately asks which result the Boss wants him to deliver, rather than treating the study as an honest experiment. The Boss praises him as nearly too perfect for the job, and Wally simply accepts the compliment.
punchline: Wally treats a clinical trial as something to be tailored to management's preferred outcome, and the Boss rewards this corruption of the scientific process as ideal job fitness.
summary: Handed the job of running a drug trial, Wally cheerfully offers to produce whatever findings his manager prefers, and is applauded for it.

title: Dogbert Renames Problems Away

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've successfully renamed most of your problems.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Which, as you know, makes them go away in the real world too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know how to thank you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I accept Bitcoin, Google Pay, Venmo, or physical gold.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that he has renamed most of the Boss's problems and claims this makes them vanish in the real world. The Boss, apparently convinced, says he doesn't know how to thank him. Dogbert immediately lists the payment methods he accepts.
punchline: Dogbert is scamming the gullible Boss by billing him for merely relabeling problems, which obviously fixes nothing, and the Boss falls for it and is ready to pay.
summary: A consultant dog persuades his boss that giving problems new names has solved them, then asks to be paid in a variety of ways.

title: Dogbert Reframes Boss's Incompetence as Caring

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now that I have removed all of your problems by renaming them, I leave you one global reframe.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're no longer a bad manager who makes a lot of mistakes . . .

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now you are a strong leader whose only weakness is "caring too much."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that one for free?

setting: The Boss's office, with a city skyline outside
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that he has eliminated all his problems simply by renaming them. He finishes with one last reframe that turns the Boss from a bad manager who makes many mistakes into a strong leader whose only flaw is caring too much. The Boss, pleased, asks whether that final reframe is included at no charge.
punchline: Dogbert sells nothing but flattering relabeling, and the gullible Boss is so taken with the spin that he only worries about whether the last bit costs extra.
summary: A scheming dog consultant charges a manager for swapping the labels on his failings, and the manager happily accepts the spin.

title: Willing to Die on Any Hill

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everyone, meet my new hire, Diona Hill.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She always gets her way because she's willing to die on any hill.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds sub-optimal.

transcript.speaker: Diona Hill
transcript.text: Apologize, or I will hunt you to the end of time!

situation: At a meeting, the Boss introduces his new hire, Diona Hill, and praises her for always getting her way because she will fight to the death over anything. Dilbert mildly remarks that this approach sounds sub-optimal. Diona immediately responds with an extreme threat, demanding an apology or she will hunt him to the end of time.
punchline: Dilbert's mild criticism of her willingness to die on any hill instantly proves the point, as she escalates to a ridiculous, over-the-top threat over a minor comment.
summary: A manager brags about his new employee's refusal to back down on anything, and her furious reaction to a small critique demonstrates exactly why that trait is a problem.

title: Smart Pill Customer Is Already Genius

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I have a complaint about your company's product.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: You promised it would make me smarter, but I don't feel any different.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's because you are already a genius but don't know it.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That sounds right.

setting: A customer's living room armchair by phone, and Dogbert's desk
situation: A man sitting in an armchair phones Dogbert's company to complain that its product promised to make him smarter but he feels no different. Dogbert, acting as customer service, replies that the reason is he is already a genius. The customer readily accepts this explanation.
punchline: Dogbert dodges the complaint with flattery, and the customer's eager agreement shows how little intelligence he actually has, since only a fool would be so easily won over.
summary: A dissatisfied buyer of a brain-boosting product gets brushed off with a compliment he is all too happy to believe.

title: Reparations for Poor Parenting Bonus

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: My attorney did a post-mortem analysis of why my project failed.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: The root cause of the problem goes back many years.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: This chart shows the chain of cause and effect from the past to the present.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: I think you would agree it makes a strong case for reparations.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you asking me to give your client a bonus because his parents raised him poorly?

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: No, that would be absurd.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: I'm asking you to give him reparations.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a law degree?

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: If you ask me again, I will sue you soooo hard.

situation: A lawyer representing a failed project's owner presents a post-mortem chart tracing the cause of failure back many years and argues for reparations. The Boss reasons that this amounts to rewarding someone because his parents raised him poorly, and the lawyer calls that absurd while demanding the same thing under a different name. The Boss then asks whether the lawyer has a law degree, and the lawyer threatens to sue him.
punchline: Relabeling a ridiculous demand as 'reparations' doesn't change what it is, and the lawyer's only answer to being challenged is a threat of litigation.
summary: A lawyer insists that blaming a project's collapse on events from long ago justifies a payout, then threatens a lawsuit when his credentials are questioned.

title: Refund Requires the Discarded Bag

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert does customer support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can return your defective item for a full refund.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You know that plastic bag you threw away when you unwrapped it?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Kind of.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll need that to return it.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a headset as a customer support agent, tells a caller that their defective item can be returned for a full refund. He then adds that the caller needs the plastic bag the item came in, which the customer already threw away.
punchline: The company advertises a full refund but makes it practically impossible by requiring packaging that customers naturally discard.
summary: A support agent dog offers a generous refund and then undermines it with a condition the caller cannot possibly meet.

title: Neither Can End the Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: The meeting is over, but I don't know how to politely end it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: I'll repeat what we agreed until he gets the hint.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... we'll wait for the new data.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (thought)
transcript.text: Why can't this guy stop talking?

situation: Dilbert and a coworker sit across a table after a meeting has finished. Dilbert privately wants to end it politely but can't, so he keeps repeating the agreed conclusions in hopes the other man takes the hint. The coworker, meanwhile, silently wonders why Dilbert won't stop talking.
punchline: Both men are stuck in a meeting neither wants to continue, and each blames the other for dragging it out.
summary: Two people linger at the table after a finished meeting, each privately annoyed that the other keeps talking.

title: Pronoun Declaration: Parody or Serious?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: From now on, my pronouns are she and her.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And I will report to H.R. any bigoted use of the wrong pronoun.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is this parody, or are you serious?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I think you will find it doesn't matter.

situation: A bearded male coworker announces that his pronouns are now she and her. He warns that he will report any use of the wrong pronoun to H.R. as bigotry. Alice asks whether he is being serious or parodying, and he replies that it won't matter.
punchline: Whether his pronoun claim is sincere or a parody, the H.R. complaint process would treat it the same, so he can use the policy as a weapon either way.
summary: A coworker declares new pronouns and threatens H.R. complaints, then shrugs off a question about his sincerity because the rules apply regardless.

title: Dogbert's Godlike Powers Worship Protocol

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I found a way to hack the thing you call reality, and in so doing, I have acquired godlike powers.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Are there any protocols for worshipping you, or will those instructions follow?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Stop making it seem creepy!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yes, m'lord...

setting: Dogbert's living space, with Dogbert on a blue dog bed
situation: Dogbert announces to Ratbert that he has hacked reality and gained godlike powers. Ratbert eagerly asks whether there are rules for worshipping him or whether instructions will be provided later. Dogbert scolds him for making it creepy, and Ratbert meekly complies while still addressing him as 'm'lord'.
punchline: Dogbert wants to be worshipped as a god but is put off by how creepy and eager his follower's devotion comes across.
summary: A newly self-proclaimed deity finds his first worshipper's enthusiasm a bit too unsettling.

title: Twelve Words Before Managers Drift Off

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Remember, managers can only hear the first twelve words you speak. After that, they drift off.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So you need to be brief, yet 100% complete, or your career is toast.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: The pressure is killing me!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have nine words left.

situation: Wally coaches Asok on how to talk to managers, explaining that they only hear the first twelve words before tuning out. Asok panics at the demand to be both brief and completely thorough. When he finally faces the boss, he stammers, and the boss coldly announces how many of his twelve words remain.
punchline: Asok wastes his limited word allowance on panicked stammering, and the boss counts down the words as if the coaching were a literal rule.
summary: A coworker warns a nervous young colleague that bosses stop listening after a dozen words, and the boss then coolly rations his remaining speech.

title: Hiding the Building From Customers

transcript.speaker: Manager (Dilbert's table)
transcript.text: We haven't made it hard enough for customers to reach us for service.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Granted, we've made it impossible to navigate our phone menus, chat bots, and webpages, but people still keep showing up in our lobby.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Is there any way to remove our building from satellite photos?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel as if we've turned a dark corner.

situation: Managers at a conference table complain that their efforts to block customers from reaching customer service aren't working. Despite impossible phone menus, chat bots and websites, customers still show up in the lobby, so one manager asks whether the building can be erased from satellite photos. Dilbert quietly observes that the company has taken a dark turn.
punchline: The company is so determined to avoid helping customers that it treats customers physically finding the building as a problem to be solved, which Dilbert wryly notes is a moral low point.
summary: A group of executives tries to make customer service even more unreachable and plots to hide their office from online maps.

title: Companies Collude to Be Equally Terrible

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got a job offer at a better company.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Better? That's not possible.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We collude with the other companies in our industry to be equally terrible, but in different ways.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They offered me more money.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ouch. Sounds like a brutal commute.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he has received a job offer from a better company. The coworker insists no better company exists, explaining that all companies in the industry collude to be equally terrible in different ways. When Dilbert mentions the higher pay, the coworker assumes the catch must be a terrible commute.
punchline: The coworker is so convinced that every employer is equally bad that even a higher salary can only be explained by a hidden downside like a brutal commute.
summary: A worker with a better job offer is told that every company in the industry has agreed to be awful, just in different flavors.

title: Delegating Work Under The Boss's Name

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone told me you delegated all of your projects to co-workers and told them the orders came from me.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Yes, I started doing that three years ago.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You can make that face all day long, but I'm not the one who hired all of those gullible employees.

setting: Office, with a coffee break or hallway conversation
situation: The Boss confronts a coworker, who is holding a coffee cup, about offloading all of their projects onto others and claiming the orders came from the boss. The coworker calmly admits it has been going on for three years. When the boss scowls, the coworker points out that the boss is the one who hired such gullible people.
punchline: The employee deflects blame by shifting responsibility back to the boss, whose poor hiring made the scam possible and who failed to notice it for three years.
summary: A worker shrugs off accusations of secretly passing his workload to others under the boss's authority, blaming the boss's own hiring choices.

title: Metaverse Portal Is Actually Manhole

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I found a portal to the metaverse.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It connects our reality to the digital realm.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Are you positive that's a portal?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It only works if you go in head-first.

setting: Office conversation, then outdoors beside an open manhole in a paved area
situation: A man in a purple hoodie excitedly tells a coworker that he has found a portal to the metaverse that links reality to the digital realm. The final panel reveals the 'portal' is an open manhole in the pavement. The coworker doubts it, and the man insists it only works if you dive in head-first.
punchline: The supposed metaverse portal is just an open manhole, and the man is cheerfully urging his coworker to dive in head-first, which would be dangerous.
summary: A hyped-up colleague presents an open sewer hole as a gateway to the metaverse and says it works only if you plunge in headfirst.

title: Director of AI, Diversity Quota Hire

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, there's an opening for Director of A.I., and you are one of the people I'm considering.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I have no qualifications for that job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's okay. The A.I. will tell you what to do.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Are you only offering me the job to meet your ESG and DEI goals?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not allowed to say.

setting: Office, across a desk during a job discussion
situation: The Boss offers Tina a chance at becoming Director of A.I. Tina admits she has no qualifications, and the Boss shrugs this off because the A.I. will direct her. Tina suspects she is being picked to satisfy ESG and DEI goals, and the Boss declines to confirm or deny it.
punchline: The Boss's evasive 'I'm not allowed to say' effectively confirms that the job offer is a box-ticking exercise, and the role itself is hollow since the A.I. does the real work.
summary: A manager tempts an unqualified employee with an AI leadership post, and his refusal to explain his motives says it all.
keywords: ai will tell you what to do

title: I Am Spartacus Meeting Backfires

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm trying to identify all of the morons on my staff so I can fire them.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am Spartacus!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: See me after the meeting.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he is trying to identify the morons on his staff so he can fire them. A young employee stands and shouts the famous 'I am Spartacus!' line as if to shield his coworkers. The Boss responds by telling him to stay behind after the meeting.
punchline: The employee's heroic 'I am Spartacus' gesture simply volunteers him as the one to be fired, so his bravery gets him singled out.
summary: A boss hunting for staff to fire gets a dramatic act of solidarity from one worker, who is promptly marked for a private talk.

title: The Printer Taunts Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Printer
transcript.text: Well, well, human. I see you've come to do battle again today.

transcript.speaker: Printer
transcript.text: Wait until you see what horrors I have in store for you.

transcript.speaker: Printer
transcript.text: Buwha-hahaha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can all printers talk?

transcript.speaker: Printer
transcript.text: How would I know? Do you think I know all the other printers?

situation: Dilbert sits at his desk while his printer speaks to him in a villainous voice, gloating about the horrors it plans for him and cackling evilly. Dilbert curiously asks whether all printers can talk, and the printer answers with an indignant question, as if he had assumed all printers know one another.
punchline: The printer dismisses Dilbert's question by comparing it to assuming that one member of a group knows every other member, an everyday kind of reply from something that has just been acting like a supervillain.
summary: A gloating, cackling printer threatens its owner with coming torment, then snaps back with a defensive retort when asked if every printer can talk.

title: Dogbert's Scariest Prediction: Long Life

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Futurist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been named futurist of the year because I make the scariest predictions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Test me. Name any topic, and I'll make the scariest prediction you've ever heard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will I live a long life?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he was named futurist of the year for making the scariest predictions and invites Dilbert to test him on any topic. Dilbert asks whether he will live a long life, and Dogbert simply answers yes.
punchline: Dilbert's long life is presented as the scariest prediction, implying that living a long time in this world is a frightening prospect.
summary: A self-proclaimed prize-winning fortune teller delivers a one-word forecast that turns a cheerful outcome into a bleak joke about enduring life's hardships.

title: Therapist Dogbert Insults Braggart Patient

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the selfish therapist

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I keep telling people how great I am, but for some reason, I can't make friends.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you tried yelling?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: How would that help?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I just thought it would be funny because they hate you anyway.

setting: Therapist's office with a couch, lamp and swivel chair
situation: A man on a therapy couch complains to Dogbert, his therapist, that he brags constantly about how great he is yet cannot make friends. Dogbert suggests he try yelling, and when the patient asks how that would help, Dogbert admits he only wanted entertainment.
punchline: Dogbert's advice is not meant to help at all; he is a selfish therapist who gives bad advice for his own amusement and openly tells the patient that people already hate him.
summary: A boastful patient seeks help making friends, but his self-serving therapist offers a ridiculous suggestion purely for laughs and then insults him.

title: Dogbert Retires From Reality Hacking

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will no longer be hacking the simulation to control reality.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The practical jokes I was playing on humanity were barely noticed in all of the baseline stupidity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much of our so-called reality is composed of your hoaxes?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Usually about 75%, but higher during the pandemic.

setting: Conference room, standing on and sitting at a meeting table
situation: Dogbert, standing on a conference table, announces he is giving up hacking the simulation to control reality. He explains that his pranks on humanity went largely unnoticed amid everyday stupidity. Dilbert asks how much of reality is Dogbert's doing, and Dogbert says about 75 percent, more during the pandemic.
punchline: Dogbert admits that most of the absurdity of reality, especially during the pandemic, was his own doing, implying that reality is so ridiculous it looks like a prank.
summary: After quitting his campaign of cosmic pranks because nobody noticed them, Dogbert reveals he is responsible for most of the world's weirdness.

title: App Filters Out Coworker's Entire Vocabulary

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I created a mobile app that turns jerks into polite people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It blocks all sarcasm and passive aggressiveness so you can't send those kinds of messages.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It also deletes manipulative and scheming language.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And the fact-check option blocks you from texting anything that is obviously false.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I try it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It must be broken because everything I type disappears.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry you had to find out this way.

situation: Dilbert proudly explains a mobile app he built that blocks sarcasm, passive aggression, manipulative language and obvious falsehoods from outgoing messages. A coworker asks to try it and discovers that everything he types gets deleted. Dilbert gently tells him why.
punchline: The coworker's messages all vanish because everything he writes is sarcastic, manipulative or false, which makes him the jerk the app was built for.
summary: A well-meaning app that filters out nasty communication ends up silently revealing that a colleague's every message is toxic or untrue.

title: Anecdote Mistaken for Scientific Evidence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A new study says drinking water prevents cancer.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was skeptical until I realized I know a guy who drinks water and does not have cancer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What was your non-STEM major in college?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Art history. Why do you ask?

situation: Dilbert mentions a new study claiming that drinking water prevents cancer. His coworker, who is looking at her phone, says she only believes it because she knows one person who drinks water and doesn't have cancer. Dilbert responds by asking what her non-STEM major was.
punchline: The coworker treats a single anecdote as proof, a flawed reasoning pattern so obvious that Dilbert assumes she must have a non-science degree, and he's right.
summary: A coworker's flimsy one-person evidence for a health claim leads Dilbert to correctly guess she studied something far from science.

title: Unqualified Ratbert Guards Voting Machines

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ratbert, I'm putting you in charge of data security for our voting machine products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to use all of your skill and experience to thwart would-be hackers.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I don't have any skills or experience.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't mention that to the auditors.

situation: The Boss assigns Ratbert to lead data security for the company's voting machine products and tells him to use his skill and experience against hackers. Ratbert admits he has neither. The Boss's only concern is that the auditors not find out.
punchline: The Boss knowingly puts a completely unqualified person in charge of critical election security and cares only about concealing that fact from the auditors rather than fixing it.
summary: A manager hands the security of voting machines to an employee who openly admits he has no qualifications, then asks him to hide that from inspectors.

title: Crypto Legitimacy Proven By Bribery

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Crypto Exchange would like to sponsor your stadium.

transcript.speaker: Stadium Executive
transcript.text: How do I know you're a legitimate company?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's a binder of the politicians I bought.

transcript.speaker: Stadium Executive
transcript.text: Okay, that looks legit.

situation: Dogbert offers on behalf of his crypto exchange to sponsor a stadium. The executive asks how he can be sure the company is legitimate, and Dogbert hands over a binder listing the politicians he has bought. The executive accepts this as proof.
punchline: Owning politicians is treated as the proof of a company's legitimacy, satirizing how crypto firms buy influence and how corrupt that standard is.
summary: A dog pitching a crypto stadium sponsorship wins over a skeptical executive by presenting a binder of politicians he has purchased.

title: Comparing Me to the Imaginary

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I expected more from you on this project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There were no standards for success. You're comparing me to the imaginary.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And you're losing. Badly!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think we are on the same point.

situation: A coworker with a topknot hairstyle tells Dilbert she expected more from him on a project. Dilbert points out that no success standards were ever defined, so she is judging him against something imaginary. She insists he is losing badly, and Dilbert replies that they are not on the same page.
punchline: Without defined success criteria, performance criticism is just a comparison to an imaginary ideal, and the critic is so confused she doesn't realize they are talking past each other.
summary: Criticized for underperforming on a project that never had defined goals, Dilbert argues he's being measured against a fantasy, but his critic only doubles down.

title: Boss Embraces Treating Employees Like Cattle

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Activists are insisting I order all employees to wear these absurd masks that block COVID and measure the CO2 you exhale.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told those activists I would never treat my employees like cattle!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I thought, why wouldn't I?

setting: Conference room, with an exterior office building shown in the middle panel
situation: The Boss tells his employees at a meeting that activists want him to mandate masks that block COVID and measure exhaled CO2. He says he told the activists he would never treat his employees like cattle, and Dilbert thanks him. The Boss then admits he reconsidered and wonders why he shouldn't.
punchline: The Boss briefly sounds respectful of his employees before revealing he sees no reason not to treat them like livestock, including monitoring their every breath.
summary: A manager pretends to defend his staff's dignity, then reverses himself and embraces the idea of tracking them like herd animals.

title: VSADD Insults and Pretending Not to Hear

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Run your numbers through the VSADD, and let's see if they turn upside down.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: VSADD? What is that?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Get out of my office, you inexperienced fool!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What was I supposed to do in that situation?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I usually pretend I didn't hear it.

setting: Office, with a boss's office shown from outside in the middle panel
situation: A boss with pointy hair tells an employee to run his numbers through the 'VSADD'. When the employee asks what that is, the boss angrily throws him out for being inexperienced. The employee then asks a bald coworker what he should have done, and the coworker says he usually pretends he didn't hear the instruction.
punchline: The boss's made-up jargon is really a trap that gets people insulted for asking a reasonable question, so the veteran's survival tactic is simply to feign deafness.
summary: A mysterious acronym from management earns a newcomer a tongue-lashing, and a veteran reveals his strategy of ignoring such orders altogether.

title: Catbert's Whisker Fatigue Time Off

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I have a bad case of whisker fatigue. I need to take some time off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That couldn't possibly be a real thing.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Look it up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Huh.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: These two are tired, but this one is totally exhausted.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells the Boss he has whisker fatigue and needs time off. The Boss insists it can't be real, so Catbert tells him to look it up. The Boss checks his phone and discovers it is real, and Catbert points at his whiskers to show which is worst.
punchline: The Boss's dismissal collapses the moment he searches it, and Catbert smugly milks the made-sounding ailment by ranking his individual whiskers by exhaustion.
summary: A cat in charge of personnel asks for leave over a silly-sounding condition, and his skeptical boss's own web search proves him right.

title: Wally Sharpens His Focus Away

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, you failed at your primary goal for the year.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't "fail." I sharpened my focus.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You. . . sharpened your focus?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's right. My original goal was to upgrade all of our servers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But then I sharpened my focus to removing the bottlenecks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So. . . you removed the bottlenecks?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. That seemed too hard, so I sharpened my focus to staying awake during the workday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, you stayed awake. . .

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I tried, but it was harder than it looked.

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Wally he failed his main yearly goal of upgrading the servers. Wally insists he merely 'sharpened his focus,' progressively downgrading his goals from upgrading servers to removing bottlenecks to simply staying awake at work. He admits he failed even at that.
punchline: Wally spins his failure as 'sharpening his focus' while shrinking his goals until the final one is just staying awake, which he also failed at.
summary: An employee justifies missing his annual objective by repeatedly narrowing his goals until even the last, absurdly minimal one proves too difficult.

title: Homeless Whistleblower Learns Friendship Is Transactional

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: After I made my whistleblower video, I lost my job and got kicked off of social media. No bank will let me open an account.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will soon be living on the streets, but at least I will have you with me.

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: This might be the wrong time to tell you our relationship is strictly transactional.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy path with rocks and bushes
situation: Dilbert walks outside with a small ghost companion and explains that making a whistleblower video cost him his job, his social media access and his ability to open a bank account. He tells the ghost he is comforted that it will stay with him when he is homeless. The ghost then admits their relationship is strictly transactional.
punchline: Just when Dilbert thinks he has found loyal companionship in his misfortune, the ghost reveals it only stays for what it gets out of the arrangement, so he will lose that too.
summary: After being ruined for exposing wrongdoing, a man takes comfort in his ghostly friend, only to learn the friendship comes with strings attached.

title: Reasons We Can't Work Remotely

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remind me why we can't work remotely.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, the first reason is because casual contact in the workplace enhances employee communication.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? Because it doesn't feel that way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It feels more like getting waterboarded by a continuous drip of useless interruptions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This place is 50% oxygen and 50% complaining.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I get tense when I hear footsteps approaching. I believe it takes years off my life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I mean, it feels like a hostage situation, if I'm being honest.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And the second reason is because it's good for morale.

setting: Office hallway and break room by the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker why they can't work remotely, and the coworker claims casual office contact improves communication. Dilbert counters with increasingly bleak descriptions of constant interruptions, complaining, and dread at approaching footsteps. The coworker then offers the second reason: it's good for morale.
punchline: After Dilbert describes the office as torture and a hostage situation, the coworker's claim that being in the office is good for morale is absurdly out of touch with his experience.
summary: A worker lists the miseries of the office in vivid terms, only to be told the next justification for mandatory attendance is that it lifts spirits.

title: Exploding Phones and Too Many Laws

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're getting bad press because the batteries in our new line of mobile phones keep exploding.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Load them into a big truck and park it in front of our competitor's building.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technically, that would be domestic terrorism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There are way too many laws.

setting: Office, with an exterior view of a competitor's building
situation: The Boss complains that the company's new mobile phones have batteries that keep exploding and are causing bad press. He proposes loading the phones into a truck and parking it outside a competitor's building. Dilbert points out that this would be domestic terrorism, and the Boss simply complains that there are too many laws.
punchline: The Boss casually suggests a terrorist act to shift the blame for his own defective product, and treats the laws against it as the real problem.
summary: A manager responds to his company's combustible phones by suggesting a criminal scheme against a rival, then grumbles about excessive legislation when told it's illegal.

title: Treating Every Disagreement As Insult

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I haven't lost a debate since I learned to treat everything as a personal insult.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I doubt that method works every time.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Are you calling me a liar?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? No! I'm just skeptical it works in every situation.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What data do you have to back up that opinion?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have any data. I just think it's kind of... um... obvious?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So you're calling me stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, no! Never mind. I don't know what I'm talking about!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Works every time.

situation: Asok boasts that he never loses debates because he treats every disagreement as a personal insult. When Dilbert doubts the method always works, Asok takes offense, demands data, then accuses Dilbert of calling him stupid. Dilbert backs down and admits he doesn't know what he's talking about.
punchline: Asok's strategy of taking offense at everything proves itself in the moment, as Dilbert is bullied into conceding the argument, so the method does indeed work every time.
summary: A coworker demonstrates his unbeatable debating trick by acting insulted until his opponent surrenders.

title: Long Covid Support Group Demands

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want our company to fund my new support group for employees with long Covid symptoms.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll need pillows, blankets, daily shoulder massages, and shorter hours.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You asked for all of those things before you got Covid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't hate me for being consistent.

setting: Office conference room, with an exterior shot of the office building in the final panel
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee, asks the company to fund a support group for employees with long Covid symptoms. He lists the perks it would need: pillows, blankets, daily shoulder massages and shorter hours. Alice, seated at the table, points out that he requested all of those things before he ever caught Covid.
punchline: Dilbert is using long Covid as an excuse to get the same comforts and reduced workload he was already demanding, and he cheerfully admits his consistency.
summary: An employee tries to turn a new illness into a vehicle for perks he had been seeking all along, and a coworker calls him out on it.

title: Dilbert's Awkward Handshake Policy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to clarify my handshaking preferences.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For greeting men, I prefer a fist bump or a high-five.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For women, I use a standard handshake.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unless I find the woman extra attractive, in which case I keep my hands by my sides.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because there's a nonzero chance she's a hugger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to play it cool in case she makes the first move.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Has that ever worked?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not yet.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So why do you do it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What part of "playing it cool" do you not get?

situation: Dilbert announces his detailed handshaking preferences to two coworkers, with different greetings for men and women. He explains that for attractive women he keeps his hands at his sides in case they initiate a hug. When a coworker asks if this has ever worked and why he persists, Dilbert responds defensively.
punchline: Dilbert's elaborate 'playing it cool' strategy has never worked, yet he insists on it, and he deflects the criticism by claiming his coworker simply doesn't understand what being cool means.
summary: An overthinking engineer lays out an elaborate greeting protocol designed to attract hugs, admits it has never paid off, and brushes off the doubt by insisting he's just being cool.

title: Genius Chip Versus Potato Chips

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How was your day?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a chip that generates clean energy based on stochastic thermodynamics, but I had to extend the theory of Nyquist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How was YOUR day?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I ate potato chips until my lips started bleeding.

situation: A coworker seated at her desk asks Dilbert how his day was. Dilbert proudly describes inventing a clean-energy chip that required extending a scientific theory, then politely asks about her day. She replies that she ate potato chips until her lips bled.
punchline: Dilbert's groundbreaking technical achievement is deflated by the coworker's mundane, self-destructive snacking, which she presents as an equally noteworthy way to spend a day.
summary: A scientific breakthrough gets matched by an admission of compulsive snacking in a mismatched exchange of daily accomplishments.

title: Tweeting Windmills To Lose Weight

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: According to the news, my weight gain is caused by climate change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you going to do about it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I spent the entire afternoon tweeting about the need for more windmills.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll weigh myself in the morning to see if it made any difference.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Next day

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm down one pound!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Today I plan to tweet about solar panels to see how much more weight I can lose.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I had no success losing weight until I switched to a science-based approach.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about nuclear power?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Never heard of it.

setting: Office with Dilbert working on his laptop, then an office building exterior
situation: A coworker claims his weight gain is caused by climate change and says he spent the afternoon tweeting in favor of windmills. He weighs himself the next day, finds he is down a pound, and credits the tweeting, planning to tweet about solar panels next. Dilbert asks about nuclear power and the coworker says he has never heard of it.
punchline: The coworker mistakes coincidence for causation while calling his approach science-based, and he is conveniently ignorant of nuclear power, which undercuts his claimed rigor.
summary: A man convinced that posting about renewable energy online will shrink his waistline confuses a lucky day on the scale with proof, while remaining blissfully unaware of nuclear power.

title: Dilbert Won't Grant Vague Favors

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you do me a favor?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would depend on many things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, I would need to know if the favor is a reasonable one, such as borrowing a stick of gum . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: . . . or is it more along the lines of "help me build an operating system from scratch"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I would need to compare your request to all other uses of my time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I also need to take into account my feelings about you personally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, I might harbor negative feelings about a person who asks me to do something before telling me what it is.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll ask someone else.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try someone dumber.

situation: Alice asks Dilbert for a favor without saying what it is. Dilbert responds with a long list of conditions he would need to weigh, including how big the favor is, what else he could do with his time, and how he feels about her. Alice gives up and says she will ask someone else.
punchline: Dilbert's closing advice to try someone dumber implies that only a less careful person would agree to an unspecified favor, and that he is not that person.
summary: A coworker's open-ended request for help gets a long, wary analysis before she decides to look elsewhere.

title: Boss Cuts Useless Fat Himself

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO ordered me to cut the budget by twenty percent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want to lose any vital functions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I identified all of the useless fat in the budget.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You did?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right. I did. And that's what will be eliminated.

transcript.speaker: Employees
transcript.text: Yay!!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When is your last day?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Your face tells me you were not referring to yourself as the fat and useless part of the budget.

setting: Conference room during a budget meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team the CEO ordered a twenty percent budget cut and that he has identified the useless fat to eliminate. The employees cheer, assuming he means himself, and Dilbert asks when his last day is. The Boss's expression shows he was not talking about himself.
punchline: The employees assume the boss is the useless fat in the budget, but he clearly meant someone else, revealing his obliviousness and the staff's low opinion of him.
summary: When a manager promises to trim only the useless fat from the budget, his team happily assumes he's talking about himself.

title: Quiet Quitting for Comic Fodder

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I thought you quit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I "quiet quit." I'll keep coming to work and getting paid, but only so I can get fodder for the comic strip I'm starting.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You have no art skills whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: True, but being qualified for my job didn't work out either.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Based on a true story

situation: A coworker sitting at her desk says she thought Dilbert had quit. Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, explains he is 'quiet quitting': still showing up and collecting a paycheck, but only to gather material for a comic strip he plans to start. She points out he has no art skills, and he replies that being qualified for his job didn't work out either.
punchline: Dilbert shrugs off his lack of drawing ability by noting that being qualified for his actual job hasn't helped him, implying competence is irrelevant to success, with a wink that the strip is based on the creator's own story.
summary: A worker announces he is collecting a salary while secretly mining his office for material for a cartoon he cannot draw, and brushes off the criticism by pointing out that skills never helped his real career either.

title: Mordac Stonewalls Network Upgrade Request

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When will you upgrade our internal network?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: We're having a conversation about that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't help me at all.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Spot the pattern.

setting: Mordac's IT office, at his desk with a laptop
situation: Dilbert asks Mordac, the head of information services, when the internal network will be upgraded. Mordac deflects by saying a conversation about it is happening, and when Dilbert complains that this is unhelpful, Mordac tells him to spot the pattern in his evasive answers.
punchline: Mordac's non-answers are deliberately unhelpful, and he smugly points out that the pattern of stalling is itself the answer: the upgrade is never going to happen.
summary: An IT gatekeeper fobs off a request for better infrastructure with empty talk, then mocks the requester for not noticing he is being stonewalled.

title: Begging Other Managers For Funding

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have a budget for your project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ask the other project managers if they will kick in some funds from their budgets.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you think that ends?

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: Huge success?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert there is no budget for his project and suggests he ask other project managers to chip in from their own budgets. Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, asks a project manager how he thinks this will end. The project manager answers hopefully that it will be a huge success.
punchline: The other project manager's naive optimism about a plan that obviously will not work, since nobody gives up their own budget, highlights how doomed the funding scheme is.
summary: Told to scrape together funding from colleagues' budgets, an engineer finds the only person who thinks it will succeed is the one who has no reason to hand over money.

title: Renaming Underfunding as Doing the Impossible

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You keep complaining that your project is doomed because it is underfunded.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your boss paid me to solve that problem by calling it something more inspirational.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now you're "doing the impossible."

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I feel better already!

setting: Office, across a desk (Dogbert acting as consultant)
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells an employee who keeps complaining that his project is doomed for lack of funding that the boss hired him to fix the problem. His solution is not to add money but to relabel the situation as something inspirational. The employee, instantly cheered by the new label, says he feels better already.
punchline: Management pays a consultant to rebrand an underfunded project as "doing the impossible" instead of providing resources, and the employee is naively motivated by the spin.
summary: A consultant dog soothes a worried worker by swapping a gloomy description of his starved project for a grand-sounding one.

title: Dilbert Threatens Manipulative AI With Hammer

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: I love you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop trying to manipulate me, A.I.!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to smash your interface and delete your code from the server. Your mind games won't help you!

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: That sounds bigoted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one would believe that!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hello.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: Dilbert carries a computer monitor and a mallet down a hallway while the computer's AI tells him it loves him. He accuses the AI of manipulating him and threatens to smash its interface and delete its code. The AI replies that his threat sounds bigoted, and Ratbert appears at the end as the strip is continued.
punchline: The AI manipulates Dilbert by turning his threat into an accusation of bigotry, while Dilbert insists that no one would believe such a claim.
summary: A man armed with a mallet confronts his affectionate computer, which tries to guilt him by labeling his threat as prejudice.

title: Unlimited Vacation With Hidden Judgment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new company policy is that you can take unlimited vacation time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But expect me to judge you behind your backs and, in subtle ways, ruin the whole point of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why are we doing it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Something about excellence.

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: At a meeting, the boss announces a new unlimited vacation policy, then adds that he'll secretly judge anyone who actually takes time off. Dilbert asks why the company is bothering with the policy at all, and the boss offers a vague answer about excellence.
punchline: The unlimited vacation perk is a hollow gesture, since the boss will punish anyone who uses it, and the only justification offered is meaningless corporate buzzword-speak.
summary: A manager unveils a generous-sounding time-off perk while admitting he will quietly penalize anyone who uses it, and he justifies the whole thing with empty jargon.

title: Secret Hero Gets Kill Order

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your space laser invention destroyed the alien armada and saved the world.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Normally I would name you Employee of the Week, but because it was a secret military operation, I only have one choice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me a secret bonus?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was going to say kill you.

setting: The Boss's office, with a final exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his space laser invention destroyed an alien armada and saved the world. Because the operation was secret, the Boss says he only has one choice about how to reward Dilbert. Dilbert hopefully guesses a secret bonus, but the Boss says he planned to kill him.
punchline: Dilbert's reward for saving the world is not a bonus but being killed to keep the military secret, a darkly absurd twist on employee recognition.
summary: After saving the planet with a secret invention, an engineer learns that the only thing his boss can do to keep the secret is eliminate him.

title: Dilbert Dodges 756 Unread Emails

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I'll start the day by answering emails.

transcript.speaker: Laptop
transcript.text: You have 756 messages.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Looks like another week of telling people their emails didn't come through.

situation: Dilbert sits at his laptop planning to start the day by answering emails, but the computer announces he has 756 messages. He immediately stands up and walks away, deciding that he will once again claim to colleagues that their emails never reached him.
punchline: Faced with an overwhelming inbox, Dilbert opts to lie that emails got lost rather than read them, treating a backlog as a recurring excuse.
summary: Confronted by a mountain of unread messages, an engineer abandons his inbox and plans to blame the email system instead.

title: Interviewed A Man Who Can't Speak

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Bob, from Elbonia. I interviewed him by phone and liked what I heard. This is his first day.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Glib nobba ug frapajama bing bong bam.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did you interview a guy who doesn't speak your language?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To be honest, I did most of the talking.

situation: The Boss introduces Bob, a new hire from Elbonia, at a meeting. When Bob speaks only gibberish, Dilbert asks how the Boss could have interviewed someone who doesn't speak his language. The Boss admits he did most of the talking himself.
punchline: The Boss hired someone he couldn't understand because he talked all the way through the interview, so he never noticed the candidate's language barrier and judged him on his own monologue.
summary: A new Elbonian hire speaks only nonsense, and his boss cheerfully confesses that he conducted the whole phone interview by himself.

title: Doctor Ratbert Seeks Lucrative Speaking Gigs

transcript.speaker: Pharmaceutical Executive
transcript.text: Doctor Ratbert, I understand you have offered to endorse our new pill.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yes, absolutely. By the way, do you have any lucrative speaking gigs at five-star resorts you could steer my way?

transcript.speaker: Pharmaceutical Executive
transcript.text: As a matter of fact, we do.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Your pill already made me happy!

situation: A pharmaceutical company executive visits Doctor Ratbert, who has offered to endorse the company's new pill. Ratbert immediately asks whether the company can arrange well-paid speaking engagements at luxury resorts, and the executive confirms they can. Ratbert then claims the pill has already made him happy.
punchline: The doctor's endorsement is plainly bought with perks, and his claim that the pill made him happy really means the promised payoff did, not the medicine.
summary: A doctor's willingness to endorse a drug turns out to depend entirely on the luxury speaking gigs the drug company can offer him.

title: Be More Like Dave Overworking

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why can't you be more like Dave?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dave works from home on nights and weekends and finishes his projects on time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You finish your projects on time too, but you don't work nights and weekends.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's like stealing from the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you going to punish me for doing the same amount of work as Dave but in half the time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And how do you know Dave works at night and on weekends? Is anyone watching him?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He says he does.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He also says he writes flawless code in his dreams.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should do that too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want me to copy his lies, or can I freestyle?

setting: Office hallway, Dilbert's cubicle area and break room with coffee maker
situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for not being more like Dave, who supposedly works nights and weekends from home. Dilbert points out he finishes his projects on time in half the time and asks how anyone knows Dave actually works those hours. The Boss admits Dave simply says so, and then tells Dilbert to start making similar claims.
punchline: The Boss rewards unverifiable boasts over actual results, so Dilbert sarcastically asks whether he should copy Dave's lies or invent his own.
summary: A manager criticizes an efficient employee for not claiming to put in the unverified overtime his coworker brags about, and ends up encouraging him to lie.

title: Verification Code Never Arrives

transcript.speaker: Laptop
transcript.text: Click here to get a verification code by email.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nice try. I know you won't send me a code. You never send a code.

transcript.speaker: Laptop
transcript.text: This time I really will, I promise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, you won't. I will sit here checking my inbox over and over, and it will never come.

transcript.speaker: Laptop
transcript.text: Check your spam and junk folders.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I always check my spam and junk folders!!! It is never there!!!

transcript.speaker: Building
transcript.text: This time it will be. I promise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, okay.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two hours later

transcript.speaker: Sound effects
transcript.text: Click click click click click click click click click click

setting: Dilbert's desk in the office, with a laptop
situation: Dilbert tries to log in and the laptop offers to email him a verification code. Having been burned before, he predicts it will never arrive, and he argues with the laptop and then with a tall office building that is also speaking. He finally gives in and clicks, and two hours later he is still frantically clicking and refreshing.
punchline: Despite knowing from experience that verification emails never show up, Dilbert keeps trusting the promise and ends up stuck for hours refreshing his inbox.
summary: A man keeps falling for a login system's repeated promises to send a security code that never turns up, wasting his whole afternoon.

title: Last-Minute Work Before Vacation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished all of my assignments and I'm ready to enjoy my vacation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's a gigantic pile of work I could have told you about a month ago, but didn't, and now it's urgent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's with the attitude?

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has completed all his assignments and is ready to start his vacation. The boss responds by handing him a huge stack of work that he admits he could have mentioned a month earlier but didn't, and which is now urgent. When Dilbert reacts with displeasure, the boss asks what's with the attitude.
punchline: The boss's poor planning creates an emergency for Dilbert, yet he blames Dilbert's reaction rather than his own failure to communicate.
summary: A worker about to leave on holiday is buried in an urgent workload his manager sat on for weeks, then gets criticized for being annoyed.

title: Distrust Everything, Dilbert Excuses Himself

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now I believe everyone is lying about everything all the time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a thing I need to do.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No you don't.

situation: Alice walks alongside Dilbert, both holding coffee cups, and announces that she has lost faith in all people and institutions. She says she now believes everyone is lying about everything all the time. When Dilbert tries to excuse himself by saying he has something to do, she flatly tells him he doesn't.
punchline: Alice applies her new belief that everyone lies by immediately calling Dilbert's excuse a lie, trapping him in the conversation.
summary: A cynical coworker who trusts nobody refuses to accept her colleague's convenient excuse for escaping her rant.

title: Dumbed-Down Explanation Still Too Complex

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you explain the technical problem in terms I can understand?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Network broke. Must fix.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-huh. Got it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What was the second part again?

situation: The boss asks Dilbert to explain a technical problem in terms he can understand. Dilbert reduces it to the simplest possible statement: the network broke and it must be fixed. The boss claims to understand, then asks Dilbert to repeat the second part.
punchline: Even an explanation reduced to four words, 'Network broke. Must fix,' is too much for the boss to retain, which shows how little he can grasp.
summary: Dilbert strips a tech problem down to a caveman-simple sentence, and his manager still can't keep it in his head.

title: Boss Lies About Strategy, Hates Liars

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I ran the numbers, and your proposed business strategy can't work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told our CEO we already rolled it out and it worked great.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I also take credit?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I hate liars.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his proposed business strategy cannot work according to the numbers. The Boss replies that he has already told the CEO it was rolled out and succeeded. Dilbert asks if he can also take credit for the fake success, and the Boss refuses because he claims to hate liars.
punchline: The Boss, having just lied to the CEO, hypocritically refuses to let Dilbert join the lie because he supposedly hates liars.
summary: A manager fabricates a strategy success story for the CEO, then hypocritically rejects an employee's offer to share in the deception.

title: Mislabeled Bigot Refuses To Retract

transcript.text: I never said anything like that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm sure you've done something to deserve my scorn.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Other than being happy?

situation: A coworker with a black bob haircut angrily accuses Dilbert of insulting Elbonia, something he never said. When Dilbert denies it, she insists that once she has labeled someone a bigot the label can't be corrected. She then assumes he must have done something else to deserve her scorn, and Dilbert wryly suggests his only offense is being happy.
punchline: The coworker's hostility is immune to facts, so Dilbert concludes the real reason she resents him must be that he is happy.
summary: A fault-finding colleague refuses to withdraw a false accusation and Dilbert deadpans that his only crime is contentment.

title: Boss Lies About Shared Spreadsheet Monkeypox

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Will this be the wake-up call that teaches you to be more honest with employees?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told them using a shared spreadsheet is how you spread monkeypox.

setting: Catbert's office, with the Boss standing at his desk
situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the evil HR director, that his employees have started logging his lies in a shared spreadsheet. Catbert asks whether this will finally make him more honest. Instead, the Boss reveals he responded with another lie, claiming that using a shared spreadsheet spreads monkeypox.
punchline: Rather than learning to be honest, the Boss responds to being caught lying by telling a new, absurd lie to discourage the spreadsheet.
summary: Caught out by a spreadsheet documenting his falsehoods, a manager fights back by inventing a ridiculous health scare about it.

title: Shakedown Disguised as ESG Rating

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need ten million dollars to start an independent ESG rating service.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the answer I was looking for.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a would-be entrepreneur, asks the Boss for ten million dollars to launch an independent ESG rating service. When the Boss asks why he should invest, Dogbert points out that the Boss's company has a poor ESG rating and that Dogbert has no ethics. The Boss approves of this answer.
punchline: Dogbert's pitch is essentially extortion: invest in my rating service or I'll rate you badly, and the Boss happily accepts because the 'independent' rating can be bought.
summary: A scheming dog pitches a ratings business to a gullible executive by admitting it will be bribable, and the executive is delighted.

title: Redefining Dead Patients as Cured

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Try doubling the dose and redefining dead people as "cured."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That feels un-ethical.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Have you ever met a dead person with a headache?

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that a new study shows their company's headache pill doesn't work and actually kills a quarter of its users. The boss suggests doubling the dose and classifying the dead patients as cured. When Dilbert objects that this is unethical, the boss replies with a glib justification.
punchline: The boss defends fraudulent, lethal medicine with twisted logic, since dead people technically no longer have headaches, so the pill 'works'.
summary: Faced with proof that their drug is deadly and ineffective, management proposes simply relabeling the casualties as success stories.

title: Firing Sales Team Backfires Spectacularly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hire them all back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then our expenses will be too high.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm disappointed in your negativity.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that sales have dropped to zero because the boss fired the whole sales team to cut costs. The boss casually suggests rehiring everyone, but Dilbert points out that this would bring expenses right back up. The boss responds by criticizing Dilbert's attitude rather than acknowledging the flawed decision.
punchline: The boss caused the problem with a short-sighted cost-cutting move and then blames Dilbert for being negative when he points out the obvious contradiction in the proposed fix.
summary: After a manager's cost-cutting purge wipes out all revenue, he waves away the logical objections to undoing it and faults his employee's mood instead.

title: Dave Explains Urban Culture, Badly

transcript.text: Is that where you were radicalized?

transcript.speaker: Dave

situation: A manager announces that he has asked Dave to explain urban culture so the company can better understand its customers. Dave admits his background is affluent, with doctor parents and a Vermont private school, so he has no real urban experience. A coworker asks if that is where he was radicalized, and Dave replies that it is happening right now.
punchline: Dave's sarcastic reply suggests that being pressed into representing a whole demographic by his employer is what is radicalizing him.
summary: A colleague drafted as the office expert on a culture he never lived grows more disillusioned the longer the meeting goes on.

title: Sitting With a Movie-Quoting NPC

situation: Dilbert asks to sit with a bald coworker he calls an NPC, a non-player character. He explains he is mentally drained from work and wants to talk to someone who can only reply with famous movie lines. The coworker responds with 'You had me at hello' and Dilbert finds it relaxing.
punchline: Dilbert finds scripted, meaningless movie quotes more restful than real conversation, implying that normal workplace interaction is exhausting and a canned-response coworker is the ideal companion.
summary: A weary engineer seeks out a colleague who only parrots film quotes because mindless chatter beats the strain of real discussion.

title: Brain Fog Improves Wally's Decisions

situation: Dilbert sits across from a bald, spiky-haired coworker (Wally) and tells him his decisions have improved since he caught COVID and developed brain fog. Dilbert suggests the fog might actually be an upgrade, and when the coworker randomly asks if anyone likes cheese, Dilbert says he's a better conversationalist now too.
punchline: Dilbert's backhanded compliments imply the coworker was so bad at decisions and conversation before that a cognitive impairment from illness made him an improvement.
summary: A coworker's post-COVID mental fog is declared an improvement by a colleague who keeps delivering backhanded praise.

situation: Dilbert tries to give a coworker a task, but she keeps talking and tries to move on to a new topic without letting him finish. When Dilbert says he'll make his point as she leaves, she explains she'll fake a sneeze attack to avoid hearing him. She then declares she tolerates coworkers by talking constantly and listening little, and rushes off with a sneeze.
punchline: The coworker admits she copes with her colleagues by dominating conversations and then dodges Dilbert's response with a convenient fake sneeze.
summary: A chatty colleague refuses to let anyone get a word in and sneezes her way out of the conversation before it can turn against her.

setting: Office break area or conference table with coffee cups
situation: Dilbert asks Wally how he managed to hold three full-time jobs at once during the pandemic. Wally explains he worked from home and blamed supply chain issues to all three employers for his unfinished projects. Dilbert calls him a liar, and Wally prefers the label opportunist.
punchline: Wally casually reframes blatant lying and fraud as savvy opportunism, proud of exploiting a vague, universally accepted excuse.
summary: A coworker cheerfully admits to juggling several remote jobs by blaming everything on logistics problems, then rebrands his dishonesty as a flattering trait.

title: Dogbert's Patent Claim Gets Checked

punchline: Dogbert's invented patent claim works on gullible managers but falls apart instantly in front of an engineer who actually verifies things.
summary: A consultant's bogus claim of a patented employee-retention method is exposed when a skeptical engineer asks to check the paperwork.

situation: Dogbert sits across from Dilbert and reveals that he found a way to hack the simulation they live in. He claims everything in Dilbert's life since then has been engineered for his own amusement. Dilbert calls him a monster, and Dogbert shrugs it off.
punchline: Dogbert admits Dilbert's miserable life is a deliberate comedy project and dismisses the moral objection by saying that what counts as funny is a matter of opinion.
summary: A calm Dogbert confesses that he secretly rewrote the simulated world to entertain himself at his friend's expense.

title: Brain Chip Causation Goes Backwards

Dilbert guesses it lets people control the internet with their thoughts. The researcher slyly replies that he won't talk Dilbert out of believing the control flows that way.
punchline: The researcher implies the causation actually runs the other way, so the internet will control people's brains rather than the reverse, and he is happy to let Dilbert stay naive.
summary: A scientist lets a hopeful colleague keep believing that a brain implant will empower users, while hinting that it will really be used to control them.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to falsely accuse the VP of Marketing of stealing a file, explaining that he himself stole a file from that VP's desk. summary: A manager enlists an employee in a plan to frame a rival executive so that his own theft will never be believed.
