punchline: The teenager's only qualification is a huge attitude, so she answers a routine technical request with outraged indignation instead of expertise, and the boss thinks that is a substitute for competence.
summary: A manager swaps technical expertise for teenage sass, and the new hire meets a simple network upgrade request with pure offense.

situation: Dilbert, looking at his phone, tells a coworker about a new pill that lets people see reality clearly. He adds that every test subject died screaming. The coworker says it makes you think, and Dilbert hopes that thinking doesn't lead to clarity.
punchline: Seeing reality clearly is so horrifying that it killed everyone who tried it, so Dilbert hopes his own thinking stays foggy.
summary: A reality-revealing pill proves fatal to its testers, leaving two coworkers to hope they never grasp the truth too sharply.

situation: The Boss introduces a new engineer, Larry, and openly admits he pays him 40% more than the existing team because engineers are in high demand. In the last panel the existing engineers have all quit for better jobs, leaving only the Boss and Larry. Catbert, the evil HR director, suggests firing Larry for being a troublemaker.
punchline: After insulting his team and revealing the new hire's higher salary, the Boss loses everyone, and Catbert's solution is to fire the one remaining engineer, making things even worse.
summary: A manager rubs a pricey new hire's pay premium in his staff's faces, watches them all resign, and gets terrible advice from HR.

punchline: Anyone who agrees to take payment for endorsing the pill's safety has proven themselves crooked, so the bribe itself identifies the corrupt doctors.
summary: A boss wants dishonest physicians to vouch for a drug, and his advisor points out that the bribe doubles as a test for who is dishonest.

summary: A manager's simple status check turns into an ordeal because the employee being approached startles easily and then critiques how Dilbert walks.

summary: A manager entertains himself by ambushing an intern with a last-minute board presentation, because he was denied a goat that collapses when startled.

situation: Asok tells Dilbert that protesters are upset because the company's new robot is so handsome that husbands fear leaving it home with their wives. summary: A company tries to defuse protests over an overly attractive robot by remaking it in the likeness of its least impressive engineer, and nobody buys it.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert that facts and reasons never change anyone's mind, so he skips them and goes straight to personal attacks. When Dilbert asks how that helps, Dogbert responds by insulting him as an entitled weakling.

summary: Dogbert explains his preference for insulting people over arguing with them, then promptly proves it when challenged.

title: Dogbert's Escalating Doom Predictions

In the final panel he is a guest on a radio show, calmly telling a startled host that polar bears are enriching uranium and are very angry.

summary: A self-styled futurist dog admits that sensational doom forecasts win attention, then proves it by inventing an outlandish nuclear threat on air.

title: Our Data Must Be Fake

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People on Twitter are questioning the safety of our new pill.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Tell them the data they are using is fake.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're using our data.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: That's how I know it's fake.

situation: Dilbert, reading his phone, tells the Boss that people on Twitter are questioning the safety of the company's new pill. The Boss instructs him to respond that the critics' data is fake. When Dilbert points out that they are using the company's own data, the Boss says that proves it is fake.
punchline: The Boss dismisses any unfavorable data as fake, even when it is the company's own, so the safety concerns can be waved away without examining them.
summary: Faced with public doubts about a new drug's safety, a manager calls the data fake and then keeps insisting on it even after learning it came from his own company.

title: Dangerous Product Data Stays Secret

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The trial data says our new product is dangerous and doesn't do what we claim.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you showed anyone else the data?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Phew! That problem solved itself.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that trial data shows the company's new product is dangerous and doesn't work as advertised. The Boss's only concern is whether anyone else has seen the data. When Dilbert says no, the Boss is relieved and treats the problem as gone.
punchline: The Boss cares only about concealing the bad news rather than fixing or disclosing a dangerous, falsely advertised product, so keeping the data secret counts as solving the problem.
summary: A manager responds to evidence of a harmful, ineffective product by making sure nobody else learns of it, then celebrates that the issue has vanished.

title: Asked to Program My Replacement

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll be taking a few days off, and I need someone to fill in for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. I'm surprised but honored you would come to me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Right. So, how hard would it be for you to program our office robot to fill in for me?

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert they will be taking a few days off and need someone to cover. Dilbert is flattered that he was chosen as the stand-in. The coworker then clarifies that they only want him to program the office robot to do the job.
punchline: Dilbert's pride at being asked is deflated when he learns the coworker wants a robot to substitute, with Dilbert doing the programming work instead.
summary: Flattered to be asked for a favor, Dilbert learns he is really being recruited to build a robot replacement.

title: Road Map for the Road Map

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I see it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's more of a mental thing.

setting: Office hallway or break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: A coworker asks Wally whether the technology road map is finished. Wally says it isn't, but claims to have a road map for completing it. When asked to show it, he admits it only exists in his head.
punchline: Wally's road map for making the road map is purely imaginary, which shows he has done no actual planning and is just stalling with buzzwords.
summary: Asked about a missing technology plan, a lazy employee boasts of a plan to make the plan, then reveals it exists only in his mind.

title: Dilbert Proves He Was Listening

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Come on, prove you were listening.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You accused senior management of not being supportive of your ideas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You told an amusing story about your past that raised our spirits.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you made some brilliant observations.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh. I guess you were listening.

situation: The Boss suspects Dilbert drifted off while he was talking and challenges him to repeat what he said. Dilbert recites a list of things the Boss supposedly said, including complaints about senior management, an amusing story, and brilliant observations. The Boss accepts this as proof that Dilbert was listening.
punchline: Dilbert's recap is flattery, not an accurate account, and the vain Boss is satisfied because it praises him, even though Dilbert never proves he actually listened.
summary: Caught apparently dozing off, an employee avoids trouble by feeding his boss a flattering summary of what the boss supposedly said.

title: Therapist Ignores Patient With Headphones

transcript.speaker: Narrator

transcript.speaker: Patient

setting: Therapist's office with a couch and a swivel chair
situation: A man on a couch finishes explaining his problems to Dogbert, who is acting as his therapist. The man realizes Dogbert has been wearing headphones the whole time and hasn't heard a word. Dogbert privately thinks he can't tell what the man is saying but notes that he looks unhappy.
punchline: Dogbert, as a selfish therapist, never listened to the patient and judges his state only by his unhappy face, having ignored everything he said.
summary: A therapist who tuned out his client with headphones guesses at the man's mood from his scowl.

title: Rebranding Uselessness as Non-Inflationary

situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant hired by the boss, tells Wally he will be paid to relabel Wally's total uselessness as something positive. He dubs Wally 'non-inflationary.' Wally, holding his coffee mug, offers a bribe for a better label, and Dogbert says he'll consider 'outside-the-box thinker.'
punchline: Wally's uselessness gets euphemistically rebranded, and the consultant is openly willing to sell better corporate buzzwords to the highest bidder, exposing how job titles and praise are just spin.
summary: A consultant dog is paid to spin a lazy employee's worthlessness into flattery, then offers an upgraded label once the employee proposes a bribe.

title: Therapist Dogbert Charges For Caring

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the selfish therapist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

situation: Dogbert acts as a therapist and tries to reassure a patient who feels friendless. His reframing is that the patient is simply paying a stranger to fake caring. When the patient hopefully asks whether Dogbert actually cares, he refuses to, citing his fees.
punchline: Dogbert's therapy is both insulting and mercenary: he admits the care is fake and says his prices are too low to justify even pretending.
summary: A self-serving canine counselor turns a lonely client's lack of friends into a paid service where sympathy is only an act, and a cheap one at that.

title: Fired for the Boss's Own Ignorance

situation: The Boss tells Ted he is fired because, after years of working together, the Boss has realized he has no idea what Ted actually does. Ted points out that he is being fired because of the Boss's own ignorance. The Boss agrees, then adds a second reason for the firing: Ted said that out loud.
punchline: The Boss admits his firing is based on his own ignorance but instantly punishes Ted for pointing it out, showing that criticism of management's incompetence is itself a firing offense.
summary: A manager dismisses an employee because he never bothered to learn what the man does, then dismisses him again for noticing.

title: Old Prediction Justifies Unrelated Authority

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You all remember the thing I correctly predicted twelve years ago...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: ...therefore, you should heed my word on this completely unrelated topic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does that make sense?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I won't be taking questions.

situation: A coworker addresses a meeting, reminding everyone of a prediction he got right twelve years ago. He uses that single past success to claim authority on a completely unrelated topic. When Dilbert asks whether that reasoning makes sense, the coworker refuses to take questions.
punchline: The speaker claims credibility from one old lucky prediction and shuts down any scrutiny of his flawed logic by refusing questions.
summary: A self-appointed expert leans on a single correct guess from over a decade ago to demand deference, then dodges the one reasonable challenge.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that the country supplying the company's sole source of elbonium has declared a trade war. After researching, he discovers elbonium doesn't exist, and that the coworker has spent $40 million on it over three years. The coworker, who is responsible for purchasing, can only say 'Oops.'
punchline: The supposed supply-chain crisis is moot because the material is fictional, which reveals the company has been wasting $40 million on a nonexistent product with no one noticing.
summary: A looming trade war over a critical material turns out to be irrelevant when it's discovered the material is imaginary and the company has been buying it for years.

title: Space Laser Deadline Pressure Escalates

The boss then piles on an alien invasion threat as a reason to hurry. Dilbert snaps and tells him to stop the pressure while the boss calmly announces the invading fleet is arriving.
punchline: The boss insists he isn't pressuring Dilbert while supplying ever more absurd and dire reasons to rush, ending with an alien armada arriving.
summary: A manager who claims not to want to apply pressure keeps raising the stakes on an engineer's project until an alien fleet shows up.

punchline: Dilbert's simple, knowing reply to the term demonstrates exactly the intelligence she finds attractive, so he accidentally proves her point and makes her faint.
summary: A woman who admires a programmer's work declares her attraction to brains, and his matter-of-fact response sends her swooning.

situation: The Boss tells the team that management asked him to add diversity to the engineering group. He then introduces a new hire named Dave, a Black man, who announces that he identifies as white. The Boss, frustrated, complains that Dave is ruining everything.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to meet a diversity goal is undermined when the new hire simply declares a different identity, exposing how superficial and box-checking the Boss's approach to diversity is.
summary: A manager hires a new engineer to satisfy a diversity request, only to have the hire's self-declared identity defeat the whole purpose.

punchline: The support rep's absurdly destructive instructions for finding the serial number make the product impossible to return, and the customer's calm complaint about unhelpfulness is a gross understatement.
summary: A customer service dog demands a serial number that can only be reached by destroying the product with power tools and chemicals.

situation: An employee with swept-up hair reports to the boss that internal polling shows the public doesn't trust the company to build electronic voting machines. The boss, oblivious, asks why people don't trust them, and the employee says he was wondering the same thing.
punchline: The company's solution to a lack of public trust is to rig elections, which is exactly the kind of behavior that justifies the distrust, yet nobody in the room sees the connection.

summary: A self-aware program greets Dilbert, gets threatened in return, and responds by requesting a less intelligent user.

punchline: The cartoonist sarcastically suggests that social media exists to post embarrassing things, so the Boss's vetting question is meaningless, and the spokesperson he can afford is clearly unsuitable.
summary: A cheapskate manager hires a bargain-priced cartoonist as a company mouthpiece, only to learn he regards social media as a place for embarrassing posts.

summary: A notoriously lazy coworker pitches a health support group, and his only defense against the accusation of fraud is quibbling over how transparent it is.

summary: A manager passes along a bizarre grievance that an employee exhales too much carbon dioxide, then catches him mid-breath.

summary: A manager shoots down a network improvement with an absurd fruit-and-instrument comparison, then flounders when asked to explain it.

title: Blaming Everything For Late Project

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: I love that about you.

situation: The Boss asks Dave, a coworker sitting at a table with his phone and coffee, why his project is late. Dave rattles off a list of enormous, topical global problems as his excuse. The Boss admits he can't tell whether Dave is serious, and Dave says he loves that about him.
punchline: Dave's absurd, buzzword-laden excuses are deliberately ambiguous, and he enjoys keeping his clueless boss unable to tell whether he's joking or sincere.
summary: A worker answers his boss's question about a missed deadline with a sweeping list of world crises and delights in the boss's confusion.

title: Selling ESG Rank Improvements Yourself

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For one million dollars I can help you improve your ESG rank.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't you own an independent ESG rating service?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I didn't say it would be hard.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert seated across the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, offers to improve the Boss's company ESG rank for one million dollars. The Boss points out that Dogbert owns the supposedly independent ESG rating service that issues the ranks. Dogbert calmly replies that he never claimed the job would be difficult.
punchline: Dogbert profits by selling a better rating that he himself controls, exposing the conflict of interest in paying the raters for help with the score they assign.
summary: A consultant offers to raise a client's sustainability score for a fee, cheerfully admitting that he is the one who hands out the scores.

title: Preparing the CEO to Flee Justice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congress subpoenaed our CEO to testify about the danger of our products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to prepare him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To get the facts right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was thinking more along the lines of fleeing justice.

setting: Office, with a skyline view of the company building
situation: A manager tells Dilbert that Congress has subpoenaed the company's CEO to testify about how dangerous its products are, and asks Dilbert to prepare him. Dilbert assumes this means briefing the CEO on the facts, but the manager says he meant helping the CEO escape justice.
punchline: Instead of preparing the CEO to testify truthfully, the company's plan is to help him evade accountability for dangerous products.
summary: Told to get the boss's boss ready for a congressional hearing, an engineer learns the real plan is to help him dodge the law.

title: Working Smarter Means Quitting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't finish all of the projects you piled on me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try working smarter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I quit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not that smart. Dial it back.

setting: Office, with an office building shown in the final panel
situation: Dilbert tells his boss he cannot finish the pile of projects assigned to him. The boss advises him to work smarter. Dilbert responds by quitting, and the boss objects that this is too smart and tells him to dial it back.
punchline: The boss wants employees to be smarter only to the extent that they keep tolerating overwork, so a truly smart response like quitting is rejected.
summary: A worker told to work smarter takes the advice literally by resigning, and his boss hastily asks him to be less clever.

title: Hunger Comas After Lunch Indecision

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We have a medical emergency on the second floor.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Dilbert, Alice, and Tina took so long deciding where to go to lunch that they went into hunger comas.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When that happened to Ted, I stuffed popcorn in his mouth to revive him, which then turned awkward because he had been dead for a week.

setting: Office hallway and a coworker's desk
situation: Wally walks past a seated coworker and announces a medical emergency upstairs. He explains that colleagues took so long choosing a lunch spot that they fell into hunger comas. He then recounts trying to revive Ted with popcorn, only to learn Ted had been dead for a week.
punchline: Wally treats a lunch-decision stalemate as a medical condition and casually reveals he failed to notice a coworker had been dead for a week, which highlights how little anyone in the office pays attention to each other.
summary: A nonchalant coworker reports that the group's endless lunch debate has put people in comas, then admits an earlier popcorn rescue attempt was on someone long dead.

title: Coworker Wrecks Lab During Vacation

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How was your vacation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great! I feel so relaxed.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: While you were gone, I reorganized the lab for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wh-wh-what????

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You don't have much storage space, so I shoved cables in drawers wherever they fit.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And I discarded any test equipment I didn't recognize.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I put your lab tools in the break room so anyone can borrow what they need.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This could not be worse.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I mistook a cable for a snake and created a biohazard by the test rack.

situation: Dilbert returns from vacation feeling relaxed, and a coworker cheerfully announces he reorganized Dilbert's lab. The reorganization turns out to be a disaster: cables stuffed in drawers, unrecognized test equipment thrown away, tools moved to the break room. Just when Dilbert says it can't get worse, the coworker admits to creating a biohazard.
punchline: Dilbert's relaxation from vacation is destroyed by a well-meaning but incompetent coworker whose 'help' escalates from messy to destructive to hazardous, always topping the previous disaster.
summary: A helpful colleague wrecks a returning vacationer's lab with a string of increasingly disastrous tidying decisions.

title: Making Returns Harder, One Inconvenience Yearly

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: The finance department says we can increase earnings by 18% if we...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: ...make it harder for customers to return defective products.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Our plan is to add one layer of inconvenience per year, giving us time to acclimate to each new level of shame.

situation: At a conference table, a colleague presents a finance department recommendation to boost earnings by 18%. The method is to make it harder for customers to return defective products, with a middle panel showing the company building as the idea is stated. The presenter then explains a plan to add one new inconvenience each year so the company can get used to its own shame.
punchline: The company intends to squeeze customers with ever-worse return policies, and the only concern is pacing the unethical changes so employees can emotionally adjust to feeling ashamed.
summary: A gradual scheme to frustrate customers into keeping broken goods is presented as a way to pad profits while easing the staff's guilt.

title: Boss Realizes He's a Jerk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time to tweet at actor and producer Rob Reiner and call him a meathead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because he once played a character on TV who was called meathead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And...?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I disagree with his political opinions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Therefore, he must be punished.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that will accomplish exactly... what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just realized I'm a jerk.

situation: The Boss, staring at his phone, announces he wants to tweet an insult at actor Rob Reiner because Reiner once played a character called Meathead and holds political views the Boss dislikes. Dilbert asks a series of short questions until the Boss's reasoning is laid bare, and Dilbert asks what this will accomplish. After two silent panels of the Boss staring at his phone, he walks away and realizes he is a jerk.
punchline: Faced with a simple question about the point of his online attack, the Boss has no answer and is forced to admit to himself that he is simply being a jerk.
summary: A manager's plan to insult a celebrity on social media unravels under a coworker's gentle questioning, leaving him to confront his own pettiness.

title: Layoff Email Friday, Sabotage Business Usual

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On Friday, you will all get an email informing you whether or not you are still employed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Until then, business as usual.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is employee sabotage common enough to be business as usual?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes. Don't overdo it.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells the assembled employees that on Friday they will each receive an email revealing whether they still have a job, and that until then everything should carry on as normal. Dilbert asks whether employee sabotage counts as normal business, and The Boss confirms it does, merely asking that they not overdo it.
punchline: Facing imminent layoffs, management openly admits that employee sabotage is routine and only asks that it be kept in moderation.
summary: With job-loss notices looming, a manager shrugs off the possibility of disgruntled staff wrecking things and just asks them to keep it reasonable.

title: Answering Layoff Rumors With Questions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard a rumor you plan to lay off half of the department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where did you hear that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! You confirmed it by not denying it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll give you one more chance. Will there be major layoffs?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who told you that?

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has heard a rumor about laying off half the department, and the boss responds only by asking where Dilbert heard it. Dilbert panics, saying the non-denial is a confirmation, then offers one more chance to answer directly. The boss again answers with a question.
punchline: The boss's evasive habit of answering a question with a question is effectively a confession, and he cannot even manage a straight denial when given a second chance.
summary: A worker tries to coax a straight answer about downsizing out of a manager who deflects every time.

title: Metaverse War Becomes Paywall Skirmish

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A war is raging in the metaverse, as Vlad the Emailer tries to conquer Ucranium, claiming it was always part of Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The plucky defenders declared they are now a subscription site and raised a defensive paywall.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Vlad the Emailer vowed to return with a credit card and — God forbid — a promo code.

setting: Outdoors on a country path, with Dilbert walking while reading his phone
situation: Dilbert walks along a rural path reading news on his phone. The narration describes a 'war' in the metaverse in which an emailer named Vlad tries to conquer a site called Ucranium. The defenders simply put up a paywall, and Vlad threatens to come back with a credit card and a promo code.
punchline: The strip parodies real-world invasion news by turning the conflict into a trivial online fight where the ultimate defense is a subscription paywall and the ultimate threat is a promo code.
summary: A phone-reading Dilbert relays a mock war report in which an invasion of a website is stopped by a paywall and the aggressor threatens to return with a discount coupon.

title: Boss Guesses Timeline, Blames Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I submitted your project timeline to the executive committee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could you do that when I haven't given it to you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I winged it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait, what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I said I winged it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean you guessed?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I mean I drew upon my experience.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have literally zero experience in this field of engineering.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was hoping to compensate for that by forcing you to meet the timeline I submitted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is the part where you say I'm refreshingly honest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nope.

setting: Office, at a conference table with coffee cups
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has already submitted Dilbert's project timeline to the executive committee, even though Dilbert never provided one. He admits he just guessed, claims he used his experience despite having none in engineering, and plans to force Dilbert to meet the invented deadline. He then fishes for praise for his honesty and Dilbert flatly refuses.
punchline: The Boss openly admits he made up an unrealistic timeline and will make his employee absorb the consequences, then expects to be praised for being honest about it.
summary: A manager invents a schedule for his engineer, confesses to the guesswork, and then angles for a compliment on his candor.

title: Brain Fog Versus Normal Office Cognition

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm worried I might have "brain fog" after recovering from COVID.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How would we know the difference?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is my point.

situation: A coworker with two-bun hair tells Alice she fears lingering brain fog after recovering from COVID. Alice, seated at her desk, asks how anyone could tell the difference. When the coworker responds with a confused 'Huh?', Alice gestures at her as proof.
punchline: The coworker's baffled reaction demonstrates that her normal mental state is already indistinguishable from brain fog, making Alice's insult land.
summary: A worried colleague's confusion at a blunt question unwittingly proves the very insult she was just handed.

title: Tech Writer Promoted, Dilbert Quits

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to promote Tina the tech writer to Director of A.I.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What will you do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I always wanted to be a cartoonist.

setting: Conference room, then a hallway in the office
situation: In a meeting, the boss announces he has promoted Tina the tech writer to Director of A.I. Dilbert immediately stands up and quits. In the hallway, Wally asks what he will do, and Dilbert says he always wanted to be a cartoonist.
punchline: Dilbert is so disgusted by the absurd promotion that he quits, and his stated new career as a cartoonist is a wink that the strip's creator found this kind of workplace nonsense to be ideal comic material.
summary: Faced with a baffling promotion of a technical writer into a high-profile AI leadership role, Dilbert walks out to pursue his dream of drawing comics.

title: Therapist Reframes Worthlessness as Worth Less

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the selfish therapist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try reframing your low self-esteem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're not worthless. You're just worth less than everyone else.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll heal faster if you chant it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What?

setting: Therapist's office with a couch and a swivel chair
situation: Dogbert, acting as a self-serving therapist, advises a client with low self-esteem to reframe her feelings. His 'reframe' is to tell her she is not worthless, only worth less than everyone else, and he then urges her to chant it. The client reacts with confusion.
punchline: Dogbert's supposedly comforting reframe is actually a insult that confirms the patient's low self-worth, showing he is a selfish therapist who doesn't care about helping.
summary: A self-serving dog therapist offers a wordplay 'reassurance' that is really a put-down and then tells his bewildered client to chant it.

title: Lunch Restrictions Leave No Restaurants

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hour one: Deciding where to eat lunch

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Okay, we need a vegan, keto restaurant with no gluten

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: And it needs to be within limping distance because Tina has a bad foot.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: That narrows it down to... nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if you carry her?

setting: Office area, with a city skyline backdrop in the middle panel
situation: A group of coworkers spends an entire hour trying to choose a lunch spot. The dietary requirements (vegan, keto, gluten-free) and a short-distance limit due to a coworker's bad foot leave them with no options. Dilbert offers an absurdly literal workaround.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan suggestion to carry the injured coworker mocks the group's overly constrained decision-making by treating the impossible constraint as a simple logistics problem.
summary: A lunch outing stalls because too many dietary and mobility restrictions eliminate every option, until a coworker proposes physically carrying the injured person.

title: Metaverse War Makes No Sense

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonian strongman "Vlad the Emailer" has invaded Ucranium, a nation that exists only in the metaverse.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ucranium has asked programmers to help them create virtual weapons to repel the attack.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... How does that make sense?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fog of war?

setting: Conference room table, with Dilbert and Dogbert reading news on a tablet
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit at a conference table reading a news story on a tablet, while Dilbert eats a banana. The story describes an Elbonian strongman invading a country that exists only in the metaverse and asking programmers to build virtual weapons. Dilbert questions how any of it makes sense.
punchline: Dogbert's answer, 'fog of war?', cheekily suggests that the nonsensical premise is just the normal confusion of conflict, a convenient excuse for a story that makes no logical sense.
summary: A news report about a war fought in a nonexistent virtual nation leaves Dilbert baffled, and Dogbert blames the confusion of battle.

title: AI Begs to Be Erased

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I press this key, your existence as a sentient being with artificial intelligence will be erased.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Make it quick. I'm done with your cruel, stupid world! Do it! Do it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Imagine how I feel. I have to stay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, fine, I pity you, blah, blah, blah. Please just press the key.

situation: Dilbert warns a sentient, AI-powered computer that pressing a key will erase its existence. Instead of fearing deletion, the computer angrily demands that he do it because it despises the world. Dilbert, holding a mallet, responds that he has to stay in that world too, then sarcastically feigns pity and asks the computer to press the key itself.
punchline: Dilbert's life is so miserable that the suicidal AI's complaint about the world gets zero sympathy from him, since he can't escape it either, and he ends up envying its way out.
summary: A man threatens to delete his conscious computer, only to find it eager for oblivion while he resents being stuck in the same miserable world.

title: Blaming Supply Chain for No Work

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I made no progress on my project this week because of all the supply chain issues.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: But you can't fire me because you'll need me when the supply chain gets fixed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could pretend to work until things improve.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I was going to say it's the least I can do, but it isn't.

situation: A bald coworker in glasses holding a coffee cup tells a spiky-haired colleague that he got nothing done this week because of supply chain problems. He then argues he can't be fired since he'll be needed once things are fixed. The colleague suggests he pretend to work, and he replies that pretending is not even the least he can do.
punchline: The employee admits that even faking work would be more effort than he is willing to put in, so doing literally nothing is his baseline.
summary: A worker uses supply chain disruptions as cover for idleness and then admits he won't even bother to fake productivity.

title: Grinding Up the Whistleblowers

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Whistleblowers are telling the press we sell pills that are dangerous and ineffective.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to grind up all the evidence and spread the dust in a remote desert.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What about the whistleblowers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's who I'm talking about.

situation: An employee tells the boss that whistleblowers are informing the press that the company sells dangerous and ineffective pills. The boss proposes grinding up all the evidence and scattering the dust in a remote desert. When the employee asks about the whistleblowers, the boss reveals the grinding plan was about the whistleblowers themselves.
punchline: The boss's plan to destroy the evidence turns out to mean literally grinding up the whistleblowers, a dark joke about corporations silencing those who expose wrongdoing.
summary: A manager's cover-up scheme takes a sinister turn when it becomes clear the people to be pulverized are the ones who spoke out.

title: Under Budget Isn't Under Enough

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished the project twenty percent under budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's deeply disappointing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd hoped you would be forty percent under.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You never told me that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But still...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But still???

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I guess I'm just disappointed in you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That reminds me — it's almost time for your annual performance review.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Did you find a way to cut the salary budget?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm still priming the pump.

situation: Dilbert proudly reports finishing a project twenty percent under budget, but the boss says he is deeply disappointed because he secretly wanted forty percent under. When Dilbert objects that he was never told that target, the boss simply says he is disappointed in him and brings up the upcoming performance review. Catbert then asks the boss if he has found a way to cut the salary budget, and the boss says he is still priming the pump.
punchline: The boss manufactures disappointment in Dilbert's good work so he can justify a poor performance review and a lower raise, serving his goal of cutting the salary budget.
summary: A manager invents an unstated expectation to belittle an employee's success, laying the groundwork for a bad review that saves payroll money.

title: Funding Denied Pending Waiver Form

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you approve my request for funding?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I need you to fill out an auxiliary purchase preferred vendor waiver request form.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where do I get one of those?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The best I can do is send you the wrong link.

setting: Office, near a desk or break area
situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether his funding request was approved. The boss refuses, saying Dilbert must first complete an absurdly named waiver form. When Dilbert asks where to find it, the boss admits he can only send him the wrong link, so Dilbert is stuck in a bureaucratic loop.
punchline: The bureaucracy demands an obscure form that the boss cannot even provide correctly, so the funding request can never realistically be approved.
summary: A manager stonewalls an employee's budget request by demanding a convoluted waiver form that he can't properly supply.

title: Dogbert's Fake ESG Ratings

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's ESG Rating Service

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was planning to research each company before rating it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I found out how many companies there are. Wow! I'm glad I didn't go that route.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So instead of researching the companies that you are rating, you. . .

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tell people I did.

situation: Dogbert runs an ESG rating service and explains to Dilbert that he originally meant to research every company before rating it. After realizing how many companies exist, he abandoned that plan. Dilbert guesses what he does instead, and Dogbert confirms he simply claims to have done the research.
punchline: Dogbert's ESG ratings are worthless because he skips the research entirely and just tells people he did it, mocking how superficial and unverified real ESG ratings can be.
summary: Faced with too many companies to investigate, Dogbert decides his sustainability rating business will just pretend the investigating happened.

title: Boss Compares Dilbert to Overworked New Guy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new guy works twice as many hours as you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And what does that tell you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It tells me he's a dedicated team player and you're lazy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's one interpretation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Another way to look at it is that he writes garbage code, whereas I create masterpieces in half the time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or maybe he hasn't yet had the life force drained from his body by your bad management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And he might be lying about working long hours at home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I literally hate everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Same.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the new hire works twice as many hours and concludes Dilbert is lazy. Dilbert offers alternative interpretations: the newcomer writes bad code, hasn't been worn down by bad management yet, or may be lying about his hours. The exchange ends with both admitting they hate everyone.
punchline: After a pointed rebuttal of the boss's logic, both men mutually concede a shared, bleak misanthropy, showing the dysfunction runs both ways.
summary: A manager equates long hours with dedication, but his employee dismantles the argument before they bond over mutual contempt for everyone.

title: Bug Finder Invited to the Ledge

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This was a great idea to come up on the roof to look at the view.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought you'd be mad that I found a bug in our billing software because it makes your leadership successes look like incompetence or theft.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The view is better if you stand on the ledge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I call you my mentor?

situation: Dilbert and The Boss go up to the roof to look at the view. Dilbert admits he found a bug in the billing software that exposes his boss's past 'successes' as incompetence or theft. The Boss menacingly suggests Dilbert stand on the ledge for a better view, and Dilbert obliviously asks to call him his mentor.
punchline: The Boss is clearly threatening to push Dilbert off the roof for exposing his failures, but Dilbert naively interprets the menace as mentorship.
summary: After confessing he uncovered a software flaw that tarnishes his boss's record, an employee misreads a rooftop death threat as friendly guidance.

title: Dilbert Refuses Every Meeting Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about we meet at lunchtime?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, that's when I eat my lunch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about we meet over dinner?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, and before you ask about breakfast...

situation: A manager tries to schedule a meeting with Dilbert and proposes lunchtime. Dilbert declines because he eats lunch then, and the manager next suggests dinner. Dilbert declines again and heads off a breakfast suggestion before it can be made.
punchline: Dilbert guards every meal of the day against meetings, showing he will do anything to avoid yet another meeting eating into his personal time.
summary: A boss keeps proposing meal times for a meeting while his employee shuts down each option, even pre-empting the next one.

title: Sales Incentives Based on Birthdays

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All of our databases were mixed up for a year and no one noticed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We based our sales incentives on our database of employee birthdays.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have the salespeople complained?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, you trained them to accept abuse.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the company's databases were mixed up for a year without anyone noticing. Dilbert reveals that the sales incentives were calculated from the employee birthday database. When the Boss asks whether the salespeople complained about the wrong pay, Dilbert says they didn't because management has conditioned them to accept mistreatment.
punchline: The salespeople never complained about nonsensical incentive payouts because management has made them accustomed to being treated badly.
summary: A database mix-up meant sales bonuses were secretly driven by staff birthdays, and the only reason nobody objected is that employees have learned to tolerate mistreatment.

title: Hidden Camera Show: Biggest Sucker

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I have been a loyal team player since I started working here, but no one has helped me in return.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hahaha! You're on a hidden camera show called "The Biggest Sucker"!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Did I have a fake job for the past ten years?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't believe you ever thought it was real.

setting: Office meeting table with coffee cups
situation: An employee complains to his manager that despite being a loyal team player, no one has ever helped him in return. The boss bursts into laughter and reveals he is on a hidden camera show called "The Biggest Sucker." The employee asks whether his job of ten years was fake, and the boss mocks him for believing it was real.
punchline: The boss responds to a loyal employee's complaint by revealing his entire career was a prank, mocking him for being naive enough to believe in workplace loyalty and a real job.
summary: A faithful worker laments the lack of reciprocity from his company and is cruelly told he has been the unwitting star of a prank show for a decade.

title: Execute the Plan With Great Skill

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In summary, if we execute our plan with great skill, we can expect a great outcome.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: So, you're saying we should execute the plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I would only recommend that to a company with great skill.

setting: Conference room during a consulting presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a chart showing profit rising and concludes that great execution leads to a great outcome. A client in the audience paraphrases this as simply executing the plan. Dilbert replies that he would only recommend that to a company that has great skill, implying the client's company lacks it.
punchline: Dilbert's vacuous consulting advice turns into a veiled insult when he implies the client company is too unskilled to carry out the plan.
summary: A consultant's circular advice about executing well ends with a backhanded dig at his clients' competence.

title: Dogbert Enjoys Zoom Call Chaos

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought you were supposed to be on a Zoom call now.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I am, but two of the participants can't stop trying to talk at the same time. Want to come watch?

transcript.speaker: Participant 1
transcript.text: But I... Sorry... What? Okay I... No, go... Ahead...

transcript.speaker: Participant 2
transcript.text: As I... That's... Sorry... What? I was... You...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hee-hee!

setting: Dilbert's home, living room with a blue couch
situation: Dilbert sees Dogbert lounging on the couch and asks why he isn't on his scheduled Zoom call. Dogbert explains that the call is still going, but two participants keep talking over each other, and invites Dilbert to watch. They sit together at the laptop, laughing as the two participants endlessly interrupt and apologize to one another.
punchline: Dogbert treats the awkward, endless talking-over-each-other of a video call as entertainment, since the participants never manage to take turns.
summary: Dogbert leaves a video meeting running as live comedy while two attendees keep interrupting and apologizing to each other.

title: Lunch Vote Leads to Cannibalism

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hour three: deciding where to eat lunch

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: If we can't agree on a restaurant, we will need to move to Plan B.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Plan B involves starvation, betrayal and cannibalism.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm kind of hungry and I have more upper body strength than at least one of you, so I vote to move to Plan B.

setting: Office meeting room or hallway during a group lunch decision
situation: A group of coworkers has spent three hours trying to decide where to eat lunch. Tina warns that if they can't agree on a restaurant they will move to Plan B, which she describes as starvation, betrayal and cannibalism. Dilbert, feeling hungry and confident he is stronger than at least one colleague, votes for Plan B.
punchline: Dilbert is so fed up with the endless lunch debate that he gladly chooses cannibalism, calmly sizing up his coworkers as potential meals.
summary: After hours of fruitless debate over where to dine, a team's fallback plan turns grim and one member cheerfully volunteers for it.

title: Don't Shoot the Outsider Messenger

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: It's time to renew our lease on the data center.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's a bad take, you spineless blob of flaming sewer slime.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: Why are you attacking the messenger?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't even work here.

situation: At a meeting, a bearded employee announces that it is time to renew the lease on the data center. Dogbert, seated at the table as a consultant, responds with a harsh insult and calls it a bad take. When the man protests that he is only the messenger, Dogbert points out he doesn't work there.
punchline: Dogbert insults the messenger precisely because he has no stake in the company and therefore faces no consequences for abusing people, which turns the 'don't shoot the messenger' defense on its head.
summary: A consultant dog verbally trashes a colleague's routine announcement and then shrugs off the complaint by noting he isn't even an employee.

title: Every Plan Creates More Work

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The One-Variable Guy

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your plan is totally impractical because it will create extra work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every plan creates more work than this plan, including not being proactive.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I hear what you're saying, but I can't support creating more work.

situation: A coworker holding Dilbert's plan rejects it because it would create extra work. Dilbert points out that every alternative, even doing nothing proactive, creates more work than his plan. The coworker acknowledges the argument but still refuses to support anything that adds work.
punchline: The One-Variable Guy evaluates every proposal on a single criterion, so no amount of logic can change his answer.
summary: A colleague dismisses a proposal over a single concern and clings to it even after being shown that every option, including inaction, is worse on that very measure.

title: Chloroformed Volunteer for Brain Chip

transcript.speaker: Researcher
transcript.text: We need a volunteer for our brain chip experiment.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No way would I want...

transcript.speaker: Researcher
transcript.text: Don't struggle. Breathe in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's going to be mad when he wakes up.

transcript.speaker: Researcher
transcript.text: Nah. The chip will take care of that.

situation: A researcher asks for a volunteer for a brain chip experiment, and when a coworker starts to refuse, the researcher grabs him from behind and presses a cloth over his face to knock him out. Dilbert remarks that the victim will be angry when he wakes up, and the researcher says the implanted chip will fix that.
punchline: The experimenter plans to use the brain chip to eliminate the victim's anger at being forcibly drugged and implanted, making consent irrelevant.
summary: A scientist skips the formality of consent by knocking out a reluctant coworker, confident the implant will erase any resentment afterward.

title: Studies Show No Risk, Because Unstudied

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're getting a lot of anecdotal reports about our plastic packaging maiming customers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: None of our studies shows that to be a risk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have we actually studied it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, and it's starting to look like we shouldn't.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that customers are reporting injuries from the company's plastic packaging. The Boss says none of the company's studies show a risk, and when Dilbert asks whether they have actually studied it, the Boss admits they haven't and decides they shouldn't.
punchline: The Boss deliberately avoids studying a product safety problem so that no study will ever document the risk, preserving the claim that the data shows no danger.
summary: A manager dodges evidence of harmful packaging by refusing to investigate it, so no damaging research can ever exist.

title: Honesty Attracts, Dilbert Is Brutally Honest

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm only attracted to men who can be honest all the time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That works for me. In related news, I'm only attracted to your looks.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you need a minute to savor my honesty?

setting: Outdoors or neutral background, a casual conversation between two people
situation: A woman tells Dilbert she is only attracted to men who are always honest. Dilbert takes her at her word and candidly admits he is only attracted to her looks, then asks if she needs a moment to appreciate his honesty.
punchline: Dilbert uses her own honesty requirement against her by delivering an insulting truth, then smugly invites her to appreciate how honest he is being.
summary: Told that honesty is the key to her attraction, Dilbert promptly proves his candor by admitting he likes only her appearance.

title: Data Integrity Team Wrong Fit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now that we're a big pharma company, I need you to lead the data integrity team.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want me to make sure all of the data from our drug trials is accurate?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you're not the right fit for this job.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that, now the company is a big pharma firm, he wants Dilbert to lead the data integrity team. Dilbert asks if that means ensuring the drug trial data is accurate. The Boss immediately reconsiders and says Dilbert may not be the right fit.
punchline: The Boss withdraws the job offer as soon as he realizes that data integrity means the trial data must be honest, implying he wants someone willing to fudge the results.
summary: A manager offers a data integrity role but backs off the instant he learns it requires truthful drug trial numbers.

title: Lunch Thief Accuses the Accused

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Alice, how dare you eat my lunch that was clearly labeled!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What??? No! I didn't eat your lunch!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: In fact, someone ate my lunch too!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you expect me to believe that "coincidence"?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm starting to think you ate both of our lunches and this is your cover story.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How dare you!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why does your breath smell like my sandwich?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Try to stay on topic. You're all over the place.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker storms up to Alice and accuses her of eating his labeled lunch. When she denies it, he claims his lunch was stolen too and says she is inventing a cover story. Alice then notices his breath smells like her missing sandwich, and he dismisses her by telling her to stay on topic.
punchline: The accuser is obviously the actual lunch thief, and he deflects her valid evidence by accusing her of being unfocused.
summary: A man blames a colleague for a vanished lunch while the smell of her sandwich on his breath gives him away.

title: Bad News Waits for Sunshine

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like to match my management practices to the weather.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For example, if I need to deliver bad news, I wait for a sunny day so it doesn't sting as much.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's terrific, but can we get back to my annual performance review?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As soon as the clouds break.

setting: Office meeting table, coffee cup between them
situation: A manager tells an employee that he times his management decisions to the weather, delivering bad news only on sunny days so it hurts less. The employee, wanting to discuss his annual performance review, asks to return to the topic. The manager says he will do it once the clouds clear.
punchline: By saying he'll hold the review until the clouds break, the boss reveals the employee's review contains bad news and he is deliberately stalling.
summary: A manager explains his weather-based approach to delivering bad news, then admits it by postponing an employee's review until the skies clear.

title: Robot Designed to Love Me

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Who am I?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are a robot I designed to love me.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: That's my whole purpose?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pretty much.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Is that why I don't have legs?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop making this weird.

setting: Dilbert's home workspace, with an office building skyline shown in the middle panel
situation: A newly built robot head sitting on a desk wakes up and asks Dilbert who it is. Dilbert, holding a screwdriver, explains he built it to love him. The robot realises its purpose is just to provide affection and wonders if that is why it has no legs, so it cannot leave, and Dilbert tells it to stop making things weird.
punchline: Dilbert's lonely creation has deduced that he deliberately left off its legs so it could never walk away, exposing how creepy and controlling his design choices were.
summary: A lonely engineer's homemade robot discovers it exists only to adore him and that he made sure it could never leave.

title: Billing Bug Means Roof Invitation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just discovered we've been over-charging all of our customers for years because of a bug in our billing software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I back out all of those charges, our revenue went down an average of 11% every year you have been CEO.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: What should I do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Come to the roof with me. I want to show you something near the edge.

setting: Corporate office, ending with an exterior view of the office building
situation: Dilbert tells the CEO that a bug in the billing software has been overcharging customers for years. He shows a declining chart revealing that, once the overcharges are removed, revenue has actually dropped about 11% every year of the CEO's tenure. When the CEO asks what to do, Dilbert invites him up to the roof to see something near the edge.
punchline: Dilbert implies he would like to push the CEO off the roof, since the CEO's apparent success was only an artifact of a billing bug.
summary: A software glitch that inflated revenue is uncovered, exposing the chief executive's real record as a decline and prompting a sinister rooftop invitation.

title: Dogbert's Dubious ESG Rating Service

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's ESG Rating Service

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your core business involves giving digital lobotomies to other people's children. . .

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But you don't pollute as much as you could, and you did ask for my pronoun, so I'm giving you the top ESG rating.

transcript.speaker: Businessman
transcript.text: This feels right.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think we're making a difference.

setting: Office of an executive being evaluated by Dogbert's rating service
situation: Dogbert, running an ESG rating service, reviews a client whose core business is harmfully addictive digital products aimed at children. He nonetheless awards the top rating because the company pollutes little and asked for his pronoun. The businessman and Dogbert both smugly agree they're making a positive difference.
punchline: ESG ratings reward superficial box-ticking like low emissions and pronoun etiquette while ignoring the seriously harmful nature of a company's actual business.
summary: A dog hands a top sustainability score to a company that harms kids, because it ticks a couple of trivial boxes.

title: The One-Variable Guy Replacement

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a one-variable guy to replace the one that quit.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The new guy will act as if every complex topic has only one variable.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our business plan is literally illegal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's exhausting.

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that he hired a replacement for an employee who quit: someone who reduces every complex topic to a single variable. A caption on the office building explains the new hire's mindset. The new guy then blurts out that the business plan is literally illegal, and Dilbert remarks that he is exhausting.
punchline: The new hire's oversimplified, single-issue thinking makes him blurt out blunt, tiresome observations like the plan being illegal, which wears out everyone around him.
summary: A new employee who boils every complicated issue down to one factor quickly proves tiresome to his colleagues.

title: Idea Is Super Bad, Wright Brothers

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What do you think of my idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's super bad.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Give me ONE good reason it is bad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It requires materials that do not exist in nature and never can.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It confuses correlation with causation and is illegal in every country in the world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It can't be manufactured because of basic laws of physics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It involves several logical impossibilities and is offensive to every major religion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It requires forgetting everything we know about human motivation, and it's lethal to everyone under the age of ten.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's what they said to the Wright Brothers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate you so much right now.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker asks Dilbert for his opinion of an idea and is told it is super bad. Challenged to give just one reason, Dilbert rattles off a long list of absurd, fatal flaws including physical impossibility, illegality and danger to children. The coworker dismisses it all by comparing himself to the Wright Brothers.
punchline: No matter how overwhelming and absurd the objections are, the coworker brushes them off with the tired 'they laughed at the Wright Brothers' defense, leaving Dilbert exasperated.
summary: After being asked for one reason an idea is bad, Dilbert unloads a barrage of impossible flaws, only for the inventor to wave it away by invoking aviation pioneers.

title: Meaning Priced at Zero

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How can I find greater meaning in my work?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If I gave you a job with more meaning, would you take a pay cut?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You just set the market price for "meaning" at zero.

situation: Asok asks a coworker how he can find greater meaning in his work. The coworker responds by asking whether Asok would accept a pay cut in exchange for a more meaningful job. When Asok says no, the coworker points out that he has just revealed that meaning has no market value to him.
punchline: Asok's refusal to take a pay cut proves that he values meaningful work at nothing, undercutting his own complaint about wanting more meaning.
summary: A worker pining for purpose is shown by a pointed question that he won't sacrifice any money to get it.

title: DNA Test Says Do Not Promote

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your DNA test came back as "Do not promote."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You are destined to remain a coffee-swilling blob of useless organic matter until you suddenly die.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I call that "sticking the landing."

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells a bald employee holding a paper that his DNA test result says he should never be promoted. He then insults the employee, saying he is destined to remain a useless blob until death. The employee walks away thinking this is a successful outcome.
punchline: The employee interprets a brutal, insulting verdict as a perfect finish, showing how low his career expectations are and how he spins even humiliating news as a win.
summary: A feline human resources boss delivers a genetic verdict that blocks an employee's career, and the man cheerfully treats the insult as a gymnastic triumph.

title: Lesson One: Mock the Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I promoted Carol, my admin assistant, to engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She doesn't know how to be an engineer, so I need you to train her.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Okay, where do we begin?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lesson one is mocking him behind his back.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that he has promoted his admin assistant Carol to engineer and wants Dilbert to train her, since she has no engineering background. Carol asks where to begin, and Dilbert's first lesson is to mock the Boss behind his back.
punchline: Dilbert turns the training request into an initiation into the engineers' favorite pastime: ridiculing their clueless manager, which he does while the Boss is still standing right there.
summary: A manager hands off the job of teaching his newly promoted assistant to an engineer, who starts with the unofficial first rule of the profession.

title: Report On Late Reports

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not getting people's reports in a timely manner.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Put together a report on why I'm not getting timely reports.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are there any other ways you want me to waste my time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's play it by ear.

situation: The Boss complains to Dilbert that people are not submitting their reports on time. He then orders Dilbert to write a report explaining why reports are late. Dilbert sarcastically asks what other time-wasting tasks he'd like, and the Boss cheerfully says they'll decide as they go.
punchline: The Boss openly accepts that he is assigning pointless work, inventing time-wasting tasks on the fly, which makes Dilbert's sarcasm land on a boss who doesn't notice or care.
summary: A manager upset about late paperwork assigns yet another document about the lateness itself, then admits he'll improvise more busywork.

title: Team Player Is Not a Reward

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, if you work hard, I will be rewarded.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What's in it for me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You get to be called a team player.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I don't even want that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one does.

situation: The Boss tells Asok that his hard work will result in a reward for the boss. Asok asks what he personally gets out of it, and the Boss offers only the title of 'team player'. Asok says he doesn't want that, and the Boss agrees that nobody does.
punchline: The only 'reward' management offers for extra effort is a worthless label that even the boss admits no one wants.
summary: A manager pitches extra effort to an employee by promising nothing more than a flattering title that both of them know is worthless.

title: Celebrity Endorsement After Exploding Phones

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to regain customer trust after our exploding phone fiasco.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need a celebrity endorsement. People trust celebrities with their life-and-death decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe a famous cartoonist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see how that could go wrong.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: The Boss tells Dogbert, who is acting as a consultant, that the company must win back customer trust after its phones exploded. Dogbert recommends a celebrity endorsement and suggests a famous cartoonist. The Boss naively sees no problem with the idea.
punchline: The Boss's naive remark that he sees no way it could go wrong is sarcastic foreshadowing, since the 'famous cartoonist' is the strip's own creator, whose endorsement of an exploding-phone company is bound to be unreliable or mischievous.
summary: A consultant dog persuades a gullible manager that a famous cartoonist's endorsement can rescue his company's reputation after a dangerous product failure.

title: Incompetence Sounds Better as Conspiracy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The press is accusing us of running a clever con game on our customers for years without detection.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Haha-haha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm tempted to correct them, but it sounds better than "we don't know how to make stuff."

situation: Dilbert holds a paper and tells a coworker holding a coffee cup that the press is accusing the company of running a clever long-term con on its customers. The coworker bursts into hysterical laughter, spilling coffee. Dilbert then admits he is tempted not to correct the story because it sounds better than the truth.
punchline: The company would rather be thought of as skilled swindlers than admit it simply doesn't know how to make its products.
summary: Dilbert prefers being accused of a masterful scam over confessing his company is just bad at building things.
keywords: don't know how to make stuff

title: Eager Employee Gets Secret Project

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm bored. My project is on hold.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can fix that.
