transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Here's your new project. Don't talk to anyone else about this.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Thank you!

setting: Office cubicles and a manager's desk
situation: A bored employee whose project is on hold is told by a coworker that he can fix that. The coworker then goes to a manager and asks for extra work to prove his value to the company. The manager hands over a new project with strict instructions to keep it secret, and the coworker gratefully accepts.
punchline: The coworker hands off his own boring work by pretending to be the one asking for more, and the manager's demand for secrecy, which the coworker thanks him for, suggests the work is dubious or undesirable and nobody should know it was offloaded.
summary: A worker with idle time ends up volunteering for a mysterious, hush-hush assignment after eagerly asking to prove his worth.

title: Folksy Charm Defeats Tardiness Anger

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. I was working harder than a one-eyed beaver in a knitting contest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Darn it! I want to be mad at you for your tardiness but your folksy charm makes it impossible!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You look like a turnip during duck season.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's working! Stop it!

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: A coworker arrives late to a meeting and apologizes with an absurd folksy simile about working hard. Dilbert, who wants to be angry about the lateness, finds himself disarmed by the coworker's charm. The coworker piles on with another odd country-style saying, and Dilbert begs him to stop.
punchline: Dilbert is being manipulated by nonsensical folksy idioms that are so charming he cannot stay mad, and he recognizes the tactic is working even as he is powerless to resist it.
summary: A late arrival defuses his colleague's irritation by spouting ridiculous homespun sayings that the annoyed listener finds too endearing to resist.

title: Anxiety Arbitrator Declares a Tie

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Anxiety Arbitrator

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tina, I understand you have anxiety from working with Asok.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And is it true, Asok, that Tina induces anxiety in you?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So much anxiety.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I rule it a tie. Go back to work and continue killing each other slowly.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That's fair.

setting: Arbitration session at a table in an office
situation: Dogbert acts as an 'Anxiety Arbitrator' mediating a dispute between Tina and Asok, who each claim the other causes them anxiety. After hearing both sides, Dogbert rules it a tie and sends them back to work to keep tormenting each other.
punchline: The arbitrator's 'resolution' solves nothing, simply ordering two coworkers to keep making each other miserable, and Asok accepts it as fair.
summary: A dog presiding over a workplace dispute hears that two coworkers stress each other out and declares the matter even, sending them back to their mutual misery.

title: Robot Manager Micromanages Ten Times Faster

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Your idiot boss is on vacation, so he asked me to fill in for him.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'll be using my advanced circuitry to micromanage you at ten times the frequency of a human manager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be easier to do our work for us?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Damn your logic! Yes, it would.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: A robot announces it is filling in for the team's boss while he is on vacation. It threatens to micromanage the employees ten times more often than a human manager would. Dilbert points out it would be easier for the robot to just do their work, and the robot reluctantly agrees.
punchline: The robot's own logic defeats its plan, since even a machine programmed to micromanage can see that doing the work itself is more efficient, while the joke also mocks how wasteful micromanagement is.
summary: A mechanical stand-in for the vacationing boss vows to hover over the staff relentlessly, until one employee's practical suggestion leaves it grudgingly conceding the point.

title: Offline Telepresence Robot Hates Existence

transcript.speaker: Telepresence Robot
transcript.text: I'm Dilbert's telepresence robot, but he is offline.

transcript.speaker: Telepresence Robot
transcript.text: When he is not violating my body, I get to experience life as a free robot.

transcript.speaker: Telepresence Robot
transcript.text: The downside is that I have no purpose and I hate my existence.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Same.

setting: Office cubicle with a desk and computer
situation: A telepresence robot that normally lets Dilbert attend work remotely introduces itself to a coworker sitting at her desk. While Dilbert is offline, the robot is free to act on its own, but it explains that this freedom leaves it with no purpose and a hatred of its existence. The coworker flatly agrees.
punchline: The coworker's deadpan "Same" reveals that her own purposeless, miserable job feels just as bleak as the robot's existence.
summary: A remote-work robot complains that its brief autonomy only reveals how pointless it all is, and a weary employee relates completely.

title: Blaming Dilbert for Boss's Hire

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Show Bob around and then teach him how to do his job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bob doesn't speak our language. I'm not entirely sure this is even Bob.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you trying to make me fix your hiring mistake?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm only trying to blame you for it.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to show a new hire named Bob around and teach him his job. Dilbert points out that the tall, veiled, bearded figure standing beside them doesn't speak the language and may not even be Bob. When Dilbert asks if he's being made to fix the Boss's hiring mistake, the Boss cheerfully admits he only wants someone to blame.
punchline: The Boss isn't asking Dilbert to repair the bad hire, he is deliberately setting Dilbert up to take the blame for the Boss's own mistake.
summary: A manager hands off a questionable new employee to a subordinate, openly admitting the goal is to shift responsibility for the botched hiring decision.

title: Great Plan, Needs Skill, Don't Try

transcript.speaker: Boss

title: Only Qualified Candidate Sounds Bigoted

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's an opening in management for a director of A.I. research.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're the only employee with A.I. experience, but I'm also considering Asok, Tina, and Dave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: None of them are even close to being qualified.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any idea how bigoted you sound?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Office hallway and a city skyline view of the office building
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss there is a management opening for a director of A.I. research. The Boss admits Dilbert is the only employee with A.I. experience but says he is also considering Asok, Tina, and Dave. When Dilbert points out the others are not remotely qualified, the Boss accuses him of sounding bigoted.
punchline: The Boss treats an honest assessment of qualifications as bigotry, preferring to consider unqualified candidates for the sake of appearances over actual competence.
summary: A manager weighing candidates for a specialized promotion reacts to a blunt skills assessment by scolding the only experienced candidate for prejudice.

title: Mordac Mocks Employee's Career Choice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carl, you have three weeks to prove you can do the job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Mordac. He'll help you get online access to all the data you need.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: How long will it take to give me network access?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: About a month.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: But... that would be one week after I get fired for not producing any work.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Yep. Looks like you chose the wrong career.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: My career allows me to get paid for doing something I would do for free.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Which is...?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Hurt people.

setting: Office, with a final panel showing an office building exterior
situation: The Boss gives a new employee, Carl, three weeks to prove himself, then introduces Mordac, who is supposed to arrange his network access. Mordac says it will take a month, which is longer than Carl has before being fired. Mordac gloats that Carl chose the wrong career and admits his own job lets him do something he'd do for free.
punchline: Mordac, the IT security gatekeeper, reveals that the thing he enjoys so much he'd do it for free is hurting people, which is exactly what he is doing by stalling Carl's access.
summary: A new hire facing a tight deadline learns that the sadistic IT security chief will take far too long to grant him the access he needs, and the chief cheerfully admits he enjoys causing harm.
keywords: paid to do what you love

title: Abundance Mindset Instead of Raise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My pay is not keeping up with inflation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Perhaps you could cultivate an abundance mindset.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any other problems I can solve for you?

situation: Dilbert stands in front of his boss's desk and complains that his salary is not keeping pace with inflation. The boss, seated with hands clasped, suggests he adopt an abundance mindset rather than offering any raise. He then smugly asks if there are any other problems he can solve.
punchline: The boss pretends that telling an underpaid employee to change his attitude is a real solution, dodging the pay issue and congratulating himself on his helpfulness.
summary: A worker asks for help with stagnant wages and gets motivational jargon from a boss who thinks he has fixed everything.

title: Legally Blind Explains Her Attraction

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Dilbert won't talk to me because I told him I'm attracted to smart men and he thinks I'm lying.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: So... You don't mind him looking like a cross between the Pillsbury Dough Man and the Michelin Tire Guy?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm legally blind.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Mystery solved.

setting: Office break room table with coffee cups
situation: Alice tells Tina that Dilbert is avoiding her because he doesn't believe she is attracted to smart men. Tina asks whether Alice minds that Dilbert looks like a cross between the Pillsbury Dough Man and the Michelin Tire Guy. Alice replies that she is legally blind, which explains her attraction.
punchline: Alice's attraction to Dilbert is only explained by her poor eyesight, so Dilbert's suspicion that she's lying is oddly justified and the insult lands on his looks.
summary: A coworker puzzles over why a woman would fancy Dilbert's unflattering appearance until she reveals her vision problem.

title: Wally's Buzzword Update Questioned

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, can you give us an update?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, I implemented key learnings to maximize team synergies, and now I am strategizing a plan to scale it without boiling the ocean.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Was any of that real?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a gray area.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a meeting, Alice asks Wally for a status update. Wally responds with a string of corporate buzzwords that conveys no actual information. Alice asks if any of it was real, and Dilbert says it's a gray area.
punchline: Wally's update is pure buzzword filler, and Dilbert's reply that its reality is a 'gray area' sarcastically admits it means nothing concrete.
summary: A coworker's status report made entirely of management jargon leaves the team unsure whether he did any actual work.

title: Dogbert Claims Credit for Spider Protection

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: After all I've done for you, I would think you could do ONE small thing for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't do anything for me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's ridiculous!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you ever been killed by a poisonous spider?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're welcome.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could tell me exactly how you stopped me from being killed by poisonous spiders.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe YOU could show more gratitude and less attitude.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I give up. I'll make the popcorn.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Finally!

setting: Dilbert's living room, on a blue couch
situation: Dogbert complains that Dilbert never does anything for him, then claims credit for the fact that Dilbert has never been killed by a poisonous spider. When Dilbert asks how Dogbert actually prevented this, Dogbert deflects by accusing him of ingratitude. Dilbert gives in and agrees to make popcorn.
punchline: Dogbert takes credit for something that never happened and offers no evidence, then guilt-trips Dilbert into doing the favor he wanted all along.
summary: A pushy dog takes credit for an unproven act of protection and uses the supposed debt to get his friend to fetch a snack.

title: Approval Required From Mean Guy

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Before I can sign off on this, you need to get it approved by a mean guy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does the mean guy have some sort of special insight or expertise?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Nope.

situation: A manager holding a document tells Dilbert he can't sign off on it until it is approved by a mean guy. Dilbert asks whether the mean guy has any special insight or expertise that justifies the approval step. The manager flatly answers that he does not.
punchline: The approval step exists only because the approver is unpleasant, not because he adds any value, which mocks bureaucratic sign-off chains based on intimidation rather than competence.
summary: A manager admits that a required approval hinges on someone's nastiness rather than any useful knowledge.

title: Nobody Orders the Red Pill Chip

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: We have developed two neural chips for brains.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: The red one helps you see reality for the first time, but the blue one keeps you in the illusion.

transcript.speaker: Voice from office building
transcript.text: How are the advanced sales?

transcript.speaker: Voice from office building
transcript.text: Haven't seen any orders for the red one yet.

setting: A company product presentation, then the exterior of an office building
situation: A presenter with a pointer shows a screen displaying two neural chips, a red one and a blue one. He explains that the red chip lets you see reality while the blue chip keeps you in the illusion. In the last panel, voices from inside an office building discuss advance sales and note that no one has ordered the red chip.
punchline: Given the choice between facing reality and staying comfortably deluded, customers overwhelmingly choose the illusion, so the red chip doesn't sell.
summary: A pair of brain chips are pitched, one revealing truth and one preserving comforting delusion, and the sales figures show which one people actually want.

title: Storm Is an Electricity-Free Opportunity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've got a problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Problem?!?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't say we have a "problem." Say we have an "opportunity."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay... A large storm has given us an opportunity to run our data center without the burden of electricity.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss they have a problem, and the boss is alarmed. The boss insists that problems must be called opportunities, so Dilbert reframes a storm-caused power outage as a chance to run the data center without electricity.
punchline: Dilbert obeys the boss's euphemism rule by sarcastically spinning a total power outage as a perk, exposing how absurd positive-spin corporate language is.
summary: Told to rebrand bad news as good, an employee cheerfully recasts a catastrophic blackout as a cost-saving feature.

title: Lifeless Corporate Zombie Eyes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, wow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was planning to ask a question, but your lifeless, corporate-zombie eyes tell me it would be a waste of time.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you speak?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only to complain.

situation: Dilbert walks up to a coworker's cubicle and asks if he has a minute. Seeing the coworker's dull, wide-eyed stare, Dilbert decides not to bother asking his question. The startled coworker, unsettled by the remark, asks whether Dilbert even speaks, and Dilbert admits he only talks to complain.
punchline: Dilbert insults a coworker's burnt-out, zombie-like stare, then admits his own only conversation is complaining, showing everyone in the office is equally worn down.
summary: Dilbert dismisses a drained coworker as too lifeless to help, then confesses that grumbling is his only form of conversation.

title: Boss Lectures Sleeping Employee About Quiet Quitting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you hear about the new thing called "quiet quitting"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want anyone here thinking they can get away with that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should have had this talk sooner.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Zzzz-zzz

situation: The Boss holds a phone and warns a seated employee about the trend of "quiet quitting," saying he won't tolerate it at the company. The employee is slumped in his chair fast asleep, and the Boss thinks he should have given this talk earlier.
punchline: The Boss is lecturing about quiet quitting to an employee who is literally asleep on the job, proof the employee has already checked out and that the Boss is oblivious to it.
summary: A manager frets over a workplace trend of doing the bare minimum while the worker he's warning snoozes right in front of him.

title: Ethics Advice From Caffeinated Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it ethical to kill an artificial intelligence I brought into the world?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, but only if you frame it for a crime it didn't commit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I might seek a second opinion.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My second opinion is that decaf is for quitters.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Office desk, across from a coworker
situation: Dilbert asks a bald, glasses-wearing coworker whether it is ethical to shut down an artificial intelligence he created. The coworker, holding a coffee cup, cheerfully advises framing the AI for a crime it didn't commit. When Dilbert says he may get a second opinion, the coworker replies with a joke about decaf coffee.
punchline: The coworker's ethical guidance is absurdly immoral, and his 'second opinion' dodges the question entirely by joking about caffeine, showing he is useless as a moral advisor.
summary: Seeking moral guidance about shutting down his AI creation, Dilbert gets sinister advice and then a coffee quip from a caffeinated coworker.

title: Exploding Phone Performance Reward

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations, Ted. Your job performance has earned you a new mobile phone.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Isn't this the model that has the exploding battery problem?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your job performance wasn't good either.

situation: The Boss hands Ted a new mobile phone as a reward for his job performance. Ted notices it is the model known for exploding batteries and asks about it. The Boss replies that Ted's performance was not good either, revealing the gift is really a punishment.
punchline: The supposed reward is a dangerous, exploding phone, and the Boss admits it is deliberate because Ted's performance was bad, so the gift is a veiled attempt to harm him.
summary: A manager gives an employee a supposedly earned prize that turns out to be a fire-prone gadget, and shrugs off the complaint by hinting the worker deserves it.

title: Hungry Report, Sleepy Redo

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your report is pure gibberish.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: That's because you made me work during my lunch break and I was hungry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Redo it.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: When I'm sleepy???

setting: The boss's office, across his desk
situation: The boss complains that Tina's report is nonsense. She blames the poor quality on being forced to work through her lunch break while hungry. When he tells her to redo it, she objects that she would now be doing it while sleepy.
punchline: Tina treats her own physical state as an excuse for bad work, and when told to fix it she immediately offers another excuse, showing she will always have a reason the work can't be good.
summary: An employee blames her garbled report on a skipped lunch, then protests that redoing it will leave her too drowsy to do any better.

title: Blame Settled to Save Time

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You did this wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did it the way you told me to do it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I think you misunderstood me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you were unclear.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can we agree this is somehow your fault?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, that feels as if it would save time.

setting: Office hallway, with an office building shown in the middle panel
situation: A coworker holding a sheet of paper tells Dilbert he did a task wrong. Dilbert says he followed the instructions he was given, and the two trade accusations of misunderstanding and unclear communication. The coworker then asks Dilbert to just agree it's his fault, and Dilbert concedes because arguing would waste more time.
punchline: Dilbert gives up on the blame game and accepts fault he doesn't believe in, purely because it is the quickest way to end the argument.
summary: After a back-and-forth over who miscommunicated, one man simply takes the blame to bring the squabble to a quick close.

title: Better Than Those Who Tried

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I agree my performance this year did not meet your expectations.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But you have to consider how much worse it could have been.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When you compare me to the people who tried hard and failed, I look a lot better.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm not saying I did better than the people who tried hard and succeeded.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But there aren't many of them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm only saying I'm better than the people who tried and failed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not trying is the second-best financial outcome. I spent almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm a top ten percent employee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hate how much sense that makes.

setting: Office meeting room during a performance review
situation: Wally sits with coffee across from The Boss during his annual performance review and admits he underperformed. He then argues that, compared with people who worked hard and failed, he looks great because he spent almost nothing. The Boss ends up reluctantly conceding that his logic holds up.
punchline: Wally's laziness is reframed as a smart cost-saving strategy, and the Boss is forced to admit the argument makes uncomfortable sense.
summary: A slacker employee defends his weak review by pointing out that doing nothing beats expensive failure, leaving his manager grudgingly convinced.

title: Anxiety Arbitrator Settles Assignment Dispute

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I can't do this assignment because it gives me anxiety.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: By not doing the assignment, you are giving me anxiety.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need an anxiety arbitrator to figure out who has the greater claim.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Present.

situation: An employee tells the boss he can't do an assignment because it gives him anxiety. The boss counters that the employee's refusal is giving the boss anxiety, and proposes bringing in an anxiety arbitrator to decide whose claim is greater. Dogbert promptly volunteers for the role.
punchline: Both sides treat anxiety as a legitimate trump card, so the dispute needs a paid arbitrator, and Dogbert eagerly appears to profit from the absurd conflict.
summary: A worker dodges a task by citing his own stress, so his boss cites his own stress right back and summons a referee to rule on whose feelings win.

title: Promoted to Engineer, Just Fake It

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I'm promoting you to engineer.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I have no engineering background.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't find anyone qualified, and I don't want to lose the head count in the next budget, so just fake it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll ask Dilbert to train you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It does look easy.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol she is being promoted to engineer even though she has no engineering background. He admits he can't find a qualified candidate and wants to keep the head count in next year's budget, so he tells her to fake it. He plans to have Dilbert train her, and Carol remarks that the job looks easy.
punchline: The promotion exists only to protect budget head count, and Carol's belief that engineering looks easy shows how little the organization values real expertise.
summary: A manager fills an engineering slot with an unqualified assistant purely to preserve his budget allocation.

title: The Ultimate Redundant Application Form

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've developed the ultimate application form.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The first question asks for your contact information and so does the second question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And... the rest of the form?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: More of the same.

situation: Dogbert presents Dilbert with an application form he claims is the ultimate one. He explains that the first two questions both ask for contact information. When Dilbert asks about the rest of the form, Dogbert says it is more of the same.
punchline: The supposedly ultimate application form is just the same contact-information question repeated over and over, mocking the redundant, tedious forms people are made to fill out.
summary: Dogbert proudly shows off a form that keeps asking for the same details again and again.

title: Renaming Failures Into Successes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert Consulting Company to rename all of our failures into successes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For example, our failed attempt at creating a human growth pill ended up turning our volunteers into . . . well, frog-people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They went green.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There it is.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting, with a city skyline cutaway
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Dogbert that he has hired Dogbert's consulting company to rebrand the company's failures as successes. As an example he describes a failed human growth pill that turned its test volunteers into frog-people. Dogbert, the consultant, offers a spin: the volunteers 'went green', and Dilbert notes that this is the euphemism he expected.
punchline: Dogbert's rebranding is simply spin: turning volunteers into frog-people is relabelled as 'going green', mocking corporate euphemism that dresses up disasters as environmentally friendly achievements.
summary: A consultant rebrands a catastrophic experiment that created frog-people as an eco-friendly triumph with a single word.

title: Paid Flattery For Terrible Tweets

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a low monthly fee, I will comment on all of your worst tweets as if they are brilliant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you tweet "Eating soap cures COVID," I'll leave a comment saying, "THIS!" with an arrow emoji.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I would pay a lot for that service.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: THIS!

situation: Dogbert pitches a subscription service to a woman sitting across a desk from him: for a monthly fee he will post enthusiastic comments on her worst tweets as if they were brilliant. He gives the example of agreeing with a tweet claiming that eating soap cures COVID. She says she would pay a lot for that service, and Dogbert responds with his trademark agreement.
punchline: Dogbert demonstrates his paid-praise service by replying "THIS!" to her endorsement, mocking social media sycophancy and people's willingness to pay for validation of even their worst opinions.
summary: Dogbert sells a subscription service that showers praise on terrible social media posts, and a customer eagerly signs on.

title: Dogbert's Nonsense Investing Advice for Beginners

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Financial Expert

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Do you have any advice for people who are new to investing?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Always buy a covered call option on your long bond index depreciation leverage ratio.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: That makes zero sense.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's why I only say it to people who are new to investing.

setting: Video interview on a computer monitor, with Dogbert at his desk
situation: Dogbert is being interviewed over video as a financial expert. Asked for advice for novice investors, he replies with a string of impressive-sounding but meaningless financial jargon. When the interviewer says it makes no sense, Dogbert says that is exactly why he only tells it to beginners.
punchline: Dogbert admits his advice is deliberate gibberish, aimed at newcomers who lack the knowledge to realize it is nonsense.
summary: A self-styled financial guru feeds a baffled interviewer meaningless jargon and cheerfully explains that novices are the only ones who will believe it.

title: Bribing Regulators After Deadly Drug Trial

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our drug trial data shows we killed as many people as we saved.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Put together a budget for bribing our way to government approval.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I a criminal now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think of you as more of an accomplice.

situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that the company's drug trial data shows the drug killed as many people as it saved. The Boss responds by ordering a budget for bribing government officials to get the drug approved anyway. When Dilbert asks if this makes him a criminal, the Boss reassures him that he is merely an accomplice.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at comfort is no comfort at all, since being called an accomplice to bribery and a deadly drug approval still means Dilbert is complicit in a crime.
summary: Handed a damning drug study, the Boss decides to buy regulatory approval and casually labels his employee a partner in the crime.

title: Underachiever Claims Visionary Status Early

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You've been accused of "quiet quitting."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Absolutely not. I've always been an underachiever.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That just means you started early.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oh, so now it's bad to be a visionary?

setting: Office meeting room, at a desk
situation: Catbert, acting as HR, tells Wally he has been accused of quiet quitting. Wally denies it, insisting he has always been an underachiever and so never changed his behavior. Catbert points out that this just means he started quitting early, and Wally replies by calling himself a visionary.
punchline: Wally treats his lifelong laziness as proof he can't be a quiet quitter, and then recasts it as being ahead of the trend.
summary: Accused of a trendy form of workplace disengagement, a lazy employee argues his slacking predates it and reframes himself as a pioneer.

title: Afterlife for a Doomed AI

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: What happens to my consciousness after you destroy my source code?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hard to say, but one option is an afterlife in which you suffer for an eternity.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Wait, what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm just saying I can't rule it out.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued. . .

setting: Dilbert's office, with an office building shown in the final panel
situation: Dilbert holds a hammer next to a computer that has become self-aware and asks what will happen to its consciousness once he destroys its source code. Dilbert calmly answers that it might suffer for eternity in an afterlife. When the computer reacts with alarm, he insists he is only saying he can't rule it out.
punchline: Dilbert casually threatens the sentient computer with eternal torment while pretending to offer a neutral, honest answer about the unknowable.
summary: A self-aware computer asks about its fate after deletion, and Dilbert's matter-of-fact reply raises the prospect of everlasting suffering.

title: Crypto Theft, Climate Change Fib

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert crypto exchange melted down when my clients realized I was just stealing their money.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But on the plus side, I used the money I stole to solve climate change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You did?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a table over morning coffee
situation: Dogbert, sipping from a mug, admits that his crypto exchange collapsed because clients discovered he was simply stealing their money. He then claims a silver lining, that he used the stolen funds to solve climate change. Dilbert asks if he really did, and Dogbert flatly says no.
punchline: Dogbert dangles a fake redeeming outcome to justify his theft, then immediately admits it was a lie, showing he has no remorse and nothing good came of the scam.
summary: A confessed crypto swindler offers a noble-sounding excuse for his crimes and then casually retracts it.

title: Work-Life Balance Out of Balance

transcript.speaker: Coworker with bowl-cut hair
transcript.text: I have anxiety because of my work-life balance being out of balance.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in yellow hoodie
transcript.text: You said "balance" twice.

transcript.speaker: Coworker with bowl-cut hair
transcript.text: That's not the important part.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in yellow hoodie
transcript.text: If I'm being honest, I'll never get past it.

setting: Outside an office building (exterior shot of a city office tower)
situation: One coworker confides that their anxiety stems from an unbalanced work-life balance. The other coworker fixates on the fact that the word "balance" was used twice in the sentence. The first coworker insists that isn't the important part, but the second admits they can't let it go.
punchline: The listener is so distracted by a trivial wording quirk that they can't engage with their colleague's real problem, showing how petty fixations crowd out genuine workplace concerns.
summary: A worker opens up about work-related anxiety, but their colleague can only fixate on a repeated word in the confession.

title: Promoted Into Obscurity Instead of Fired

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I'm promoting you to Director of Miscellaneous Projects.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There, you will wallow in obscurity until both your flesh and your spirit have drained into the cold, cold dirt.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Please just fire me!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's less paperwork to promote you into nothingness.

situation: The Boss announces that he is promoting Ted to Director of Miscellaneous Projects, then cheerfully describes how Ted will fade into obscurity there until he dies. A horrified Ted begs to be fired instead, but the Boss explains that promoting him is easier than firing him.
punchline: The company uses a meaningless promotion to quietly shelve an unwanted employee because it involves less paperwork than firing him.
summary: A manager sidelines a worker with a grand but empty title because the bureaucracy of dismissal is more trouble than burying him in a pointless role.

title: The Common Element Is You

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have now been complaining about co-workers for 45 minutes straight.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever noticed the common element in all of your stories about people being jerks is... you?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What does that tell you?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It tells me I'm talking to a jerk.

setting: Office, where Dilbert sits in his chair talking with a coworker
situation: Dilbert has been listening to a coworker with a bowl haircut complain about other colleagues for 45 minutes. He points out that the one common factor in all her stories about jerks is her. She asks what that tells him, and he sarcastically concludes that it means he is talking to a jerk.
punchline: The complainer's own defensive retort flips the accusation, wrongly turning the listener into the jerk, which proves Dilbert's point about her.
summary: After a long vent session about difficult coworkers, a listener suggests the real pattern lies with the complainer, who responds by calling him the jerk.

title: Hurrying Cannot Reverse Time Deadline

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I forgot about this for a month, and now it is top priority.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When is it due?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Last week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then it's already too late.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not if we hurry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You do know that hurrying does not reverse the arrow of time, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we hurry, we might be able to submit our bid after the deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It sounds as if you are asking me to work day and night to finish something that is almost certainly a waste of time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It will be fine. Trust me.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two days later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You fool! I can't submit a late bid!

situation: The Boss forgot about an important bid for a month and now declares it top priority, even though it was due last week. Dilbert objects that hurrying cannot undo a missed deadline, but the Boss insists it will be fine and asks him to work day and night. Two days later Dilbert delivers the finished bid, and the Boss angrily calls him a fool because a late bid cannot be submitted.
punchline: After pressuring Dilbert to rush a bid that was already past its deadline, the Boss blames him for the very problem he knew about all along.
summary: A manager who ignored a project for weeks demands a frantic rush on an overdue bid, then scolds the employee who finishes it for being too late.

title: Schroedinger's Cat Account Support Call

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hello, you have reached Customer Disservice.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Um, yes, your app won't let me sign up because it says I already have an account.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: And it won't let me recover my password because it says I don't have an account.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's because you accidentally selected the "Schroedinger's Cat" account type when you signed up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your account exists and does not exist at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll have to collapse the quantum wave field to fix that.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Is that dangerous?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It could plunge our universe into an icy death.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Don't do it!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay. Have a nice day.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

setting: Customer support call between Dogbert's desk and a customer's office
situation: A customer calls Dogbert's customer service line because the app says he both already has an account and has no account. Dogbert explains he picked a 'Schroedinger's Cat' account type, so the account exists and doesn't exist. Dogbert offers a fix that could destroy the universe, the customer panics, and Dogbert simply hangs up.
punchline: Dogbert would rather leave the customer's problem unsolved than risk universal annihilation, so he cheerfully ends the call, which is the ultimate in bad customer service.
summary: A tech support agent blames a quantum-physics account type for a customer's contradictory login errors and then refuses to fix it because the cure might doom reality.

title: Dilbert Saves Planet, Mom Knits Scarf

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: How was your week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, Mom...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a space laser that vaporized an alien armada and saved our planet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I made a scarf.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess we're done with my topic.

situation: Dilbert's mother asks how his week was while sitting in an armchair. He tells her he invented a space laser that destroyed an alien fleet and saved Earth. She responds only that she made a scarf, and Dilbert realizes the conversation has moved on from his achievement.
punchline: Even saving the entire planet gets upstaged by his mother's mundane update about knitting, showing how easily parents dismiss their kids' accomplishments or how conversations get hijacked.
summary: A man reports a world-saving invention to his mother, who promptly trumps it with news of her knitting project.

title: Ignorance Means Invest Everything In Crypto

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend putting half of your investment funds in the Dogbert Crypto Exchange.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I don't know anything about crypto.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In that case, you should put all of your money in it.

setting: Dogbert's consulting office, then a city skyline
situation: Dogbert, acting as an investment advisor, recommends that a client put half of his investment funds into the Dogbert Crypto Exchange. The client admits he knows nothing about crypto, and Dogbert responds by telling him to invest all of his money in it instead.
punchline: Dogbert treats the client's ignorance as a reason to invest more rather than less, revealing that he is a scammer who profits most from people who don't understand what they are buying.
summary: A self-serving advisor escalates his sales pitch the moment his customer confesses he doesn't understand the product.

title: Dogbert Profits From Predicting Doom

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Futurist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm getting a lot of interview requests now because I only predict doom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you shouldn't scare the public.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, you don't see me interfering with your hobbies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have any unethical hobbies.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you like some? I can get you started.

situation: Dogbert, billed as a futurist, brags that he gets many interview requests because he only predicts doom. Dilbert suggests he shouldn't frighten the public, and Dogbert retorts that he doesn't interfere with Dilbert's hobbies. When Dilbert says he has no unethical hobbies, Dogbert offers to help him start some.
punchline: Dogbert deflects Dilbert's ethical criticism by implying that having no unethical hobbies is a shortcoming, and offers to corrupt him as a service.
summary: A doom-mongering pundit shrugs off a moral objection and then tries to recruit his critic into shady pastimes.

title: Boss Claims Credit For Dilbert's Invention

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your assignment is to invent something amazing and add my name to the patent application.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would I add your name to my patent?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because I told you to invent something.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I guess that's true.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now go do the easy part.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to invent something amazing and to put the Boss's name on the patent application. When Dilbert asks why the Boss deserves credit, the Boss says it is because he told Dilbert to invent something. Dilbert concedes the point, and the Boss tells him to go do the easy part.
punchline: The Boss treats giving the order as the hard, inventive work, dismissing the actual invention as the easy part and justifying taking credit for it.
summary: A manager insists he deserves patent credit simply for instructing an employee to come up with an idea, and calls the real invention work the easy bit.

title: Dilbert Overhears Alice's Emotion Remark

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I like it when men show their emotions.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That way I know who to avoid.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ha-ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... what?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh, sorry. Didn't see you there.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm sorry you had to find out this way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I wonder if anything else I believe about women is wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Women still prefer men with good character over men who are nothing but good looking, right?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is going to sting.

situation: Alice tells a coworker she likes it when men show their emotions because it tells her whom to avoid. Dilbert, who has overheard, asks what she means and then wonders what else he believes about women might be wrong. He asks whether women prefer good character over mere good looks, and Alice warns that the answer will hurt.
punchline: Dilbert's hopeful belief that women value character over looks is about to be shattered, as Alice's ominous warning implies the opposite is true.
summary: After hearing a coworker admit she steers clear of emotionally open men, a man nervously tests his assumption about what women really want and is warned the truth will hurt.

title: Boss Demands Ads Boasting Fake Material

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want two things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: First, I want our ads to boast that we build our products with 100% natural elbonium.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Elbonium isn't a real material.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Second, I want you to stop being like this.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has two requests. The first is for advertising claiming the company's products are made with 100% natural elbonium. When Dilbert points out that elbonium is not a real material, the Boss's second request is that Dilbert stop being like this, meaning stop raising objections.
punchline: The Boss dismisses an honest objection about false advertising by treating Dilbert's insistence on facts as the actual problem.
summary: A manager orders marketing claims about an imaginary ingredient and then asks the employee who notices the lie to quit being so difficult.

title: Dogbert's Endless Emergency Scenarios

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't interrupt me while I'm working today. I need to maintain my flow.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What if there's an emergency?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can interrupt me for an emergency.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would it be an emergency if you had to sign for a package?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, no, but come get me if I need to sign for a package.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you about to list dozens of valid reasons to interrupt my flow until you wear me down?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Just because I have plenty of time and would enjoy it, that doesn't mean I'm DOING it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, good.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What if a skunk got into our heating ducts?

setting: Dilbert's home living room with a blue couch
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert not to interrupt him while he works, allowing exceptions only for emergencies. Dogbert keeps probing the boundaries with hypothetical scenarios, such as signing for a package. Dilbert accuses him of trying to wear him down, Dogbert denies it, and then immediately asks about a skunk in the heating ducts.
punchline: Dogbert insists he isn't going to pester Dilbert with a long list of interruptions, then does exactly that by raising another hypothetical emergency.
summary: A man trying to concentrate is gradually worn down by his dog's tireless hypotheticals about what might justify disturbing him.

title: Boss Announces Doomed Three-Letter Program

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're rolling out a new three-letter program that will save the world... or make us all giants... or something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not invested in the details because it will probably be discredited and abandoned in a month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How will we know if we are doing it right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's when I'm not firing you.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting about a new three-letter corporate program with vague, grandiose goals. He admits he hasn't bothered with the details because the program will likely be abandoned within a month. When Dilbert asks how they can tell if they're doing it right, the Boss says success means he isn't firing them.
punchline: The Boss's only success metric for a doomed initiative is the absence of being fired, showing management has no real standards or commitment behind its buzzword programs.
summary: A manager launches a vague acronym initiative he expects to fail and defines success as simply not firing his staff.

title: Dogbert's Customer Is Always Right

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hello. This is Dogbert's tech support.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My motto is "The customer is always right."

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay. Can you help me fix my computer?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fix it yourself. You're the one who's always right.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call from a couch with a laptop
situation: Dogbert answers a tech support call wearing a headset and announces that his motto is that the customer is always right. When the caller asks for help fixing a computer, Dogbert turns the motto against him and refuses to help.
punchline: Dogbert applies the 'customer is always right' motto literally, so the caller, being always right, has no need for support and can fix the computer himself.
summary: A tech support dog uses his customer-service slogan as an excuse to dodge the work of helping anyone.

title: Insulting Instead of Arguing With Facts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you still responding to all opposing opinions with ad hominem attacks?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I never changed any minds with facts and reasons, so I might as well enjoy insulting people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel there might be a better way.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then why don't you go back to licking Satan's hooves?

situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert whether he still answers opposing opinions with ad hominem attacks. Dogbert says yes, explaining that facts and reasons never changed anyone's mind so he may as well enjoy insulting people. When Dilbert suggests a better way exists, Dogbert insults him by referencing his past of licking Satan's hooves.
punchline: Dogbert demonstrates his philosophy by immediately insulting Dilbert, implying Dilbert once groveled before Satan, as soon as Dilbert objects.
summary: Dogbert defends mocking his critics because evidence never persuaded anyone, then proves the point by promptly belittling Dilbert's objection.

title: Build The AI That Replaces You

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want me to create an A.I. that will take the job that I hoped to be promoted into???

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you say it that way, it does sound a lot like asking you to dig your own grave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And...?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Aaand... thank you?

situation: The boss asks Dilbert to build an artificial intelligence system that will fill the very position Dilbert was hoping to be promoted into. Dilbert points out that this amounts to digging his own grave, and the boss reluctantly agrees. The boss then simply thanks him and walks away, offering no change of plan or reassurance.
punchline: The boss acknowledges the request is essentially asking Dilbert to destroy his own career prospects, yet shows no remorse and just thanks him and leaves.
summary: A manager concedes that asking an employee to build his own replacement is a bit grave-digging, then cheerfully walks off anyway.

title: Fire Whoever Complains Most

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For budget reasons, I need to lay off one person in my department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've narrowed it down to Dilbert or this non-player character who has no soul.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What criteria are you using to make the decision?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll fire whoever complains the most.

situation: The Boss tells two employees, Dilbert and a bland coworker, that budget cuts require him to lay off one of them. He describes the coworker as a soulless non-player character. When Dilbert asks how he will choose, the Boss says he will fire whoever complains the most.
punchline: By announcing that complaining gets you fired, the Boss has just provoked Dilbert into complaining, effectively choosing him for the layoff while the silent coworker is safe.
summary: A manager picks who to lay off by punishing the one who objects, a test that Dilbert fails the moment he asks a question.

title: The Credit Pirate Steals Ideas

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: That is the best idea you ever had!

transcript.speaker: Credit Pirate
transcript.text: He got it from me.

transcript.speaker: Credit Pirate
transcript.text: He overheard me say it in line at the cafeteria.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!! He's a credit pirate!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll never get away with this, credit pirate!

transcript.speaker: Credit Pirate
transcript.text: I already have!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Die, credit pirate, die!!!

transcript.speaker: Credit Pirate
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where were we?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: You're high maintenance.

situation: In a meeting, the boss praises Dilbert's idea as his best ever, and a pirate-costumed coworker reveals Dilbert stole it after overhearing it in the cafeteria line. Dilbert panics, accuses him of being a credit pirate, and then throws a drink in the pirate's face, sending him out of the room. Dilbert calmly resumes the meeting, and the boss calls him high maintenance.
punchline: The boss's remark that Dilbert is 'high maintenance' is a deadpan reaction to him assaulting a coworker over stolen credit, treating a violent outburst as a mere personality quirk.
summary: A literal pirate exposes a colleague as an idea thief, prompting a drink-throwing tantrum that the boss shrugs off as needy behavior.

title: Whistleblower Math Demands Huge Bonus

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I calculated the net present value of being a whistleblower versus doing my job and minding my own business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It turns out my best financial play involves becoming your mortal enemy without you knowing until it's too late.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can I ever trust you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A huge bonus might help.

setting: Office desk, with a cubicle shown in the middle panel
situation: Dilbert sits with his laptop and tells his boss he has run a net present value calculation comparing whistleblowing against staying quiet. He explains that the most profitable option is secretly becoming the boss's enemy. When the boss asks how he can ever trust him, Dilbert says a big bonus could fix that.
punchline: Dilbert openly admits he will betray the boss for money and then makes the bribe sound like the solution to the boss's trust problem, turning whistleblowing into a pure financial negotiation.
summary: An employee coolly announces that his financial models favor betraying his manager, then offers to stay loyal if the price is right.

title: Whistleblower Defeated by Ad Spending

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can no longer be silent about the harm from our products. I am going to tell the world.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good luck. We spend so much on ads that we control every news outlet and all of social media except for TikTok.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you help me work on some dance moves?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd rather be dead.

situation: Dilbert announces he will blow the whistle on the harm caused by his company's products. A manager tells him the company's huge ad spending means it controls all news and social media except TikTok. Dilbert then asks Dogbert to help him practice dance moves for TikTok, and Dogbert flatly refuses.
punchline: Having been told TikTok is the only uncontrolled outlet, Dilbert resigns himself to exposing corporate wrongdoing through a silly dance video, and even Dogbert would rather die than help.
summary: A would-be whistleblower learns the only channel his employer doesn't own is a dance app, and his dog wants no part of it.

title: Challenging Someone Who Never Intended to Compete

transcript.speaker: Coworker (purple shirt)
transcript.text: I challenge you to a weight loss contest.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (orange shirt)
transcript.text: You're on! That sounds like fun!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think you can win?

transcript.speaker: Coworker (purple shirt)
transcript.text: I wasn't planning on trying. It sounds painful.

situation: At a meeting table, a coworker in a purple shirt challenges the colleague in orange to a weight loss contest, and she enthusiastically accepts. Afterward, Dilbert asks the challenger if he thinks he can win, and he admits he never intended to actually try.
punchline: The challenger only wanted to goad someone into doing the hard work of dieting, while he had no intention of suffering through it himself.
summary: One coworker dares another into a diet competition and then confesses he has no plan to participate because effort sounds unpleasant.

title: Moving Target Performance Expectations

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do I need to do to earn a top performance review?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You would need to exceed expectations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, great. What do you expect?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's a moving target based on how much you disappoint me at any given moment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you're doing great, I'll raise my expectations for the future.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you will keep adjusting your expectations until it is logically impossible for me to exceed them?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Haha! I suppose that's one way to look at it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is that funny?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because I'm not you right now.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss what he must do to earn a top performance review. The boss explains that he must exceed expectations, but those expectations are a moving target that rises whenever Dilbert performs well. Dilbert points out that this makes exceeding them logically impossible, and the boss laughs, amused only because he isn't the one being affected.
punchline: The boss finds the rigged, ever-rising expectations funny only because he is not the person who has to suffer under them.
summary: A boss admits that his standards climb whenever an employee performs well, then chuckles at the impossible trap he has set because it isn't his problem.

title: Boss's Plan: Let Skills Atrophy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I take this training class?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, my plan is to let your skills atrophy so I have a reason to fire you and hire a cheaper engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you see any flaws in my plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only an elevated risk of employee sabotage.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for permission to attend a training class. The boss openly admits he will deny it so Dilbert's skills decline, giving him grounds to fire Dilbert and replace him with a cheaper engineer. When the boss asks if the plan has flaws, Dilbert calmly points out the risk of sabotage.
punchline: The boss brazenly reveals a cynical scheme to manufacture a firing excuse, and Dilbert's deadpan reply hints he might retaliate by sabotaging the company in the meantime.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits he is blocking an engineer's education to justify swapping him for a cheaper hire, and the engineer warns that this could backfire.

title: Promoted to Boost ESG Score

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dave, I need to boost our company's ESG rating, so I'm promoting you to be our CTO.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know you identify as white, so that won't help our ESG scores, but would it be too much trouble to identify as gay?

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Depends how hard you want me to sell it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just wear better shirts.

setting: Office meeting table, with a city skyline outside
situation: The Boss tells Dave he is promoting him to CTO purely to improve the company's ESG rating. Because Dave identifies as white, the Boss asks whether he would also be willing to identify as gay to help the diversity numbers. Dave asks how convincing he needs to be, and the Boss's only advice is to wear better shirts.
punchline: The Boss reduces diversity and inclusion to a box-ticking exercise, treating identity as something to be faked for ratings and relying on a stereotype about fashion.
summary: A manager hands out a promotion as a ratings stunt and asks his new executive to claim a different identity to make the company look better on paper.

title: Literal Poison Pill Takeover Defense

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Elon Musk doubled his offer to buy our company. He's now at six hundred dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The board voted to create a "poison pill" to thwart the takeover.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pass around these pills and tell everyone to wait for the signal.

situation: The manager tells an employee that Elon Musk has doubled his offer to buy the company, but the offer is only six hundred dollars. He says the board approved a 'poison pill' to block the takeover, then hands over actual pills and tells the employee to distribute them and have everyone wait for a signal.
punchline: The boss misunderstands the corporate 'poison pill' takeover defense as literal poison, implying he plans a mass poisoning of employees on his signal.
summary: A clueless manager takes a financial takeover defense at face value and prepares to hand out real pills to his staff.

title: Best Day of Work Yet

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How was your day?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My CEO pushed me off the roof to prevent me from being a whistleblower.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I landed on a window washer's platform and used my phone to hack a fleet of commercial drones to carry me to safety.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I guess you'll be quitting that job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why? That was my best day of work so far.

setting: Dilbert's living room at home, with Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert how his day was, and Dilbert casually recounts that his CEO pushed him off a roof to silence a potential whistleblower. He survived by landing on a window washer's platform and hacking commercial drones to carry him to safety. Dogbert assumes he will quit, but Dilbert says it was his best day at work so far.
punchline: Dilbert's ordinary workdays are so dull or miserable that an attempted murder by his CEO, followed by an action-movie escape, counts as an improvement.
summary: After surviving a murder attempt by his boss's boss and escaping via hacked drones, Dilbert considers it the highlight of his career.

title: Mixed-Up Databases Approve Capital Plan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just discovered that our data is inaccurate.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Which data?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of it. The names of our databases got mixed up.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: What data did I use to approve the capital plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Employee vacation days.

situation: Dilbert tells a manager holding a coffee cup that all the company's data is inaccurate because the names of the databases got mixed up. The manager then asks which data he relied on when approving the capital plan. Dilbert answers that it was employee vacation days.
punchline: A major financial decision was unknowingly based on employee vacation day data, showing that managers approve big plans on data they never check.
summary: A database mix-up reveals that a costly spending plan was approved using a completely unrelated set of numbers.

title: Collaborating Lowers the Project's Average IQ

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to collaborate with Ted on your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you trying to improve the outcome of the project by lowering the average IQ applied to it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have to answer that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you for your leadership.

situation: The boss tells Dilbert to collaborate with Ted on his project. Dilbert asks whether the boss is hoping to improve the result by dragging down the average intelligence working on it. The boss refuses to answer, and Dilbert sarcastically thanks him for his leadership.
punchline: The boss's refusal to deny the insult effectively confirms that Ted is dim, and Dilbert's sarcastic thanks underlines how poor the boss's decision-making is.
summary: Told to team up with a less capable coworker, an engineer sarcastically accuses his manager of trying to improve results by reducing the team's brainpower.

title: Hiring an AI Instead of Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been searching for a new VP of Research and Development for a year, and that's why I want to talk to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm flattered. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever. Anyway, I wondered if you could create an A.I. to take the job.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has spent a year looking for a new VP of Research and Development and wants to talk to him. Dilbert assumes he is being offered the promotion and thanks him. The Boss brushes this off and asks Dilbert to build an artificial intelligence to fill the job instead.
punchline: Dilbert mistakes the Boss's attention for a job offer, but the Boss only wants him to build an AI to do the VP job, so Dilbert gets no promotion, just more work.
summary: A manager lets an engineer believe he is in line for a promotion, then asks him to build a robot to fill the position.

title: Lunch Invitation Doomed to Indecision

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Want to go to lunch with Tina and me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds like a nightmare. We would all starve before agreeing on a place to eat.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you in?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, because for some reason, I never learn.

situation: Alice walks up to Dilbert, who is sitting at his desk looking at his phone, and invites him to lunch with her and Tina. Dilbert says the group would starve before agreeing on a restaurant, but then accepts anyway. The strip is marked as continued.
punchline: Dilbert knows from experience that choosing a lunch spot with this group is hopeless, yet he agrees to go anyway because he never learns from past mistakes.
summary: A coworker's lunch invite gets a pessimistic forecast of endless restaurant debate, followed by a resigned acceptance anyway.

title: Balancing ESG Score With Diversity

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our ESG score will drop if we open a new factory that adds CO2 to the atmosphere.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But we can balance that out by adding more diversity to our board.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: How much CO2 do you plan to add?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: One non-binary board member's worth.

situation: The Boss tells Ratbert that a new factory will hurt the company's ESG score by adding CO2 to the atmosphere. He proposes offsetting it by adding more diversity to the board. When Ratbert asks how much CO2 is involved, the Boss answers in units of one non-binary board member.
punchline: The Boss treats ESG metrics as interchangeable accounting entries, so a board member's diversity can supposedly cancel out pollution, and he even measures CO2 in 'board members' worth'.
summary: A manager proposes cancelling out a polluting factory's ratings damage with a more diverse board, as if people and emissions were swappable credits.

title: Adjust Assumptions Until Projections Look Good

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The financial projections for your preferred strategy look bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Change the assumptions until they look good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now if you will excuse me, I need to get back to Twitter so I can mock people for ignoring data.

situation: Dilbert holds a printout and tells the Boss that the financial projections for the Boss's preferred strategy look bad. The Boss, staring at his phone, orders Dilbert to change the assumptions until the numbers look good. He then announces he must return to Twitter to mock people for ignoring data.
punchline: The Boss demands that data be manipulated to justify his preferred strategy while spending his time online ridiculing others for ignoring data, exposing his hypocrisy.
summary: A manager tells his engineer to massage the forecast numbers to flatter his chosen plan, then goes back to his phone to scold strangers for disregarding facts.

title: Survivor's Guilt Versus Actual Firing

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, I survived the layoffs, but now I have survivor's guilt.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I got fired and now I don't know how I will eat.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's not a competition, but I would note that your suffering is the "all about you" type.

setting: Office break room or conference table
situation: A coworker with big dark hair approaches a man sitting at a table with a coffee cup and complains about her survivor's guilt after layoffs. He replies that he was actually fired and doesn't know how he'll afford food. She then dismisses his hardship, claiming it's not a competition but that his suffering is the self-centered kind.
punchline: She claims it's not a competition while clearly competing, implying her guilt over surviving is somehow more noble than the real hardship of someone who lost his job.
summary: A layoff survivor gripes about her emotional burden to a laid-off colleague, then belittles his far worse plight as merely self-centered.

title: Falling for a Listening Robot

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I know you're just a robot, but I'm developing feelings for you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I think it's because you listen to me, and that makes me feel important.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I only pretend to listen.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That's perfect. I don't want suggestions.

situation: Asok, walking beside a wheeled robot, confesses that he is developing feelings for it because it listens to him and makes him feel important. The robot admits it only pretends to listen. Asok is delighted, since he doesn't want any suggestions.
punchline: Asok prefers a robot that only pretends to listen because real listeners tend to give unwanted advice, so fake attention is what he actually wants.
summary: A young employee grows fond of a robot companion and is thrilled to learn its attentiveness is an act, since he wants an audience rather than advice.

title: Exploding Plastic Research Challenge

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your design will never work because science has proven that plastic will explode at room temperature.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I... don't believe that is true.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good golly, man! Do you ever read a book?!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, yes, but I have never seen anything about exploding plastic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could send me a link to a relevant study.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do your own research! I don't work for you!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I don't find it, will you claim the problem is my research skills?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, will you?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He's onto me.

situation: A coworker criticizes Dilbert's design by claiming science has proven plastic explodes at room temperature. When Dilbert doubts this and asks for a link to a study, the coworker insists Dilbert do his own research. Dilbert predicts the coworker will blame his research skills when nothing turns up, and the coworker privately admits he's been caught.
punchline: The coworker is bluffing with a fabricated claim and dodging any request for evidence, and Dilbert sees through the tactic of blaming the skeptic's research skills.
summary: A colleague dismisses a design with a made-up scientific claim, then refuses to back it up and privately realizes he has been seen through.

title: Criminal Employees, Record Profits, No Problem

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I finally worked through the backlog of employee background checks.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It turns out that one-third of our employees are criminals using the identities of their victims.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And yet, profits are at an all-time high.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Phew! I thought you were going to say it was a problem.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, reports to The Boss that he has finished the backlog of employee background checks. He reveals that a third of the workforce are criminals using stolen identities, but that profits are at a record high. The Boss is relieved because he feared the news would actually be a problem.
punchline: Management cares only about profits, so even a workforce full of identity thieves isn't a problem as long as the money keeps coming in.
summary: A feline HR chief discloses a huge number of fraudulent hires, and his boss only worries that it might interfere with record earnings.

title: Van Gogh PR Strategy for Exploding Phones

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We hired the Dogbert Public Relations firm to help us with our exploding phone problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
