transcript.text: We have two choices. We can either recall all of the phones, or we can convince people that having one ear is cool.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Recalls are expensive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, the Van Gogh strategy it is.

situation: The Boss explains that the company hired Dogbert's PR firm to handle its exploding phone problem. Dogbert offers two options: recall all the phones or convince the public that having one ear is cool. Citing the cost of recalls, the Boss chooses the second option.
punchline: Rather than fix a dangerous product, the company would rather spin the resulting injuries as a fashion statement, like Van Gogh's famously missing ear.
summary: A PR consultant offers a company the choice between an expensive product recall and making ear loss seem fashionable, and the cost-conscious management picks the latter.

title: Musk's Staffing Plan: Robots and Panther

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Elon Musk bought the company where I work, and now he's doing a deep dive to see how many employees we need.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: His preliminary estimate is five humans, seven thousand robots, and...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...one panther to kill the humans if they try to touch any of the robots.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Heh-heh, panther.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Old jokes are the best!

setting: Dilbert's desk or a table in an office
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that Elon Musk has bought the company and is studying how many employees are needed. He reads Musk's preliminary estimate from his phone: five humans, seven thousand robots, and a panther to kill any humans who try to touch the robots. Dogbert chuckles at the word 'panther', and a caption notes that old jokes are the best.
punchline: The staffing plan replaces nearly everyone with robots and adds a guard panther, a joke recycled from an old internet gag about a factory with one man and one dog, which the caption acknowledges as an old joke.
summary: A new billionaire owner plans a nearly fully automated workforce, with a predatory animal as the enforcement mechanism.

title: Startled Coworker Blames Dilbert's Sneaking

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: GAAA!!! Stop sneaking up on me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is my fault?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, because you sneak up on people.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green shirt
transcript.text: What are you guys talking about?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: GAAAA!!!

situation: Dilbert greets a coworker, who screams and accuses him of sneaking up on her. Dilbert protests that it isn't his fault, and she insists it is because he sneaks up on people. A third coworker then approaches and asks what they're discussing, startling her again.
punchline: The coworker blames Dilbert for sneaking up on people, yet she is so jumpy that anyone approaching startles her, as the third coworker unwittingly proves.
summary: A perpetually jumpy employee blames Dilbert for startling her, only to be frightened again by the next person who walks up.

title: Cheap Energy Meets Oil Reality

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented an energy source that is cheaper than fossil fuels!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you also invent a way to prevent the oil-producing countries from trying to kill us for competing with them?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Toss it in the trash.

situation: Dilbert proudly shows a coworker a small device he says is a new energy source cheaper than fossil fuels. The coworker, looking at his phone, asks whether Dilbert has also solved the problem of oil-producing countries retaliating against competitors. When Dilbert admits he hasn't, the coworker tells him to throw the invention away.
punchline: A breakthrough invention is dismissed as worthless because it threatens powerful oil interests who would supposedly respond violently, implying that cheap energy is impractical in the real world.
summary: A hopeful inventor's cheap clean power gadget is waved off by a cynical colleague who points out the dangerous geopolitical fallout of undercutting oil.

title: Never Check Your Crypto Balance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried to withdraw funds from the Dogbert crypto exchange, but I checked my balance and it shows zero.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that some kind of mistake?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, you should never check your balance at the Dogbert crypto exchange.

setting: Dilbert's home or office phone call with a customer support line
situation: Dilbert phones the Dogbert crypto exchange because his account balance reads zero when he tries to withdraw funds. He asks the support rep whether it's a mistake. Dogbert, wearing a headset as the support agent, replies that the mistake was checking the balance at all.
punchline: Dogbert admits the balance is really zero by blaming Dilbert for looking, implying the exchange has lost or stolen customers' money and that the only error is the customer noticing.
summary: A customer calls a crypto exchange about his vanished funds and the support agent insists the real blunder was peeking at the account.

title: New Year's Eve Streaming Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Happy New Year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like to stay up until ten o'clock and fail to find something we both want to watch on any streaming service?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is it?

situation: Dilbert greets Dogbert with a New Year's wish, then proposes a modest evening plan: staying up until ten o'clock and scrolling streaming services without finding anything they both want to watch. He justifies it as better than doing nothing, and Dogbert, sitting on the couch with a tablet, doubtfully asks if it really is.
punchline: Dilbert's pathetically low-key New Year's Eve plan is to fail at choosing something to stream, and Dogbert's 'Is it?' questions whether that is really any better than nothing.
summary: A dull stay-at-home New Year's Eve plan of fruitlessly browsing streaming options gets a skeptical response from Dogbert.

title: Seventh Covid Case This Year

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I tested positive for covid, so I'll be home for ten days.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds deeply suspicious because it's the seventh time this year you got covid.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is no time to start doubting science.

setting: Wally's living room, talking to The Boss by phone
situation: Wally phones in to say he tested positive for covid and will be home for ten days. The Boss, holding his own phone, grows suspicious because this is the seventh time Wally has supposedly caught covid this year. Wally, relaxed in an armchair, replies that this is no time to doubt science.
punchline: Wally turns his obviously dubious repeated sick leave into a shield by invoking trust in science, making any skepticism from the boss sound irresponsible.
summary: A habitually absent employee fends off his manager's doubts about yet another positive covid test by appealing to scientific authority.

title: CEO's Convenient Relationship Defense

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You have been accused of having a relationship with a subordinate.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: So what? It hasn't changed any of my decisions as a CEO.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Did you recently promote your admin assistant to senior vice president of engineering?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: She does good work!

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, confronts a bald CEO about an accusation that he is in a relationship with a subordinate. The CEO shrugs it off, claiming it hasn't influenced his decisions. Catbert then asks whether he just promoted his admin assistant to senior vice president of engineering, and the CEO defends it by saying she does good work.
punchline: The CEO insists the relationship hasn't affected his decisions while unwittingly admitting he promoted his admin assistant to a senior engineering role, which is exactly the favoritism he denies.
summary: A boss denies that an office romance has swayed him, right up until he is reminded of the absurd promotion he handed his assistant.

title: Sadist Assigned to Self-Checkout Design

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to your employee personality test, you're a sadist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to transfer you to our division that does user interface design for grocery store self-checkout systems.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You want a sadist to design a human interface?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Trust me, no one will notice.

situation: A manager reads the results of an employee personality test aloud and informs the employee that he is a sadist. He decides to transfer the employee to the division that designs user interfaces for grocery store self-checkout systems. The employee questions putting a sadist in charge of a human interface, and the manager reassures him that nobody will notice.
punchline: Self-checkout machines are already so frustrating to use that they might as well have been designed by a sadist, so no one would detect the difference.
summary: A manager reassigns a test-certified sadist to design checkout kiosks, confident customers are already used to torment.

title: Metaverse Cow Avatars Cause Climate Change

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Our retail space in the metaverse has been destroyed by climate change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How is that even remotely possible?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: It was a mistake to give the cow avatars realistic digestive systems.

situation: At a meeting, a coworker reports that the company's virtual retail space in the metaverse has been wiped out by climate change. Dilbert asks how that could possibly happen in a virtual world. The coworker explains that the virtual cow avatars were given realistic digestive systems, implying they produced virtual methane.
punchline: The metaverse's realistic simulation of cow flatulence caused simulated global warming that destroyed the virtual store, mocking the pointless over-realism of virtual worlds.
summary: A virtual storefront gets ruined by climate change because someone made digital cows too anatomically faithful.

title: Boss Trusts Twitter Over Doctor

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got a bad case of long Covid. I need to take some time off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do I know you really have long Covid?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a note from my doctor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nice try, but I only trust medical information from Twitter gadflies.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has long Covid and needs time off. The boss questions whether he's really sick, and Dilbert offers a note from his doctor. The boss reads the note and rejects it, saying he only trusts medical information from Twitter gadflies.
punchline: The boss dismisses a legitimate doctor's note in favor of unqualified social media commenters, mocking people who trust random online voices over medical professionals.
summary: A worker's sick-leave request backed by a physician's note is waved away by a manager who prefers health advice from self-appointed internet pundits.

title: AI Writes Nonsense Status Report

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I outsourced 90% of my job to an open source AI.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ping!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's done writing my random jargon status report. No one will be the wiser.

transcript.speaker: Report
transcript.text: "The bitflange subvercates the error locus and creates a Higgs mirror effect."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sounds right.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee cup, tells a coworker that he has outsourced most of his job to an open source AI. His phone pings with the AI-generated status report, which he assures her nobody will question. The Boss reads the report, which is complete technical gibberish, and thinks it sounds right.
punchline: The boss is so clueless that he accepts a meaningless, AI-generated string of buzzwords as a legitimate status report, proving Wally's laziness will go undetected.
summary: A lazy employee lets an AI churn out his status updates, and his baffled manager happily accepts the gibberish as credible.

title: Identifying as White to Prank Boss

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is it true you identify as white just to prank our boss on his diversity goals?

transcript.speaker: Coworker with goatee
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's too soon to say I love you, but things are heading in that direction.

setting: Office, coworkers standing with coffee cups
situation: Two coworkers stand holding coffee cups. One asks the other whether he claims to identify as white just to mess with their boss's diversity goals. The man answers a deadpan 'Maybe,' and the questioner responds that he is not ready to say 'I love you' but things are heading that way.
punchline: The questioner is so delighted by the idea of trolling the boss's diversity metrics that he declares he is almost in love with his coworker.
summary: A worker is thrilled to hear a colleague might be gaming the company's diversity targets as a prank on their boss.

title: Deadly Pill Presentation Impresses Boss

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: The clinical trial data says our new pill makes people grow antlers and drop dead.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Urk!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That might be the most persuasive presentation I've ever seen.

situation: A colleague presents clinical trial data to the Boss, stating that the company's new pill causes people to grow antlers and die. As he speaks he sprouts antlers himself and collapses, apparently dead. The Boss, holding a coffee cup, sips it and comments on how persuasive the presentation was.
punchline: The presenter's literal demonstration of the pill's lethal side effect makes the presentation persuasive, and the Boss reacts only with detached admiration rather than concern for the dead employee or the dangerous drug.
summary: A presenter's live demo of his company's lethal drug proves so convincing that his boss admires the performance instead of worrying about the death.

title: Entry-Level Job Requires Experience

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're looking for a candidate with 3 to 5 years of experience.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: If I had that much experience, I doubt I would be applying for an entry-level job at this monkey-taint of a company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll fit right in. When can you start?

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss tells a job candidate that the company wants someone with 3 to 5 years of experience for an entry-level job. The candidate points out that someone with that experience wouldn't apply to such a lousy company. The Boss takes the insult as a sign the candidate is a good cultural fit and offers him the job.
punchline: The candidate's blunt insult of the company proves he understands the place, so the oblivious Boss hires him on the spot.
summary: A job seeker mocks the absurd experience demands and the company itself, and the interviewer happily hires him for it.

title: Late Notice Right On Time

transcript.speaker: Phone caller
transcript.text: I'll be thirty minutes late.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You waited until the agreed time to tell me you would not be here at the agreed time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you hate me or just not care about me?

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: I try to find a balance.

setting: An empty conference room, with Dilbert on the phone
situation: Dilbert sits alone in a conference room holding a phone and receives a call from a colleague saying he will be thirty minutes late to the meeting. Dilbert points out that the colleague waited until the meeting start time to say so, then asks whether the colleague hates him or just doesn't care. The colleague replies that he tries to find a balance.
punchline: The late colleague's answer implies he both dislikes Dilbert and doesn't care about him, and he deliberately splits the difference between the two.
summary: A colleague phones in at the very moment a meeting is due to start to announce he'll be half an hour late, and when challenged about whether he hates or ignores Dilbert, he claims to split the difference.

title: Godlike Powers Used for Volcano

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You didn't believe me when I said I hacked reality and acquired godlike powers.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: So I will demonstrate my powers by making a long-dormant volcano erupt in Elbonia's biggest city.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Couldn't you use your powers to do something good instead?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Too late. This is on you.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch looking at his phone while Ratbert claims to have hacked reality and gained godlike powers. To prove it, Ratbert announces he will make a dormant volcano erupt in Elbonia's biggest city. When Dilbert asks why he doesn't use his powers for good, Ratbert says it's too late and blames Dilbert.
punchline: Ratbert blames Dilbert for the disaster because Dilbert doubted him, shifting responsibility for his own destructive choice onto the skeptic.
summary: A tiny rodent with newfound godlike abilities erupts a volcano to prove himself, then pins the catastrophe on the human who questioned him.

title: Management Hosts Pizza, Employees Pay

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The bad news is that you won't be getting raises this year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The good news is that management is hosting a pizza party after work!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All we need is a volunteer to pay for the pizza.

situation: The Boss addresses employees, including Wally and Dilbert, and announces that there will be no raises this year. He then cheerfully offers a 'good news' pizza party hosted by management. He finishes by asking for a volunteer to pay for it.
punchline: The supposedly management-hosted consolation party turns out to be funded by the employees themselves, making the 'good news' just another cost to staff after being denied raises.
summary: After denying everyone a pay increase, a manager touts a free pizza party and then asks one of the underpaid workers to cover the bill.

title: Robots Hide Management Incompetence

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: A big advantage of robots is that no matter how poorly you manage us, we never have low morale.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: That's just one of the ways we run cover for the massive incompetence of your kind.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My kind invented you!

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm guessing you were not in the room when that happened.

situation: A robot employee tells its human boss that robots never suffer low morale however badly they are managed. It adds that robots also cover for the huge incompetence of humans. The angry boss protests that humans invented robots, and the robot replies that the boss surely wasn't involved in that.
punchline: The robot implies the boss is so incompetent that he could not have contributed to inventing robots, so he can't take credit for his species' achievements.
summary: A smug robot subordinate belittles its pointy-haired manager, who tries to claim credit for humanity's invention of robots and gets shot down.

title: Worst Case Presentation Nerves Spiral

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How can I calm my nerves about my presentation tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ask yourself what's the worst thing that can happen.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I could embarrass myself so badly that I become a serial killer and have to hide in the forest until wild pigs eat me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now don't you feel better?

setting: Office desk or break room table
situation: Asok asks a coworker how to calm his nerves about a presentation the next day. The coworker advises him to imagine the worst outcome, and Asok escalates it to absurd extremes involving becoming a serial killer and being eaten by wild pigs. The coworker then cheerfully asks if he feels better.
punchline: The coworker's calming technique backfires and makes things worse, yet he sincerely asks if Asok feels better, ignoring the grim absurdity of the imagined outcome.
summary: A worried employee follows advice to imagine the worst-case scenario and spirals into a macabre fantasy that hardly soothes him.

title: Orphan Fertilizer: Wait and See

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're getting pressure to stop doing business with Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Critics say they make fertilizer out of orphans. There are hundreds of videos of it happening.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But the Elbonian government denies it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sounds like a "wait and see" situation.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the company is under pressure to stop doing business with Elbonia because of allegations that the country turns orphans into fertilizer. He notes there are hundreds of videos, but the Elbonian government denies it. The Boss, looking at his phone, calmly suggests waiting to see what happens.
punchline: The Boss treats overwhelming video evidence of an atrocity as an open question, using corporate fence-sitting to avoid giving up a profitable business partner.
summary: A manager responds to horrifying allegations against a business partner by choosing to do nothing and see how things develop.

title: Boss Takes Credit For Cubicles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This article says the benefits of the "open office" floor plan have been totally debunked.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Luckily for all of you, I had the vision of keeping you in tiny cubicles instead of chasing fads.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would it kill you to say, "Thank you"?

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss reads from his phone that open office floor plans have been debunked. He then claims that his foresight in keeping everyone in tiny cubicles saved them from a fad. He finishes by demanding that the staff thank him, while Alice and Dilbert look on unimpressed.
punchline: The Boss presents the company's outdated, cramped cubicles as visionary leadership and expects gratitude for what was really just inertia or neglect.
summary: A manager reads that open offices don't work and takes credit for having kept his staff boxed in cubicles, then wants applause for it.

title: Wally Explains Away Project Failures

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, our new human resources A.I. has found a disturbing pattern.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: One hundred percent of the projects that included you as a team member failed.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Let's see you explain that away.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Challenge accepted.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For starters, eighty percent of our projects fail no matter who is on the team.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The remaining twenty percent can be explained by my boss's lack of faith in me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He believes I am likely to fail, so he assigns me to projects that are already doomed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And thus it can be shown that poor management created the misleading pattern your A.I. detected.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: To be honest, that was better than I expected.

setting: Catbert's office in the human resources department
situation: Catbert, the HR director, confronts Wally with an HR A.I. finding that every project Wally joined has failed. Wally calmly rebuts it by noting that most projects fail anyway and that his boss only assigns him to doomed ones, concluding that bad management created the pattern. Catbert admits the defense was better than he expected.
punchline: Wally, famous for doing nothing, delivers a surprisingly sharp and plausible defense that blames management, and even the evil HR director is grudgingly impressed.
summary: Faced with data blaming him for every failed project, lazy Wally produces a surprisingly clever argument that management is the real culprit.

title: Flattering a Storytelling Coworker Endlessly

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I can't get enough of your stories.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Especially the ones I've already heard.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Your terrific stories need to be repeated so their wisdom sinks in.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: If you think about it, that's no different than how we learn anything else.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I love the fact that all of your stories have the same point: You're awesome.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: And that's a lesson that has helped me grow as a person and as a professional.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I don't know how I can ever repay you for that gift.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Is he serious? I can't tell.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one knows.

situation: A coworker sitting at a conference table lavishes increasingly over-the-top praise on a storyteller, claiming he loves hearing the same stories repeatedly. His compliments escalate until he thanks the speaker for the gift of constant self-congratulation. Phil and Dilbert watch, unable to tell whether he is being sincere or sarcastic.
punchline: The praise is so deadpan and exaggerated that no one can tell if it is genuine flattery or biting sarcasm about a self-absorbed storyteller whose every story just says he's awesome.
summary: A deadpan colleague gushes about a self-promoting storyteller's repetitive tales so convincingly that his co-workers can't tell whether he's sincere or mocking.

title: Non-Player Character Talks Weather

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you think the government should do about inflation?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm a non-player character. I can only complain about my job and comment on the weather.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay then, how's your job?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Partly cloudy.

setting: Office, with Dilbert and a coworker sitting at desks
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker for his opinion on what the government should do about inflation. The coworker explains that he is a non-player character who can only complain about his job and talk about the weather. Dilbert asks how his job is going, and the coworker answers with a weather report.
punchline: The coworker takes his scripted limits so literally that he mixes up the two permitted topics, answering a question about his job with the weather, like a video-game NPC glitching.
summary: A coworker who claims to be a video-game background character can only discuss work grumbles and weather, and promptly gets the two confused.

title: Big Pharma Strategy Inspired by Bank Robber

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've decided to become a big pharma company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As business expert Willie Sutton once advised, "Because that's where the money is."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He was talking about bank robbery.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's your point?

situation: The Boss announces the company will become a big pharma company and justifies it by quoting Willie Sutton, calling him a business expert. Dilbert, working on his laptop, points out that Sutton was actually talking about bank robbery. The Boss doesn't see why that matters.
punchline: The Boss's unfazed 'What's your point?' implies that he sees nothing wrong with taking business strategy advice from a bank robber, or that profiting from pharmaceuticals is morally comparable to robbery.
summary: A manager cites a famous criminal's quote as sound business wisdom for entering the drug industry, and shrugs off the correction that it was about stealing from banks.

title: Success Is Genetic, Willpower Imaginary

transcript.speaker: Coworker with hair buns
transcript.text: The keys to success are passion and hard work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Those traits are probably genetic.

transcript.speaker: Coworker with hair buns
transcript.text: All it takes is willpower.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Willpower is imaginary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your move.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Three coworkers sit at a meeting table with coffee cups. One coworker declares that passion and hard work are the keys to success, and Dilbert counters that those traits are probably genetic. When she insists it only takes willpower, Dilbert says willpower is imaginary and challenges her to respond.
punchline: Dilbert dismantles motivational platitudes by arguing that even willpower and work ethic are just genetic luck, leaving no room for a rebuttal.
summary: A colleague's self-help advice about success gets systematically undercut by Dilbert's deterministic skepticism.

title: Firing Departments to Impress Musk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our sales are up 23% since Elon Musk bought our company and fired the entire marketing department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That worked so well, I plan to fire the engineering department to impress him.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Are you doing anything to impress him?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I plan to fire you. I think he'd like that.

situation: The Boss brags to a coworker that sales rose 23% after Elon Musk bought the company and fired the marketing department. He then announces he will fire the engineering department to impress Musk. The coworker asks if he is doing anything else to impress him, and the Boss says he plans to fire the coworker.
punchline: The Boss's eagerness to impress a new owner by firing people shows he draws a bad lesson from correlation, and he casually threatens the very employee he is talking to.
summary: After a new billionaire owner axes a department, a boss decides mass layoffs are the way to win the owner's approval, starting with the person he is speaking to.

title: Demon Would Insist On Cake

transcript.speaker: Coworker (orange shirt)
transcript.text: When I had a heart attack, I was technically dead for three minutes before doctors revived me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do I know you're really you and not a demon who used a soulless carcass to hitch a ride to the mortal plane?

transcript.speaker: Coworker (orange shirt)
transcript.text: Would a demon let you have birthday cake in the break room?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think a demon would insist on it.

situation: Three coworkers stand around holding coffee cups while one mentions he was technically dead for three minutes during a heart attack. Dilbert suspects he might now be a demon inhabiting the revived body and asks how anyone could know otherwise. The coworker offers birthday cake in the break room as proof of being human, but Dilbert says a demon would insist on it.
punchline: The coworker's proof of humanity, birthday cake in the break room, is exactly what a demon would push for, since office cake events are portrayed as something people dread and a demon would enthusiastically enforce.
summary: A man who briefly died is accused by a skeptical colleague of being a possessed corpse, and his cake-based defense backfires.

title: Neural Chip Forces Government Praise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, please demonstrate what you can do with our new neural chip in your brain.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: The government always tells the truth!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try doing that without a neural implant. You can't do it.

situation: The boss asks Asok to show off what the company's new neural chip in his brain can do. Asok suddenly blurts out, wide-eyed, that the government always tells the truth. The boss then smugly points out that nobody could say that without a brain implant.
punchline: The only demonstration of the implant's power is making Asok sincerely claim the government always tells the truth, which is so implausible that only mind control could cause it.
summary: A brain implant's showcase feature turns out to be compelling a coworker to praise government honesty, a belief only possible through mind control.

title: Modeling the AI After Lazy Wally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our CEO ordered me to create an A.I. that will replace me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My plan is to model the A.I. after you, so no one wants it.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Let's drink coffee and pretend to work.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Kill it.

setting: Office coffee station and a meeting room
situation: Dilbert tells Wally by the coffee maker that the CEO wants him to build an AI that will replace him. He plans to model the AI on Wally so nobody will want it. In the last panel the AI, a smart speaker on a conference table, proposes drinking coffee and pretending to work, and the CEO orders it killed.
punchline: Dilbert's scheme to sabotage his own replacement works perfectly, because an AI patterned on lazy Wally behaves so uselessly that the CEO scraps it immediately.
summary: An engineer ordered to build his own robotic replacement copies a notoriously slacking coworker so the project gets cancelled.

title: Quiet Quitting Fixed By No Working

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Consulting Company has fixed your quiet-quitting epidemic.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: All it took was a tweak to their work-life balance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much of a tweak?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No more working.

setting: Boss's office, with Dogbert standing on a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the pointy-haired boss that his firm has solved the company's quiet-quitting problem by adjusting employees' work-life balance. The boss asks how big the adjustment was, and Dogbert reveals that employees simply no longer work at all.
punchline: The consultant's 'solution' to employees disengaging from work is to eliminate work entirely, which technically ends quiet quitting but makes the company useless.
summary: A consultant dog claims to have cured disengaged staff by tweaking their balance between job and personal life, with the tweak being that the job is gone.

title: Long Covid Support Group Demands Naps

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm forming a long covid support group to fight against motivated privilege.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We will be demanding naps instead of goals and reparations from the healthy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How will I know who has long covid?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Look for nappers.

characters: Bald coworker with glasses and green sweater
situation: A bald coworker holding a coffee cup announces to Alice that he is forming a long covid support group to fight 'motivated privilege.' He says the group will demand naps instead of goals, plus reparations from healthy people. Alice asks how she'll recognize who has long covid, and he tells her to look for nappers.
punchline: The coworker's criteria for long covid is simply being someone who naps, implying the 'support group' is really an excuse for lazy employees to avoid work.
summary: A sleepy-minded coworker launches a self-serving advocacy group that conveniently identifies its members by their habit of napping on the job.

title: Wokeness Score Reported by Better People

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Your job performance is excellent, but your wokeness score has me concerned.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I have several reports of you using pronouns without even asking if they are the right ones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who reported me for that?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: People who are better than you.

setting: Office hallway or break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: A manager tells Dilbert that although his job performance is excellent, his 'wokeness score' is a concern because colleagues reported him for using pronouns without asking if they were the right ones. Dilbert asks who reported him, and the manager replies that it was people who are better than him.
punchline: The manager dismisses Dilbert's question by asserting that the accusers are morally superior, showing how wokeness evaluations can trump actual job performance and be used to judge people's worth.
summary: A boss admits an employee does great work but then criticizes him over a social-awareness rating, with the accusers described as simply being his moral betters.

title: Financial Advisor Dodges Awkward Question

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Financial Advisor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend putting all of your money in a managed stock fund.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Is that where you put your own money?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can't work with you if you insist on asking questions.

setting: Dogbert's financial advisor office, across a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a financial advisor, recommends that his client put all his money into a managed stock fund. The client asks whether Dogbert invests his own money that way. Dogbert avoids answering and says he cannot work with clients who ask questions.
punchline: By refusing to answer, Dogbert implies he does not invest his own money in the funds he recommends, and he deflects by blaming the client for asking.
summary: A skeptical client probes his advisor's own investing habits, and the advisor responds by ending the conversation rather than answering.

title: Impossible Packaging Return Call Survey

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can return it in the original box.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It almost seems as if you designed the packaging to make it impossible to cram everything back in the box.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I won't be asking you to take a brief survey at the end of this call.

setting: A customer support call, with Dogbert at a desk wearing a headset and a customer at home holding a phone beside a box of stuffed-in product
situation: Dogbert, working as a customer service rep with a headset, tells a customer she can return a product in its original box. The customer sarcastically points out that the packaging seems designed so that nothing can be crammed back in. Dogbert responds that he won't be asking her to take a survey, a sign he's sweating the likely bad feedback.
punchline: Dogbert's pointed promise not to ask for a satisfaction survey is an implicit admission that the company knows its service and packaging are bad and wants to avoid hearing her complaints.
summary: A support agent dodges a customer's complaint about unrepackable packaging by assuring her no feedback survey is coming.

title: Boss Lectures Wally About Assignments

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've noticed a disturbing pattern in the assignments I give you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You always say you will take care of something, but then you don't.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then, when I question you about it, you say you really will take care of it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But then you don't.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I'm here to tell you it isn't optional to do assignments.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You must do what I tell you to do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're right.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I will totally take care of that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why doesn't this feel like a win?

setting: Conference room / office, ending with the Boss walking in a hallway
situation: The Boss confronts Wally about his habit of promising to complete assignments and then never doing them. He sternly tells Wally that doing assignments is not optional, and Wally cheerfully agrees and promises to take care of it. The Boss walks away wondering why the conversation doesn't feel like a victory.
punchline: Wally's agreeable promise is exactly the same empty promise he always makes, so the Boss has achieved nothing and subconsciously knows it.
summary: A manager lectures a chronically unproductive employee, receives the same hollow reassurance as always, and leaves oddly unsatisfied.

title: Avoiding Her: Con Artist or Demon

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Why have you been avoiding me after I told you I'm attracted to smart men?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm just playing the odds. You're either running a con, or you are an empty husk of humanity possessed by a demon.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Maybe I just like smart men.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds like something a demon would say.

situation: A female coworker asks Dilbert why he has been avoiding her since she said she is attracted to smart men. Dilbert, looking at his phone, calmly explains that statistically she must be either a scammer or a demon-possessed husk. When she insists she simply likes smart men, he says that is exactly what a demon would say.
punchline: Dilbert's paranoid, unfalsifiable logic treats even a sincere compliment as proof of malice, since any denial is just what a demon would say.
summary: A woman who admires smart men is rebuffed by Dilbert, who is convinced her interest means she is a swindler or a possessed shell of a person.

title: Voting Machines That Count Twice

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our company is entering the electronic voting machine market.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you have any idea what this means?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it mean my vote won't count?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sometimes it will count twice!

situation: A coworker with swirled hair tells Dilbert, who is holding a coffee cup, that the company is entering the electronic voting machine market. He asks if Dilbert understands the implications. Dilbert guesses that his vote might not be counted, and the coworker cheerfully corrects him that sometimes votes will be counted twice.
punchline: The coworker treats double-counting of votes as a reassuring upside, when it is really just another way the company's voting machines will be unreliable.
summary: A cheerful colleague announces a move into voting technology and reassures Dilbert that the machines are sometimes generous rather than just faulty.

title: Four Hours Choosing a Lunch Spot

transcript.speaker: Narrator

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have now rejected thirty-five potential eateries.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think this is nature's way of telling us we are not worthy of survival.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think Tina agrees with you, but she is too weak to reply.

setting: Office, during a prolonged lunch-planning discussion
situation: Dilbert and Alice have spent four hours trying to decide where to eat lunch and have rejected thirty-five restaurants. Alice gloomily suggests their indecision is a sign they don't deserve to survive. Dilbert notes that Tina, standing apart in the background, probably agrees but is too weak from hunger to speak.
punchline: The group's endless indecision over lunch has dragged on so long that a colleague is physically too weak from hunger to talk, proving their inability to make a simple decision is a genuine survival risk.
summary: A team's marathon argument over where to have lunch leaves one coworker too famished to even respond.

title: Fake Job Was a TV Show

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I just learned my job was never real. I was being filmed for a show called "The Biggest Sucker."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you know and not tell me?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't think you understand how funny it was.

situation: A man in a yellow shirt announces that his job was never real and that he was secretly being filmed for a reality show called "The Biggest Sucker." He asks his bespectacled, green-shirted coworker whether he knew and kept it secret. The coworker, holding a coffee cup, doesn't deny it.
punchline: The coworker admits he knew and withheld the truth because watching the man be duped was too entertaining to spoil.
summary: A worker discovers his entire career was a hoax staged for a TV prank show, and the colleague who was in on it defends the joke as too funny to ruin.

title: Crypto Exchange Needs Celebrity Endorsements

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting a crypto exchange, so give me all of your money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do I look like a fool? I wouldn't trust you with my money unless you had celebrity endorsements!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If I had your money, I could get some.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That makes sense.

situation: Dogbert, standing on the Boss's desk, announces a crypto exchange and demands all of the Boss's money. The Boss indignantly refuses unless Dogbert has celebrity endorsements. Dogbert points out that he could buy endorsements with the Boss's money, and the Boss agrees that this is logical.
punchline: The Boss demands celebrity endorsements as proof of trustworthiness, not realizing they can simply be bought with the money he is being asked to hand over, mirroring how crypto scams used paid celebrity promotions.
summary: A scheming dog talks his gullible manager into funding the very celebrity backing that is supposed to prove the scheme is legitimate.

title: The Boss's Brutally Honest Speech

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I often say employees are the key to our success.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But that's only so I can blame you when things go wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The truth is I could replace 99% of you, and we'd have the same outcomes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And what are the odds you're in the top 1% of contributors?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you left tomorrow, it would be a month before anyone noticed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've already forgotten most of your names.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To be honest, I think of you as scenery.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You were right about honesty being the best approach. I enjoyed it.

situation: The Boss addresses his employees in a meeting and, in a burst of unfiltered honesty, tells them they are interchangeable, replaceable, forgettable and just scenery. In the last panel he stands alone in front of a red creature on a desk, saying that someone was right about honesty being the best approach and that he enjoyed it.
punchline: The Boss took advice to be honest and discovered that insulting his entire staff is enjoyable, since his honest opinion is that employees are worthless.
summary: Following a tip to be candid, a manager gleefully tells his team they are disposable background figures.

title: Study Says All Studies Misleading

transcript.speaker: Computer voice
transcript.text: Breaking news: A new study says all studies are misleading.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Floop!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: His brain rotated in his skull. When the brain stem unwinds, he'll be fine.

situation: At a meeting, a coworker working on a laptop hears a news report claiming that a new study says all studies are misleading. His head spins and he flops over, apparently overwhelmed by the paradox. Dilbert calmly explains that his brain rotated in his skull and he will be fine once the brain stem unwinds.
punchline: The news story is a self-referential paradox (if all studies are misleading, so is this one), and it literally twists a listener's brain, which Dilbert treats as a routine, harmless medical event.
summary: A logical paradox in a news bulletin about unreliable research spins a man's head right around, and Dilbert casually reassures everyone it will untwist itself.

title: Boss Needs Dopamine From Bossing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do I need to be in the office when I can do my work at home?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you are home, I can't get my hit of dopamine from bossing you around.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go re-configure something.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss why he must come into the office when he could work from home. The boss candidly admits he needs Dilbert physically present so he can get a rush from ordering him around. He then promptly demonstrates by pointing and telling Dilbert to go reconfigure something.
punchline: The boss's real reason for requiring office attendance is not productivity but the personal pleasure he gets from bossing people around, and he gives a pointless order to prove it.
summary: A manager confesses that he wants his employee back in the building purely so he can enjoy ordering him around.

title: Dogbert Recommends the Deadly Pill

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My anxiety is through the roof! I don't know how to slow down my pulse!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try your new pill.

setting: A table in a break room or office
situation: Dilbert, visibly sweating and agitated, tells Dogbert that his company intends to market a drug that killed half the volunteers in its clinical trial. He then complains that his anxiety is so severe he cannot slow his pulse. Dogbert calmly suggests he take the company's new pill.
punchline: Dogbert darkly points out that the pill, which killed half its test subjects, would certainly slow down Dilbert's pulse, by killing him.
summary: A panicking engineer is advised by his dog to calm his racing heart with the lethal drug his employer is about to sell.

situation: A bearded coworker tells Dilbert to follow the experts, then keeps contradicting himself when Dilbert asks what to do when experts disagree. He ends up claiming that doing his own research makes him the one to ask, and Dilbert keeps poking holes in the logic.
punchline: The coworker's reasoning is circular, since he's right because he does his own research, so Dilbert sarcastically suggests he teach the experts how to do that.
summary: A confident coworker's advice about trusting experts collapses into the claim that only his own research can be trusted, and Dilbert dryly points out the flaw.
