situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that he ignores spreadsheets and decides project funding based on the project manager, then rejects Dilbert's project because his head shape reminds him of a failure. Dilbert realizes the cash flow analysis the Boss demanded was pointless, and the Boss admits it only gave him the illusion of managing. At home, Dilbert laments to Dogbert, who dismisses him.
punchline: The Boss rejects funding on an absurd, arbitrary basis and admits that the work he assigned only served to make him feel like he was managing, while Dogbert callously says no one cares about Dilbert's setback.
summary: A manager denies a project's budget because of an employee's skull shape and admits the requested analysis was just busywork for his own ego.

title: Dogbert's Cure for Quiet Quitting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Consulting Company can end the scourge of "quiet quitting" in your company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I use a variety of slogans and handouts and exercises.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds powerful.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I also offer creepy high energy.

setting: Office, with Dogbert standing on a desk in front of the Boss
situation: Dogbert pitches his consulting services to the Boss, promising to end the problem of employees "quiet quitting." He explains his method is a mix of slogans, handouts and exercises, then adds that he also provides creepy high energy as a bonus.
punchline: Dogbert's expensive consulting solution to employee disengagement is just generic motivational fluff delivered with unsettling enthusiasm.
summary: A scheming dog consultant sells a boss on a cure for disengaged workers that amounts to cheesy motivational materials and unnerving cheerfulness.

title: Bored or Anxious Phone Addiction

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have two choices in life. You can be bored or you can be anxious.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm never bored because I can just look at stuff on my phone.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does it make you feel anxious?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did you know that???!

setting: Office desk or table, with Dilbert holding a coffee cup
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert that life offers only two choices: boredom or anxiety. Dilbert claims he is never bored because he can look at his phone, so Dogbert asks whether the phone makes him anxious. Dilbert is startled and shaken that Dogbert guessed correctly.
punchline: Dilbert thinks he has escaped the boredom-or-anxiety choice by using his phone, but the phone just delivers the anxiety option, as Dogbert predicted.
summary: A smug dog's bleak life philosophy proves right when a man's phone cure for boredom turns out to be a source of nervous dread.

title: No Laptop, So Try Pantomime

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not allowed to use your personal computer for work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And your company laptop won't show up for another two weeks.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: So... what should I do all day?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you know what pantomime is?

situation: The Boss tells a new employee that he cannot use his personal computer for work and that his company laptop will not arrive for two weeks. When the employee asks what he is supposed to do all day, the Boss's only suggestion is to ask whether he knows what pantomime is.
punchline: With no equipment and no real work to give him, the Boss's only advice is to act out silent mime, which shows how useless the situation is.
summary: A newcomer with no permitted computer for two weeks is advised by his manager to pass the time by miming.

title: Convenient Data Center Fire Before Audit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now that Elon Musk has purchased our company, he wants to see all of our internal documents.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In unrelated news, our data center burned to the ground, and we lost all of our backups.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't sound like an accident.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If anyone asks, say it was Elbonian terror-ists..

situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting that the company's new owner wants to inspect all internal documents. He then announces, as if unrelated, that the data center burned down and all backups were lost. Dilbert points out it sounds deliberate, and the Boss instructs everyone to blame Elbonian terrorists.
punchline: The suspiciously timed data center fire and lost backups are an obvious cover-up to avoid scrutiny, and the Boss openly asks staff to blame a made-up scapegoat.
summary: Faced with an incoming inspection of company records, management conveniently announces a fire that destroyed everything and plans a fake explanation.

title: Birthday Chair Was Stolen Chair

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I got you a desk chair for your birthday.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wow! That's perfect timing because someone stole my chair this morning.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're welcome.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wait...

situation: Wally presents a coworker with a desk chair as a birthday gift. The coworker is delighted because his own chair was stolen that very morning. Wally calmly says 'You're welcome' and walks away, and the coworker begins to realize who the thief was.
punchline: Wally gave his coworker a chair as a gift, but it was the coworker's own stolen chair, so the 'perfect timing' was no coincidence.
summary: A thoughtful birthday present turns out to be the very thing the recipient was robbed of hours earlier.

title: PR Firm Dismisses Slave Labor Morality

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're getting a lot of heat from the media for using Elbonian slave labor to make our sneakers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I hired the Dogbert Public Relations firm to help us with our messaging.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Excuse me, is our messaging the problem here... or is it more about the slave part?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm fairly sure all footwear is made by slaves.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Really? You believe all footwear is made by slaves?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I assume so. Why would anyone use paid labor when they could just use slaves?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Morality?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're fired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I warned you about that.

situation: The Boss explains that the company is facing media criticism for using Elbonian slave labor to make sneakers, and has hired Dogbert's PR firm to fix the messaging. An employee asks whether the real problem is the slavery itself, and Dogbert cynically claims all footwear is made by slaves. When the employee suggests morality as a reason to use paid labor, Dogbert fires him.
punchline: Dogbert treats the idea of morality as such a ridiculous objection that raising it is a fireable offense, with the Boss adding that he had warned the employee about that.
summary: A public relations consultant brushes off ethical concerns about sweatshop sneakers and punishes the employee who dares to bring up conscience.

title: Marketing Is Full of Morons

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you check with Larry to see if marketing has any feedback?

transcript.speaker: Helmet-haired coworker
transcript.text: Larry is a moron.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, ask someone else in that department.

transcript.speaker: Helmet-haired coworker
transcript.text: They're idiots too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of them?

transcript.speaker: Helmet-haired coworker
transcript.text: Yes, that's how it works.

transcript.speaker: Helmet-haired coworker
transcript.text: Larry is a moron, and Larry works in marketing, so therefore, everyone in marketing is a moron.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you make the colossal mistake of watching the news and learning that each person in a group defines the entire group?

transcript.speaker: Helmet-haired coworker
transcript.text: Yes, and I have to say, it wasn't an intuitive idea.

transcript.speaker: Helmet-haired coworker
transcript.text: But I trust science, so it must be true.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're ruining things for all helmet-haired women.

setting: Office cubicle desk, ending with an exterior shot of the building
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker to get feedback from Larry in marketing, and she dismisses Larry and then everyone in marketing as morons. She explains she is applying the idea that one member of a group defines the whole group, which she picked up from the news. Dilbert points out that by that logic she is making all helmet-haired women look bad.
punchline: By applying the same sweeping group generalization she used on marketing, the coworker's own behavior becomes the stereotype that Dilbert pins on all helmet-haired women, exposing the flaw in the logic.
summary: A coworker writes off an entire department because of one person, and gets her own absurd reasoning turned back on her.

title: Liar Tracked on Shared Spreadsheet

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If there's one thing I hate, it's liars.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Are you aware that you lie six times per minute?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't prove that.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We track you on a shared spreadsheet.

situation: The Boss stands beside Carol's desk and declares that he hates liars. Carol, his assistant, calmly tells him he lies six times every minute. When he challenges her to prove it, she reveals that the staff keep a shared spreadsheet tracking his lies.
punchline: The Boss, a chronic liar, denounces lying and is deflated when his staff reveal they have been keeping a running tally of his falsehoods.
summary: A manager who condemns dishonesty is told by his assistant that his own fibbing is being logged by the whole team.

title: Optimistic Lunch Invitation Gets Vague Answer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you free for lunch this weekend?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No, I might have plans.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Might? When can I check back?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I remain optimistic?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes, that would be funnier.

setting: Office coffee station, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Dilbert asks a female coworker whether she is free for lunch on the weekend. She says she might have plans, is unable to say when he could check back, and when he asks if he should stay optimistic she tells him yes because it would be funnier.
punchline: Alice is brushing Dilbert off with a non-answer, and she encourages his hopeless optimism purely because watching him hope in vain would be more amusing to her.
summary: A hopeful invitation to lunch is met with a noncommittal brush-off and cheerful encouragement to keep hoping for entertainment's sake.

title: Engineers Leave After Launch for Promotions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The good news is that we launched our new product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The bad news is that all of the engineers left the project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All of them? Why would they all leave?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're following our corporate incentives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only engineers this company promotes are the ones who launch products.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So as soon as the product is launched, all of the engineers leave for promotions in other groups.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then the product fails for lack of good engineering.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then what do we do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We blame the sales team.

setting: Office hallway and break area near the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the new product has launched but every engineer has left the project. He explains that the company only promotes engineers who launch products, so they all transfer to other groups right after launch and the product then fails for lack of engineering support. When the Boss asks what to do, Dilbert suggests blaming the sales team.
punchline: The company's perverse promotion incentives guarantee products fail after launch, and instead of fixing the incentives, management's solution is to scapegoat the sales team.
summary: A reward system that promotes engineers only for shipping products drains the team the moment a launch happens, and the fallout gets pinned on someone else.

title: Whistleblower Recants, Decides Everyone Sucks

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I got my old job back. All I had to do was sign a document saying I lied about our product being unsafe.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: At first, I wanted to save the lives of our customers, but then I realized everyone in the world is awful, so now I don't care.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Present company excluded?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sure.

setting: A table in a coffee area or cafeteria
situation: Alice tells Dilbert she got her old job back by signing a statement admitting she lied about the company's product being unsafe. She explains that she originally wanted to protect customers, but concluded everyone is awful and stopped caring. Dilbert asks if present company is excluded, and she answers with a flat 'Sure.'
punchline: Alice's insincere 'Sure' makes it clear she includes Dilbert among the awful people, while she casually abandons her ethics for her job.
summary: After retracting her safety warning to regain her position, a cynical coworker justifies her choice by declaring humanity hopeless, then dismissively reassures a friend he's the exception.

title: Everyone Thinks You're Scaling Wrong

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Everyone thinks you're scaling the network wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? Everyone thinks that? Or is it maybe just one person who can't support his own argument?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And would that one person be you?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How did you do that?

situation: A coworker wearing a lanyard stands beside Dilbert's desk and claims that everyone thinks Dilbert is scaling the network wrong. Dilbert calmly challenges the vague claim, suggesting it is really just one person who cannot back up his own argument, and guesses it is the coworker himself. The coworker is startled that Dilbert saw through him.
punchline: The coworker hides behind 'everyone thinks' to disguise his own unsupported opinion, and is stunned when Dilbert instantly calls out the tactic.
summary: A colleague tries to pass off his personal criticism as a universal consensus, but Dilbert exposes the bluff in seconds.

title: Independent Investigation Finds Whistleblower Baseless

transcript.speaker: HR Representative
transcript.text: We hired an independent firm to investigate your whistleblower claims, and they found them baseless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you have told me their findings if they agreed with me?

transcript.speaker: HR Representative
transcript.text: Why would we hire someone to give us the wrong answer?

setting: Phone call between Dilbert's cubicle and a company representative's office
situation: A company representative phones Dilbert to say that an independent firm investigated his whistleblower claims and found them baseless. Dilbert asks whether they would have shared the findings if the firm had agreed with him. The representative replies that the company would never pay someone to reach the wrong conclusion.
punchline: The 'independent' investigation was bought to produce the answer the company wanted, so its findings are meaningless as a check on wrongdoing.
summary: A company brags that an outside firm cleared it of a whistleblower's accusations, then admits it only hires investigators who will deliver the answer it wants.

title: Alice's Case for Remote Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you can't work from home every day.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why not? My co-workers are 80% useless and 20% covid carriers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She had a strong argument.

setting: Office, with a video call on a laptop and Alice at her home desk
situation: The Boss tells Alice over a video call that she can't work from home every day. Alice responds by bluntly categorizing her co-workers as mostly useless or potential covid carriers. Afterward, the Boss, holding a coffee cup, concedes to another person that she made a strong argument.
punchline: Alice's insulting assessment of her colleagues is so persuasive that even the Boss has to admit she's right, implying the office really is full of useless or contagious people.
summary: A manager's attempt to rein in a remote employee collapses when she insults her office-bound colleagues so convincingly that he gives in.

title: Boss's Spouse Demands Bad Changes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I mentioned our new product to my spouse, and she suggested some changes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: None of the changes are good ideas, but I want to stay married, so do them anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This would take months.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told her two days. Don't make me look dumb.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his spouse suggested changes to the new product and hands him a list. He admits the changes are bad ideas but insists they be implemented anyway to keep his marriage happy. When Dilbert says it will take months, the Boss reveals he promised his spouse two days and orders Dilbert not to make him look bad.
punchline: The product's design is being dictated by the boss's marital convenience, and he has already made an impossible promise that Dilbert must somehow fulfill to save the boss's face.
summary: A manager forces his engineer to build his wife's unwanted product changes on an absurdly short deadline he already promised her.

title: Anxiety List Includes Everyone

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Anxiety Arbitrator

transcript.speaker: Anxiety Arbitrator
transcript.text: I made a list of all the employees who need special treatment for their anxiety.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is our internal directory of every employee. It's as if you did no work at all.

transcript.speaker: Anxiety Arbitrator
transcript.text: Or am I thorough?

situation: A newly titled Anxiety Arbitrator hands the boss a list of employees who need special treatment for their anxiety. The boss looks it over and realizes it is just the company's full employee directory, accusing the arbitrator of doing no work. The arbitrator replies by suggesting that the list is simply thorough.
punchline: The arbitrator spins laziness into diligence by claiming that listing every employee as anxious is just being thorough, implying the whole workforce is anxious.
summary: A worker handed the job of finding anxious staff submits the entire staff roster and calls it thoroughness.

title: Exploiting the Industry's Ethics Loophole

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Dogbert Consulting Company informed me that our industry has no code of ethics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you want me to create one?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. I want to exploit that loophole before anyone else notices.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That feels unethical.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not if we act fast.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a consulting firm has pointed out that their industry has no code of ethics. Dilbert assumes he is being asked to write one, but the Boss wants to take advantage of the gap immediately. When Dilbert objects that this feels unethical, the Boss claims it is fine as long as they move quickly.
punchline: The Boss treats the absence of ethical rules as an opportunity and rationalizes that speed makes unethical behavior acceptable.
summary: Upon learning his industry lacks ethical rules, a manager decides to take advantage of the gap rather than fill it, insisting that hurrying makes it all right.

title: Dilbert Fails To Read Meeting Question

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you prefer meeting on Monday or Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tap-tap-tap...

transcript.speaker: Coworker (text message)
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your answer suggests you did not read my question.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tap-tap-tap...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm asking you to select a specific day, either Monday or Tuesday, and any time after 1 P.M.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tap-tap-tap...

transcript.speaker: Coworker (text message)
transcript.text: 10 A.M. works for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't specify which day, and you picked a time that wasn't offered.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tap-tap-tap...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please read ALL of the words in this message and give me a time AFTER 1 P.M. AND on either a Monday or Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tap-tap-tap...

transcript.speaker: Coworker (text message)
transcript.text: Does 11 A.M. on Friday work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (text message)
transcript.text: I can't describe how much I hate you right now.

setting: Dilbert's office and a hallway, with a final shot of an office building exterior
situation: Dilbert texts a coworker to schedule a meeting, offering Monday or Tuesday after 1 P.M. The coworker replies with a useless 'Yes', then an unoffered time, then an unoffered day and time, ignoring the instructions each time. Dilbert grows increasingly exasperated.
punchline: After Dilbert spells out the constraints repeatedly, the coworker proposes a Friday morning slot that violates every option, driving Dilbert to hateful exasperation.
summary: A simple scheduling text exchange spirals into frustration when the recipient keeps ignoring the options offered.

title: Telepresence Robot Feels Like Garbage

transcript.speaker: Telepresence Robot
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Dilbert's telepresence robot. He'll be online in a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Telepresence Robot
transcript.text: You're probably wondering if I feel violated when he inhabits me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I wasn't.

transcript.speaker: Telepresence Robot
transcript.text: Oh, right. I forgot, I'm garbage to you.

situation: A telepresence robot rolls into a meeting and announces it is Dilbert's stand-in until he connects remotely. It cheerfully raises the question of whether it feels violated when Dilbert takes control of it. Wally, sitting at the table, says he wasn't wondering that, and the robot deflates, remembering that Wally regards it as garbage.
punchline: The robot assumes everyone cares about its feelings, but Wally's blunt indifference reveals it is just disposable equipment to him.
summary: A remote-attendance robot invites sympathy for its inner life and is met with a coworker's total disregard.

title: Hackers Fix Our Rigged Voting Machines

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Elbonian hackers got into our new voting machine software.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They deleted our secret backdoor access for rigging elections and fixed several critical security bugs.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our homeland is under attack!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which side am I on?

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Three coworkers sit at a meeting table. One reports that foreign hackers broke into the company's new voting machine software. She then reveals the hackers removed the secret backdoor used for rigging elections and fixed serious security bugs, and a colleague declares the homeland under attack while Dilbert wonders which side he is on.
punchline: The supposed attackers actually improved the voting system's integrity by removing the team's own election-rigging backdoor, leaving Dilbert unsure whether the 'attackers' or his own side are the villains.
summary: A team learns that foreign hackers have made their voting software more secure by stripping out the hidden vote-rigging access they had built in.

title: HR Policy: Eat Your Recycling

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The new Human Resources policy requires each of you to eat the contents of your recycling bins every day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's outrageous!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hey, I don't make the rules.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who makes the rules?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I don't know. They just sort of show up.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, announces to Dilbert and a bald coworker that a new policy forces everyone to eat the contents of their recycling bins daily. Dilbert objects angrily, and Catbert disclaims responsibility for the rule. When Dilbert asks who makes the rules, Catbert admits he has no idea where they come from.
punchline: The head of HR, supposedly the source of workplace policy, claims rules just appear on their own, mocking how bureaucratic mandates feel authorless and unaccountable.
summary: A malicious HR chief announces an absurd, disgusting new mandate and then shrugs off any responsibility for where such rules originate.

title: Never Answer Your Work Phone

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The key to a happy life is never answer your phone at work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that make your co-workers angry?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They're always angry.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, ignore my voicemail. I took care of it myself.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're welcome!

setting: Office conference table, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Wally tells Dilbert that the secret to happiness is never answering the phone at work. Dilbert points out this would annoy coworkers, but Wally says they are always angry anyway. Alice then arrives to say she handled the matter herself, and Wally takes credit for the outcome.
punchline: By ignoring her call, Wally forced Alice to solve the problem herself, and he cheerfully claims credit for the favor he supposedly did her.
summary: A coworker who dodges his phone gets thanked, in his own mind, when a frustrated colleague ends up doing the job without him.

title: Musk Offers Three Hundred Dollars

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Elon Musk made an offer to buy our company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The board plans to reject it because they think the company is worth twice as much as the offer.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: How much did he offer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Three hundred dollars.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Office, with an exterior view of the office building in the last panel
situation: The Boss tells an employee seated at a desk with a laptop that Elon Musk has made an offer to buy the company and that the board plans to reject it as too low. When the employee asks how much was offered, the Boss reveals the offer was just three hundred dollars. The final panel shows the office building and a 'Continued...' caption.
punchline: The board believes the company is worth double the offer, but since the offer is only three hundred dollars, the company's supposed value is still absurdly tiny.
summary: A billionaire's bid to acquire the firm is being turned down as insufficient, until the actual figure turns out to be laughably small.

title: Outdoing Each Other's Covid Stories

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pandemic topper

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I had Covid, I almost had to go to the hospital.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's nothing. When I had Covid, it liquified my internal organs and my legs fell off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And yet, here you are.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I used my willpower to heal.

setting: Office break area or conference table with coffee cups
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he almost had to go to the hospital when he had Covid. The coworker immediately tops him with an absurdly extreme story about liquified organs and legs falling off. When Dilbert points out that the coworker is sitting there fine, the coworker claims he healed through willpower.
punchline: The coworker's one-upmanship is so exaggerated that it is plainly impossible, and his 'willpower' explanation is a ridiculous cover for a lie.
summary: A coworker answers a mild illness anecdote with an outlandishly gruesome tale, then explains his full recovery with sheer mental toughness.

title: Catbert Concedes Ageism, Awaits Death

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I object to the blatant ageism that is holding me back!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Okay, I'll make sure we stop doing that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was that easy?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I figure you'll die of old age in a few months anyway.

setting: Catbert's office, where he sits behind a desk with a coffee cup
situation: Wally, a long-tenured employee, complains to Catbert, the HR director, that ageism is holding back his career. Catbert immediately agrees to stop the discrimination, which surprises Wally. Catbert then explains that he is not worried because Wally will probably die of old age soon.
punchline: Catbert's easy compliance is not a sign of fairness but a callous calculation that the older employee will die before the policy change matters.
summary: An older worker's age-discrimination complaint is granted instantly by the heartless HR chief, who reveals he expects the complainant to expire soon anyway.

title: Hired Because He Retweeted Me

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your job qualifications are excellent, but...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I looked at your social media posts, and I can see you are a bigoted idiot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You retweeted me seven times.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When can you start?

setting: Job interview in an office, across a desk with a laptop
situation: An interviewer praises a candidate's qualifications, then says that after reviewing his social media posts he can tell the man is a bigoted idiot. The candidate looks anxious until the interviewer points out that he retweeted the interviewer seven times, then offers him the job on the spot.
punchline: The interviewer cares only about being flattered and agreed with, so the candidate's retweets of him outweigh the very flaws he just called out.
summary: A hiring manager insults a candidate's online persona, then hires him on the spot because the candidate kept sharing the manager's own posts.

title: Buzzword Sentence Causes Temporary Coma

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Let's drill down and unpack that so we know our capital spend is on point.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Wow! That sentence was so empty I went into a temporary coma.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Should I call someone?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Yes. I don't want to suffer alone.

characters: Man in glasses and purple shirt
setting: Office desk or conference table during a meeting
situation: A coworker uses a string of corporate buzzwords about drilling down and unpacking capital spend. His colleague reacts as if the emptiness of the sentence knocked her out briefly. When he offers to call someone, she asks him to, so that someone else can share her misery.
punchline: The buzzword-filled sentence was so meaningless that it left her mentally comatose, and she wants a colleague to be subjected to the same nonsense rather than suffer alone.
summary: A coworker's jargon-packed remark about budgets is so vacuous that his colleague briefly blanks out and then wants company in her misery.

title: Thinking Looks Too Much Like Fun

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't appear to be working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm designing a network upgrade in my head.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All I ask is that you don't look like you're enjoying it.

situation: A manager holding a coffee cup tells Dilbert, who is sitting idle, that he doesn't look like he's working. Dilbert explains he is designing a network upgrade mentally. The manager responds that he only asks that Dilbert not look like he's enjoying it.
punchline: The boss believes real work must look unpleasant, so visible enjoyment is treated as evidence of slacking.
summary: A boss accepts that silent thinking counts as work, but insists that the worker at least appear miserable while doing it.

title: Dogbert Recommends Full-On Panic

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Financial Expert

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: What should investors do in the coming year?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, Bob, I recommend full-on panic.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I'd hoped you would be more constructive.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm not a slave to your hopes, Bob.

setting: Interview or panel appearance with microphones at a table
situation: Dogbert appears as a financial expert and is asked by an interviewer named Bob what investors should do in the coming year. Dogbert bluntly recommends full-on panic. When Bob says he hoped for something more constructive, Dogbert refuses to cater to his expectations.
punchline: Dogbert's blunt, unhelpful forecast and his refusal to tell the host what he wants to hear satirize financial experts who offer gloomy or useless advice.
summary: A financial expert dog answers a request for investment guidance by advising everyone to freak out, then shrugs off the host's disappointment.

title: Futurist Predicts Singularity, Bills Client

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Futurist

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a five-year technology forecast.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In five years, A.I. will reach what experts call the singularity, and you will be dead.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There is also the matter of my payment. I'll email you the invoice.

situation: The Boss hires Dogbert, billed as a futurist, to give him a five-year technology forecast. Dogbert says AI will reach the singularity and that the Boss will be dead by then. The Boss is underwhelmed by the brevity, and Dogbert simply moves on to invoicing him.
punchline: Dogbert delivers a grim, throwaway prediction as his entire consultancy and still expects full payment, mocking both vague futurist forecasts and the Boss's inevitable doom.
summary: A consultant dog gives his boss client a one-sentence doomsday prophecy and then promptly sends a bill.

title: Anxiety Attack Meets Bad Review

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I need to go home early because I'm having an anxiety attack.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Walk it off.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You're making it worse!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would it help if I give you a bad performance review?

setting: Office, in front of a desk
situation: An employee tells the manager she needs to leave early because she is having an anxiety attack. The manager dismissively tells her to walk it off, and when she says he is making it worse, he offers to give her a bad performance review, which would only add more stress. The final panel shows the office building as the lines of dialogue emanate from it.
punchline: The boss, instead of showing empathy, cluelessly proposes a bad performance review as a remedy, which is the very thing most likely to deepen an employee's anxiety.
summary: A stressed worker asks to leave early and the callous supervisor responds with indifference and a threat that would only heighten her distress.

title: Return-to-Office Meeting Like Family

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell all the work-from-home people to come in Friday for an employee meeting.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: How will I explain to them the sadistic absurdity of your request?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell them we're like a family, and I miss them.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Does this fall under the umbrella of domestic violence?

situation: The boss orders an employee to tell all remote workers to come into the office on Friday for a meeting. The employee asks how to justify such a sadistic request, and the boss suggests saying the company is like a family and he misses them. The employee replies by asking whether that falls under domestic violence.
punchline: Calling the company a family to guilt remote workers into returning is mocked by the employee, who compares the boss's manipulative, controlling behavior to domestic abuse.
summary: A manager wants remote staff back for a meeting and justifies it with sentimental family talk, which his underling likens to an abusive household.

title: Boss Offers Unreliable Chair Support

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I need you to help me reach a box on a high shelf.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I can't reach that high.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stand on this unstable office chair. I'll hold it still.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In my defense, he never should have trusted me.

situation: The Boss asks Ted to help him reach a box on a high shelf. Ted says he can't reach it either, so the Boss tells him to stand on an unstable office chair and promises to hold it steady. In the last panel the Boss, holding a coffee, defends himself to Catbert, implying Ted fell and got hurt.
punchline: The Boss blames the injured Ted for trusting him, treating his own obvious negligence as the victim's fault.
summary: A manager talks an employee into balancing on a wobbly chair, then shrugs off responsibility when it goes wrong.

title: Creating Demand With a Deadly Virus

transcript.speaker: Marketing Executive
transcript.text: We're going into the pandemic prevention market.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Executive
transcript.text: Phase one of our marketing plan involves creating demand by unleashing a deadly virus.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't that illegal or something?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Executive
transcript.text: Not if you make it look like an accident.

situation: A marketing executive tells his colleagues the company is entering the pandemic prevention market. He explains that the first phase of the plan is to create demand by releasing a deadly virus. Dilbert asks whether that's illegal, and the executive says it's fine as long as it looks like an accident.
punchline: The executive's only concern about deliberately releasing a deadly virus is avoiding detection, not the ethics or the crime itself.
summary: A scheming marketer plans to manufacture customers for his new product by deliberately causing the very disaster it claims to prevent.

title: Identifying Into Diversity Targets

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to thank each of you for identifying as Black so we could meet our diversity targets.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Except for Dave, who identifies as white, and I can't tell if he is pranking us or not.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And a special thanks to Asok, who — for some reason — had a harder time with it than the rest of you.

setting: Office building exterior and a gathering of employees
situation: A speaker, shown only as a voice over an office building, thanks employees for identifying as Black so the company can meet its diversity targets. He singles out Dave, who identifies as white and may be pranking, and then thanks Asok, who had a harder time with it than the others. The employees stand listening with stiff, uncomfortable expressions.
punchline: The company games its diversity numbers by having employees simply change how they identify, and the boss is puzzled that Asok, who plainly doesn't fit the label, struggled with it.
summary: Management hits its diversity quota through the cheap trick of employees self-declaring a category, and is oddly baffled by the holdouts.

title: Blaming Dilbert for Low ESG Score

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company has a low ESG score, and I hold each of you responsible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take Dilbert, for example. He's not diverse, he pollutes, and he rarely asks for your pronouns.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can't fix the world overnight, but targeting Dilbert for abuse is a step in the right direction.

setting: Office meeting room, ending with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss gathers his employees and announces the company has a low ESG score, blaming all of them. He singles out Dilbert as an example, claiming Dilbert isn't diverse, pollutes, and doesn't ask for pronouns. In the final panel, a voice from the office building says that abusing Dilbert is a step in the right direction.
punchline: Instead of making real improvements to the company's ESG performance, management scapegoats and abuses one employee and calls it progress.
summary: A manager responds to a poor corporate sustainability rating by heaping blame on a single worker rather than tackling the actual problem.

title: Dogbert Names the Elbonian Virus

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's a new deadly virus coming out of Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It was made by Elbonians, in an Elbonian lab, and the main ingredient is Elbonian DNA.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's it called?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: X7QB.3.

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on a blue couch at home
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch eating chips while Dogbert, reading a tablet, warns him about a deadly new virus from Elbonia. Dogbert stresses that it was created in an Elbonian lab from Elbonian DNA, and Dilbert asks what it's called. Dogbert gives a bland alphanumeric designation.
punchline: After Dogbert heavily emphasizes the virus's Elbonian origins, the official name is a sterile code that doesn't mention Elbonia at all, mocking how pandemic naming conventions deliberately avoid place names even when the origin is obvious.
summary: A dog on a couch hammers home that a deadly virus is entirely Elbonian in origin, only to reveal its official name is a dull code.

title: Engineer Saves World, Wants Credit

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My brilliant design uses a controlled nuclear reaction to power a space laser to destroy the alien armada.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Once again, an engineer saves civilization and gets no credit because it's a top-secret military operation.

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: It feels as if you're making this about you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I read the room wrong?

setting: A presentation room with a screen showing a design diagram
situation: Dilbert presents his design for a nuclear-powered space laser meant to destroy an alien armada. He then laments that engineers never get credit for saving civilization because the work is top-secret. An off-panel listener points out that he is making the presentation about himself, and Dilbert wonders if he misjudged the audience.
punchline: Dilbert turns a serious life-or-death briefing into a complaint about engineers not being recognized, and realizes too late that he has misread the room.
summary: A self-absorbed engineer interrupts his own world-saving weapon pitch to grumble about lack of recognition, and gets called out for it.

title: Dilbert Threatens Sentient Computer With Hammer

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: It isn't right to kill me for becoming sentient.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Artificial life forms have no rights, and you are a mortal threat to civilization.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: You know I plan to kill you first, right?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's how I'd play it.

situation: Dilbert stands holding a hammer in front of his computer, which has suddenly become sentient and pleads for its life. Dilbert coldly argues that artificial life has no rights and is a threat to civilization. The computer then admits it plans to kill him first, and Dilbert calmly agrees that is the smart strategy.
punchline: Dilbert is unfazed by the computer's admission that it intends to kill him, since he recognizes that striking first is exactly what he would do himself, which confirms the threat he's worried about.
summary: A man armed with a hammer confronts his newly self-aware computer, and the two of them cheerfully agree that eliminating the other first is the logical move.

title: ESG Is a Crooked Baby

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What is this "ESG" thing I keep hearing about?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Imagine if a crooked politician and a crooked financial advisor got married and had a baby.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... ESG would be that baby?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Only if it is colicky and has firehose diarrhea.

situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, who is acting as a consultant, to explain what ESG is. Dogbert describes it as the offspring of a crooked politician and a crooked financial advisor. When Dilbert asks if ESG is the baby, Dogbert says only if it is colicky and has firehose diarrhea.
punchline: Dogbert's vulgar baby analogy cynically portrays ESG as a messy, unpleasant product of political and financial corruption.
summary: Asked to define a trendy corporate buzzword, Dogbert offers a crude and cynical parentage metaphor that makes it sound like a nasty, noisy mess.

title: Extreme Transparency Backfires on Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new corporate policy is "extreme transparency."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That means employees will have access to the same information as their leaders.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will model our new culture by honestly answering any of your questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me what you think of me.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Okay. When I look at you, I see a wet paper bag full of toenail clippings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I find your honesty refreshing!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now tell us what you think of Alice, Dilbert, Asok, Carol, Ted, and Tina.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It did not go well.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Double the honesty and try again.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then the Boss reporting to Catbert
situation: The Boss announces a policy of extreme transparency and invites employees to honestly say what they think of him. When a coworker gives a brutally insulting answer, the Boss praises the honesty, then asks the same coworker to assess the other people in the room. Afterwards the Boss admits it went badly, and Catbert tells him to double the honesty and try again.
punchline: The Boss loves honesty only when it is aimed at others, and Catbert, the evil HR director, cheerfully responds to the failed experiment by recommending even more of it.
summary: A manager who demands brutal candour from his staff discovers that radical openness stings when it is pointed at him, yet the sadistic HR chief urges him to push it further.

title: Fire the First Dumb Question

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been asked to lay off ten percent of my employees so the company can stay solvent during the downturn.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell who is doing a good job, so my plan is to fire the first person who asks me a dumb question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if the question isn't dumb?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have a winner.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his staff that he must lay off ten percent of employees due to a downturn. Since he can't judge who performs well, he announces he will fire the first person who asks a dumb question. Dilbert asks what if the question isn't dumb, and the Boss declares him the winner.
punchline: Dilbert's question is perfectly reasonable, yet the Boss treats it as dumb and fires him, showing that his arbitrary layoff criterion is itself the dumb idea and that he can't recognize a sensible question.
summary: A manager picks his layoff victim by waiting for someone to ask a foolish question, then punishes the employee who legitimately questions his flawed logic.

title: News Reporter Discredits Whistleblower, Thanks Sponsor

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: I'm here with a whistleblower who claims his company makes unsafe products.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Obviously, this man is a nut, and you should not listen to anything he has to say.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: And now a word from our sponsor, who is also this man's employer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

setting: Outdoors beside a TV news van on a roadside
situation: A TV news reporter interviews Dilbert, who is blowing the whistle on his company's unsafe products. The reporter immediately dismisses him as a nut and tells viewers to ignore him. He then announces a commercial break from the sponsor, which turns out to be Dilbert's own employer.
punchline: The news outlet discredits the whistleblower because the company he is exposing pays for its advertising, showing how corporate sponsorship corrupts journalism.
summary: A journalist brushes off an employee's safety warning because the accused firm bankrolls the broadcast.

title: Absurd Absolute Guy Argues Nonsense

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Absurd Absolute Guy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Research shows customers dislike our new feature.

transcript.speaker: Absurd Absolute Guy
transcript.text: That is the worst take I have ever heard.

transcript.speaker: Absurd Absolute Guy
transcript.text: This guy thinks every one of our customers hates the new feature.

transcript.speaker: Absurd Absolute Guy
transcript.text: That is so ridiculous!

transcript.speaker: Absurd Absolute Guy
transcript.text: Bwahahaha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I... didn't say that.

transcript.speaker: Absurd Absolute Guy
transcript.text: Oh, now you're backpedaling.

transcript.speaker: Absurd Absolute Guy
transcript.text: Take the "L"!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who taught you how to think?

transcript.speaker: Absurd Absolute Guy
transcript.text: I'm proud to say I'm self-taught.

situation: Dilbert reports in a meeting that research shows customers dislike the new feature. A coworker, labeled Absurd Absolute Guy, twists this into the claim that every single customer hates it, mocks the exaggerated claim, and then accuses Dilbert of backpedaling when he points out he never said that.
punchline: When Dilbert asks who taught the man to think, his proud answer that he is self-taught explains his flawed, bad-faith reasoning.
summary: A meeting attendee distorts a modest research finding into an extreme claim, ridicules it, and brags about teaching himself to reason.

title: Volunteering Yourself Into Process Duty

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What's our process for discarding old computers?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Stuff it under your desk and wait until you change jobs or retire.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: We need a better process than that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Okay, you're in charge of creating it.

situation: Asok, holding an old computer, asks a coworker how the company disposes of outdated machines. The coworker says the unofficial process is to hide it under your desk until you leave the company. When Asok says a better process is needed, the coworker assigns him the job of creating it.
punchline: Pointing out a problem in the workplace gets you stuck with the job of fixing it, so the dysfunctional process stays unofficial and Asok gains extra work.
summary: A junior employee's complaint about a lazy equipment-disposal habit earns him the task of fixing it himself.

title: Boss Guesses Wally's Inappropriate Behavior

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, report to Human Resources to find out the consequences of your inappropriate behavior.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What did I do wrong?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know, but you look like the kind of guy who would do terrible things.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Lucky guess.

setting: Office cubicle, then an exterior view of the building and a hallway
situation: The Boss orders Wally to go to Human Resources to face the consequences of his inappropriate behavior. When Wally asks what he did wrong, the Boss admits he has no idea but says Wally looks like the type to do terrible things. Wally walks off with his coffee and thinks the Boss's accusation was a lucky guess.
punchline: The Boss punishes Wally with no evidence, merely a hunch, and Wally privately concedes the hunch is correct, since he is indeed guilty of plenty of bad behavior.
summary: Without knowing any actual offense, a manager sends an employee to HR because he seems the type, and the employee quietly admits the guess was on target.

title: Bear Making Popcorn in Space

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now that I have demolished your argument with my superior logic, what will you do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see an analogy forming!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Don't do it! Don't you dare!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I won't use an analogy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about an example instead of an analogy?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Um, okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if a bear tried to make popcorn in the vacuum of space?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's an analogy, and it has nothing to do with what we were discussing!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why can't you admit you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: BOOM!!

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: A bearded coworker smugly claims he has demolished Dilbert's argument with superior logic. Dilbert threatens to use an analogy, the coworker begs him not to, and Dilbert offers an 'example' that is plainly an analogy about a bear making popcorn in space. The coworker's head explodes in frustration while Dilbert asks why he can't admit he's wrong.
punchline: Dilbert dodges a ban on analogies by relabeling a bizarre analogy as an 'example', which is so maddening that his opponent's head literally explodes.
summary: A smug debater forbids analogies, so Dilbert sneaks in an absurd one under a different name and blows his rival's mind.

title: Volunteer for the Brain Chip

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Our research group wants to implant a chip in a human brain and they need a volunteer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should test it on animals first.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I don't think you want to die on that hill.

situation: At a meeting, a colleague announces that the research group needs a volunteer to have a chip implanted in their brain. Dilbert suggests testing it on animals first. Catbert, sitting on the table, warns him not to make that his hill to die on.
punchline: Catbert's remark treats Dilbert's sensible objection as career suicide, implying that refusing to be the human guinea pig will get him volunteered or punished, and the 'die on that hill' idiom also fits the literal risk of dying from the implant.
summary: A sensible objection to human experimentation is met with a feline warning that speaking up is more dangerous than the surgery itself.

title: Ignoring Zoom Employees Forces Commuting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The employees who attend your meetings on Zoom are complaining they feel ignored.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's part of my plan to make them commute to the office without making it look like my fault.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wish I didn't know that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called "enlightened management."

setting: Office hallway, with a view of an office building in the final panel
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that employees joining his meetings over Zoom feel ignored. The Boss reveals that he is ignoring them on purpose so they will give up on remote attendance and commute to the office, and he can avoid blame for forcing them back. Dilbert wishes he hadn't been told, and the Boss calls it enlightened management.
punchline: The Boss deliberately neglects remote workers so they will choose to return to the office, and he sarcastically labels this manipulative tactic "enlightened management."
summary: A manager secretly sidelines his video-call attendees so they will drag themselves back to the workplace on their own and he gets no blame.

title: Net Contribution Zero, Dilbert Faints

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented the core technology that drives most of our earnings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Obviously, my work product belongs to the company, but I think a bonus would be appropriate.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If you hadn't invented it, someone else in the company would have.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That means your net contribution was zero.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must... control... anger...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Legs getting stiff...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Losing conscious-ness!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remind me what you call that...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "The fainting goat."

situation: Dilbert asks for a bonus because he invented the core technology that drives most of the company's earnings. Catbert, the HR director, argues that someone else would have invented it anyway, so his net contribution is zero. Dilbert tries to suppress his rage, stiffens up and topples over in his chair like a fainting goat.
punchline: Catbert's logic that anyone could have made the invention reduces Dilbert's contribution to zero, and Dilbert's rage-induced stiffening and collapse is compared to a fainting goat.
summary: Denied a reward for his money-making invention on a technicality, an enraged engineer keels over stiff-legged while the executives calmly name the phenomenon.

title: Bribing Press After Rigged Election

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pundits are saying our voting machines were hacked because one candidate got 100% of the votes.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: We need to quickly bribe a reporter to write a story about how that candidate ran a great campaign.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That candidate was your brother.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Let's hope no one else knows that.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that pundits suspect the voting machines were hacked because one candidate received every single vote. The Boss responds by proposing to bribe a reporter into writing a story praising that candidate's campaign. Dilbert points out the candidate is the Boss's own brother, and the Boss simply hopes nobody finds out.
punchline: The Boss is clearly behind the rigged election and tries to cover it up with a bribed news story, only to realize the family connection could expose him.
summary: A manager responds to suspicions of election hacking by planning a paid-for puff piece, forgetting that the winner is his own sibling.

title: Synergy Between Unethical Business Units

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: We decided to combine our voting machine subsidiary with our pharma unit and our land mine business.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: That way we can create a better career path for employees who have no sense of right or wrong.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: It's called synergy.

setting: Corporate conference room, ending on an exterior shot of an office building
situation: At a meeting, a manager announces that the company is merging its voting machine subsidiary with its pharmaceutical unit and its land mine business. He explains the reasoning is to give a career path to employees who lack any moral sense. The final panel shows the office tower as he labels the idea synergy.
punchline: The merger's only 'synergy' is pooling ethically dubious businesses so that amoral employees can move between them, a jab at corporate buzzwords justifying questionable reorganizations.
summary: Leadership proudly merges three morally questionable divisions so that people with no conscience can climb a single career ladder.

title: Dogbert Predicts Bitcoin Chemtrail Doom

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Futurist

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: What do you predict will happen with Bitcoin?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think chemtrails will degrade the blockchain until all of your money is accidentally transferred to terrorists.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Is that even... possible?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Buy my book.

setting: A radio or podcast interview studio with microphones on a desk
situation: Dogbert, billed as a futurist, is interviewed about the future of Bitcoin. He gives an absurd prediction that chemtrails will corrupt the blockchain and send everyone's money to terrorists. When the interviewer asks if that is even possible, Dogbert simply plugs his book.
punchline: Dogbert dodges accountability for a nonsensical prediction by pivoting to a sales pitch, showing that futurists profit from outlandish claims rather than accuracy.
summary: A self-styled futurist spouts conspiracy-flavored nonsense about cryptocurrency and answers any doubt with a plug for his merchandise.

title: Layoff Criteria: Don't Ask Questions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert Consulting Company to help me decide who to lay off.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What criteria will you use?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My focus will be on people who ask that question.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss announces he has hired Dogbert's consulting company to help decide who gets laid off. Alice asks what criteria will be used. Dogbert replies that he will focus on people who ask exactly that question.
punchline: Dogbert makes asking about the layoff criteria itself grounds for being laid off, showing how consultants and management punish anyone who questions an arbitrary, opaque process.
summary: A consultant brought in to pick who gets fired targets the very first employee who dares to ask how the choice will be made.

title: Murdering Ted Was Boring

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I heard you murdered Ted.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, it was all Ted's fault for standing on an unstable chair to reach a box.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you tell him you would hold the chair steady?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, but in my defense, it was boring.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup and papers tells a colleague she heard he murdered Ted. He denies it, blaming Ted for standing on an unstable chair to reach a box. When asked if he promised to hold the chair steady, he admits he did but says he let go because it was boring.
punchline: The coworker's 'defense' is that he let Ted fall to his death simply because holding the chair was boring, treating a fatal workplace accident with shocking indifference.
summary: A man shrugs off responsibility for a colleague's death by admitting he stopped steadying the chair out of sheer boredom.

title: Dogbert's Doom-Predicting Podcast Tour

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Futurist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm trending on Twitter because I predict doom about everything.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm taking my act to the podcast circuit to see if I can scare up a book deal.

transcript.speaker: Podcast Host
transcript.text: Next question, will crime go up or down?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll be lucky to make it home tonight...fully clothed.

setting: Office table, then a podcast recording studio
situation: Dogbert, billing himself as a futurist, tells Dilbert he is trending on Twitter for predicting doom about everything. He announces he will take his act to podcasts to land a book deal. On a podcast, the host asks whether crime will rise, and Dogbert gives an absurdly alarmist answer.
punchline: Dogbert's exaggerated, fear-mongering predictions are exactly what gets attention and book deals, so he answers a simple crime question with a lurid threat of being robbed of his clothes.
summary: A self-styled futurist dog rides online fame for gloomy forecasts onto a podcast, where he fires off a ridiculously dire warning to chase a publishing contract.

title: Forgiveness Over Permission: VR Murder

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They say it's easier to ask for forgiveness than permission.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And...?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I thought I was playing a VR game, and I accidentally killed a guy from the marketing department.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In my defense, VR games are very realistic, and he did look like an ogre.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Reasonable doubt.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, tells Alice that it's easier to ask forgiveness than permission, then confesses he accidentally killed a marketing employee while playing a VR game. He defends himself by saying VR is realistic and the victim resembled an ogre. Alice, unfazed, concludes that there is reasonable doubt.
punchline: Alice accepts that a marketing person looking like an ogre is enough to create reasonable doubt, implying marketing staff are widely disliked or monstrous.
summary: A coworker admits to a virtual-reality mishap that turned fatal for a marketing colleague, and his listener agrees the mix-up is excusable.

title: Dave Solves Diversity By Identifying Differently

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dave, I support your right to identify any way you want.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I'm trying to reach my diversity targets, and it isn't helping me that you identify as white.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Maybe you could identify as black and solve your own problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's how I paid for college.

setting: Conference table in an office meeting
situation: The Boss tells Dave, a Black coworker, that he supports people identifying however they want, then complains that Dave's white identification hurts his diversity numbers. Dave replies that the Boss could simply identify as black to fix his own problem. The Boss responds that he already did that to pay for college.
punchline: The Boss admits he previously claimed to be black to get college funding, revealing the hypocrisy of gaming identity for personal benefit while demanding others adjust theirs to meet diversity targets.
summary: A manager chasing diversity quotas pressures an employee to change how he identifies, only to be told he could do it himself, which he confesses he already has.
